chapters.title: Introduction to EMS
chapters.intro: Emergency medical services grew out of battlefield transport, and for most of its history the ambulance was a vehicle rather than a place where care began. This chapter follows that shift into the modern system: how a 911 call moves from dispatcher to responder to emergency department, what the four provider levels are trained to do, and what the profession expects of an EMT in fitness, judgment and conduct. It closes with the machinery that keeps the system honest: continuing education, the National Registry, medical direction and quality improvement.

topics.heading: From battlefield transport to hospital-quality care at the scene
topics.html:
The earliest documented emergency medical service appeared in France in the 1790s, and it did one thing: it carried the wounded off the battlefield. No care was given at the scene. During the American Civil War, Clara Barton organized care for the wounded and went on to found the American Red Cross, and by the First World War volunteer ambulance corps were an established part of military medicine. The wars in Korea and Vietnam brought the major advances in field care, and those advances carried over into the civilian trauma centers that followed.

Civilian service developed more slowly. Cities began ambulance services in the early 1900s, but they too were transport only. Smaller communities did not get service at all until after the Second World War, in the late 1940s, and where they did, it was often a funeral home's hearse or the fire department that provided it.

The defining shift in the history of EMS is the one from "just transport" to care of hospital quality that begins at the scene and continues without interruption until the patient reaches the hospital. Everything that follows in this book rests on that idea.

topics.heading: Timeline
topics.html: The modern system took shape through a series of federal actions. In 1966 the National Highway Safety Act directed the Department of Transportation (DOT) to set standards for EMS. The National Registry of Emergency Medical Technicians (NREMT) was founded in 1970, and in 1973 the National EMS Systems Act became the cornerstone federal law for EMS systems. Since then control has largely passed to the states, which now run most of their own systems, although the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) still provides guidance.

topics.heading: NHTSA's 10 EMS System Standards
topics.html:
NHTSA describes a complete EMS system in terms of 10 standards, each naming a component the system must have. They are:

  • Regulation and policy
  • Resource management
  • Human resources and training
  • Transportation
  • Facilities
  • Communications
  • Public information and education
  • Medical direction
  • Trauma systems
  • Evaluation, through quality improvement, quality assurance and total quality management (QI/QA/TQM)

Several of these, medical direction and evaluation among them, are taken up later in this chapter.

topics.heading: EMS system flow (patient's point of view)
topics.html:
Seen from the patient's side, the system is a chain of handoffs. The call is answered by an emergency medical dispatcher (EMD), who sends responders; depending on the system and the call, these may be EMRs, EMTs, AEMTs or paramedics. An ambulance then carries the patient to the emergency department (ED), and from the ED the patient moves on to the rest of the hospital.

The ED is the gateway to the hospital's services, including the operating room (OR) and its specialists. Some hospitals are also specialty centers: trauma centers, which keep surgical teams available 24/7, and burn, pediatric, cardiac and stroke centers. Choosing the right facility for a patient is a critical decision, because it weighs the patient's condition against the transport time, and on-line medical direction can help you make it.

topics.heading: 911 and dispatch
topics.html:
The public reaches EMS by telephone, and the number is 911. The 911 system covers roughly 99% of the population and handles about 240 million calls a year, more than 80% of them from mobile devices. Enhanced 911 automatically identifies a landline caller's number and location, and some systems can locate wireless callers as well. For mobile devices this happens in two phases: Phase 1 identifies the caller's number, and Phase 2 identifies the physical location of the device. Calls placed over the internet (VoIP) are harder to locate, and this remains an ongoing technical challenge.

The call is answered by an emergency medical dispatcher (EMD). EMDs are specially trained and certified, and besides sending the right resources they give the caller pre-arrival instructions, such as how to perform CPR, provide ventilation or control bleeding until the crew arrives.

topics.heading: 4 levels of training (low → high)
topics.html:
Prehospital providers are trained to one of four nationally recognized levels. From the least to the most training, they are:

  • Emergency medical responder (EMR): often the first on scene; activates EMS, provides basic care for life threats and controls the scene.
  • Emergency medical technician (EMT): the minimum certification for ambulance staff; basic medical and trauma care, and transport.
  • Advanced EMT (AEMT): everything an EMT does, plus advanced airway devices, intravenous and intraosseous (IV/IO) fluids, and some medications.
  • Paramedic: all of the EMT and AEMT skills plus advanced assessment and decision-making; the highest prehospital level.

In some states, specially trained nurses (RNs) and physicians also hold prehospital certifications.

topics.heading: "Think like an EMT" — critical decision making
topics.html: Much of what makes an EMT effective is critical decision making: taking in information from the scene, from the assessment findings and from other sources, then synthesizing all of it to make the right call. When the information you have is not enough to decide, ask more questions or examine the patient further before you act. The choice of hospital is one example, because the closest hospital is not always the right destination when a specialty center is available. Giving a medication is another, because a drug that would help one patient may worsen another patient's condition.

topics.heading: EMT responsibilities
topics.html:
An EMT's responsibilities on a call follow a definite order of priority. Personal safety comes first, followed by the safety of the crew, the patient and bystanders. You work alongside other public safety professionals at the scene. Patient assessment always comes before patient care, because you cannot treat what you have not found. Care is followed by lifting and moving the patient safely, then by transport, and then by transfer of care at the hospital; a patient is never abandoned before that transfer is complete. Throughout, the EMT acts as the patient's advocate.

The role also extends to community health and injury prevention, such as noticing fall hazards or poisoning risks in a patient's home.

topics.heading: Good EMT traits
topics.html:
The job makes physical demands. A good EMT is in good health and physically fit, and is able to lift and carry 125 lb (57 kg). Good near and distance vision is needed, along with functional color vision, because color changes in the skin, lips and nail beds are diagnostic cues. Clear speech and good hearing matter as well.

The personal traits matter just as much. The EMT should be pleasant, sincere and cooperative; resourceful and a self-starter; emotionally stable; able to lead; and neat and clean in appearance. Good moral character and controlled personal habits are expected, which means no alcohol within 8 hours of duty and no smoking on duty. Finally, the EMT is a good listener who is nonjudgmental and fair with every patient.

topics.heading: Education & the NREMT
topics.html:
Certification is not permanent. Refresher training is required periodically, roughly every 2–4 years, in order to recertify. Continuing education supplements the original training rather than replacing it, and it comes in many forms: conferences, classes and videos. Both are necessary because EMS knowledge and procedures change constantly, so much so that some of what you learn will change during your own course.

The NREMT sets and maintains national standards and registers EMRs, EMTs, AEMTs and paramedics. Registration is earned by passing the NREMT practical examination and its computer-based knowledge examination. Holding national registration helps with reciprocity, the transfer of certification from one state to another, and is looked on favorably by employers. Most states use the NREMT examination as their own certification examination.

topics.heading: Quality improvement (QI)
topics.html: Quality improvement (QI) is the continuous self-review of an EMS system to identify and fix problems, with the aim of ensuring the highest quality of prehospital care. EMTs support QI in several ways: by writing accurate and complete reports, by serving on QI committees, by critiquing their own performance after each call, by gathering feedback from patients and hospitals, by maintaining their equipment, and by continuing their education.

topics.heading: Medical direction
topics.html:
Every EMS system operates under the authority of a physician. The Medical Director is the physician with ultimate responsibility for the patient-care side of the system: the protocols, oversight of training, and a central role in QI. Medical direction reaches the EMT in two forms, set out in the table below.

TypeMeaningExample
Off-lineStanding orders — act without contacting a physicianGiving naloxone for opioid overdose
On-lineReal-time order via phone/radio from an on-duty physicianCalling for permission before a medication not covered by standing orders

Off-line direction takes the form of standing orders, which let you act without contacting a physician. On-line direction is a real-time order from an on-duty physician, given over the phone or radio.

sections.title: EMS as Public Health & Evidence-Based Practice

topics.heading: EMS role in public health
topics.html:
Public health is the system that oversees the health of a population as a whole: clean water, vaccination, prenatal care and the like. EMS contributes to it in a number of ways. Geriatric injury prevention includes identifying fall hazards, running blood pressure (BP) clinics and promoting the File of Life. Youth injury prevention includes car-seat clinics and bicycle helmet programs. Many EMS agencies take part in public vaccination programs, giving flu shots and, in some regions, routine childhood vaccines. EMS also contributes to disease surveillance, because trends in call volume are an early warning of influenza, opioid overdoses and mass-casualty events.

The umbrella term for this expanded role is Mobile Integrated Health Care, also called community paramedicine. EMS is uniquely placed for it because it operates directly in patients' homes and communities rather than only in hospitals and offices.

topics.heading: Research & evidence-based EMS
topics.html:
Evidence-based techniques are those supported by scientific evidence rather than by tradition alone. The measure that matters is patient outcomes, meaning long-term results and not simply survival to the hospital. Oxygen is the classic example: O2 is not a "wonder drug," and excess O2 can worsen the outcome of a myocardial infarction (MI) or a stroke.

Adopting an evidence-based practice follows a process. A hypothesis is formed, the literature is reviewed, the evidence is evaluated together with the Medical Director, and the practice is adopted only if the evidence supports it. This is the scientific method, in use for roughly 400 years since Galileo: a general observation leads to a hypothesis, the hypothesis to a prediction, and the prediction to testing that proves or disproves it.

Research that is peer reviewed has been vetted by other experts before it is published in a journal, which makes it more reliable than EMS magazines; those are informative, but they do not publish original, peer-reviewed research. Research in EMS is hard for several reasons: the environment is unstable, patient encounters are brief, data collection is disjointed, and there are ethical issues in obtaining consent from critically ill patients.

topics.heading: Street Scenes — professionalism case study
topics.html:
Two EMTs on the same kind of call illustrate what professionalism looks like in practice. Chuck is the poor example. His uniform is unkempt, he does not introduce himself, and he is dismissive of the patient, calling the patient "hon," cutting the patient off and criticizing his partner in front of the patient. This is unprofessional behavior and poor people skills.

Susan Miller is the good example. Her uniform is neat. She introduces herself and her crew, and she has checked the equipment and reviewed procedures before the call. She reassures the patient, and when correction is needed she gives it privately and constructively, never in front of the patient. After the call she debriefs with her crew.

takeaways: 911 system – telephone access for emergencies; Enhanced 911 = auto-ID of caller info.
Evidence-based techniques – science-backed, not just tradition.
Medical direction – physician oversight of patient care (on-line/off-line).
Medical Director – the physician with ultimate responsibility for the system.
Off-line medical direction – standing orders, no direct contact needed.
On-line medical direction – real-time orders via radio/phone.
Patient outcomes – long-term survival/results, not just short-term survival.
Peer reviewed – vetted by experts before publication.
Protocols – Medical-Director-set steps for assessment/care.
Quality improvement – continuous self-review to fix system issues.
Standing orders – pre-approved actions taken without direct physician contact.

chapters.title: Well-Being of the EMT
chapters.intro: An EMT who is exhausted, exposed or hurt cannot take care of anyone else, so this chapter is about protecting the provider first. It covers standard precautions and the personal protective equipment that stands between you and infectious disease, the way stress accumulates over a career and how to manage it, what patients and families go through around death, and how to read a scene for violence, hazardous materials and rescue situations before stepping into it.

topics.heading: Well-being / healthy habits
topics.html:
Taking care of yourself is the foundation of a long career, and it rests on a few habits. The first is a support system of solid personal relationships with family, EMS colleagues and friends. Exercise builds strength, flexibility and cardiovascular fitness and helps with weight management. Sleep is just as important, because a lack of it leads to medical errors, poor decisions, more motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) and a weaker immune system. Eating right provides the fuel for long shifts and strenuous work.

Alcohol and caffeine should both be limited. Each impairs performance, decision making and reaction time, even when you feel more awake for having had them. Finally, see a physician regularly and stay current on your vaccines.

topics.heading: Standard precautions
topics.html:
Pathogens spread in two main ways: through blood and body fluids (bloodborne) or through droplets (airborne). Because you cannot tell by looking whether a patient is infected, standard precautions require you to assume that all body fluids are infectious. The decision about which precautions to take is made during scene size-up and is reassessed throughout the call as the patient's condition changes.

The law divides the responsibility. Under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), the employer must provide training, vaccines, personal protective equipment (PPE) and a written exposure control plan; the employee must follow that plan and report exposures. Federal law also provides that emergency workers can be notified if a patient they were exposed to is later found to be infected with tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis B or HIV.

topics.heading: PPE types
topics.html:
The table below sets out the types of PPE an EMT uses and when each is called for.

EquipmentWhen
Gloves (nonlatex)Any contact w/ blood/body fluids (bleeding, suction, ventilation, CPR) — carry 2 pairs
Heavy-duty glovesCleaning ambulance/equipment, broken glass
Eye protectionRisk of splash/spatter
Surgical maskBlood/fluid spatter
N-95/HEPA respiratorSuspected TB (NIOSH-approved)
Face shieldSuctioning
Gown/apronArterial bleeding, childbirth, multi-trauma

Gloves are not a substitute for handwashing. Wash your hands after every patient contact, even if you wore gloves. An alcohol-based cleaner is acceptable unless your hands are visibly soiled or anthrax is suspected.

A few common-sense rules apply: keep PPE on your person or in your kits at all times, carry 2 sets of gloves, and if in doubt, take precautions.

topics.heading: Diseases of concern
topics.html:
Several infectious diseases are of particular concern to EMS providers because of how they spread and how serious they are. The table below summarizes them.

DiseaseSpreadNotes
Hepatitis BBlood/body fluidsVaccine available; deadly without it (was the top occupational killer)
Hepatitis CBlood/body fluidsNo vaccine
TBAirborneHighly contagious; assume any productive cough = possible TB
HIV/AIDSBlood (needlestick, IV drug use, sex, transfusion)Less risk than HBV (<0.5% vs. 30% per exposure) — doesn't survive well outside the body
EbolaBlood/body fluidsHigh death rate; a vaccine and treatments exist but are limited; screen travel history
SARS/MERS/Avian fluRespiratory dropletsSevere respiratory illness, regional outbreaks

The incubation period is the time between contact with a pathogen and the first symptoms; it varies by disease.

topics.heading: Infection control & the law
topics.html:
Infection control in EMS is shaped by two pieces of federal law. The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard requires the employer to have an exposure control plan; to provide training, a free hepatitis B vaccine and PPE; to label hazards properly with the biohazard symbol; and to maintain housekeeping and decontamination procedures. The Ryan White CARE Act of 1990 gives emergency responders the right to find out whether they have been exposed to a life-threatening disease.

Notification works differently depending on the route of exposure. After an airborne exposure, such as to TB, the hospital notifies your agency's designated officer, who notifies you. After a bloodborne exposure, such as to HIV, you must request a determination yourself, through the designated officer. When caring for or transporting a suspected TB patient, or when performing a high-risk procedure such as suctioning or intubation, an N-95/HEPA respirator is required.

If you are exposed, whether by needlestick or splash, seek medical care immediately, because delay reduces the effectiveness of any preventive treatment. EMTs are also tested regularly for TB exposure, usually yearly, with the tuberculin skin test (TST).

sections.title: Stress, Grief & Scene Safety

topics.heading: Stress — Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome (3 stages)
topics.html: Resilience is toughness, the ability to recover from difficult situations, and understanding how the body responds to stress is part of building it. Selye described that response as the general adaptation syndrome, which unfolds in three stages. In the alarm stage the body mounts the fight-or-flight response: the heart rate (HR) rises, the pupils dilate, blood pressure (BP) climbs and cortisol is released. In the resistance stage the body adapts and returns to normal as it copes with the stressor. If the stress is prolonged or severe, the body reaches the exhaustion stage, when the body's resources are depleted and fatigue and stress-related illness set in.

topics.heading: 3 types of stress reactions
topics.html:
Stress reactions differ in when they appear. The table below sets out the three types.

TypeTimingExample
AcuteDuring/shortly after incidentNausea after a bad call
Delayed (PTSD)Days–years laterFlashbacks, nightmares, irritability (1+ month)
Cumulative (burnout)Builds over yearsApathy → physical complaints → depression

Not all stress is harmful. Eustress is positive, helpful stress; distress is negative stress that impairs performance. Certain calls are recognized as especially stressful: multiple-casualty incidents (MCIs), calls involving infants or children, severe injuries, abuse or neglect, and the death of a coworker. The signs that stress is taking a toll include irritability, poor concentration, changes in sleep or appetite, anxiety, guilt and isolation.

topics.heading: Dealing with stress
topics.html:
Managing stress begins with lifestyle. A better diet, less alcohol and caffeine, exercise and relaxation techniques all help, and so, when needed, does a change of shift or work location.

For patients and for EMTs alike, the mnemonic eSCAPe describes what to offer after a traumatic event, to every patient, every time:

  • S – Social support: the person is not alone.
  • C – Choice and control: offer small choices.
  • A – Anticipate: explain what happens next.
  • P – Plan and organize: reduce confusion.

Critical Incident Stress Management (CISM) is a comprehensive system of education, peer support and counseling. One of its components is critical incident stress debriefing (CISD), in which a team of peers and mental health professionals meets with responders 24–72 hours after an incident; a "defusing" is an earlier, smaller session of the same kind. Debriefing is now used less often and is not always recommended. Whatever form it takes, seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness.

topics.heading: Death & dying — 5 stages
topics.html:
Patients who are dying, and their families, commonly pass through five emotional stages:

  1. Denial ("Not me")
  2. Anger ("Why me?")
  3. Bargaining ("Let me first...")
  4. Depression ("I haven't...")
  5. Acceptance ("I'm not afraid")

Not everyone goes through all five stages, or in this order, and the family may need more support than the patient does. You can help by treating the patient with respect and dignity and talking directly to him or her, by tolerating anger without taking it personally, by listening empathetically, and by offering realistic comfort. Never give false reassurance.

topics.heading: Scene safety
topics.html: Whether a scene is safe is the most important decision you make on every call. It helps to know what actually kills EMS providers. The biggest killers are heart attacks, MVCs and air-medical crashes, not violence, and back injury ends more careers than violence does.

topics.heading: Hazardous materials & rescue
topics.html:
At a hazardous materials incident, your first task is to keep your distance. Stay well back and use binoculars to identify placards. The DOT Emergency Response Guidebook gives information on safe distances and procedures. Your job is to recognize the hazard, protect yourself and others, and notify the hazmat team; you do not act beyond that. Contaminated patients are not treated until they have been decontaminated, because treating them earlier contaminates the ambulance and the ER. Terrorism may involve chemical, biological, radiological or explosive agents, and you should know your local protocols for it.

Rescue operations follow the same principle. Call for police, fire or specialist teams as needed, and never act outside your training. The PPE for rescue work is turnout gear, eyewear, a helmet and puncture-proof gloves.

topics.heading: Violence — Plan / Observe / React
topics.html:
Protection from violence follows three steps: plan, observe and react. Planning starts before the call. Wear safe clothing, meaning nonslip shoes, reflective gear and, in high-risk settings, body armor. Carry equipment you can manage, keep a portable radio with you, and assign safety roles; one EMT can act as the observer.

Observation begins on approach and continues throughout the call. Look for signs of violence such as broken glass or arguing, for a crime scene, for drug or alcohol use, for weapons, for agitated family members or bystanders, for possible perpetrators still on scene, and for pets. Turn off your lights and siren as you near the scene so that you do not draw a crowd, and do not stand directly in front of doors.

If violence develops, react with the 3 Rs:

  • Respond: put distance between yourself and the threat and use cover, which protects you from projectiles, or concealment, which hides you but does not protect you.
  • Radio: call for police and give clear information about the location, the number of people involved and any weapons.
  • Reevaluate: do not re-enter until the police have secured the scene, and stay alert even after they have.

When you have to retreat, flee with 2 obstacles between you and the danger, ditch cumbersome gear, and take cover or concealment.

takeaways: Standard Precautions – treat all body fluids as infectious (= body substance isolation).
Pathogens – disease-causing organisms (viruses, bacteria).
PPE – equipment protecting from infection/exposure.
Contamination – introduction of disease/chemicals. Decontamination – removal/cleansing of contaminants.
Hazardous material incident – release of a harmful substance.
MCI (multiple-casualty incident) – single incident, multiple patients.
Resilience – ability to recover quickly from hardship.
Stress – state of physical/psychological arousal to a stimulus.
CISM – system to prevent/manage stress.

chapters.title: Lifting and Moving Patients
chapters.intro: More EMTs are hurt lifting and moving patients than in any other part of the job, and those injuries are almost always preventable. This chapter sets out the body mechanics that keep a lift safe, the devices that carry a patient and what each is suited to, the difference between an emergency move and one that can wait, and the positions a patient should ride in for different conditions.

sections.title: Patient Lifting & Moving
sections.note: This chapter doesn't map onto one of the practice exam's six domains — it's a standalone topic in its own right.

topics.heading: Body mechanics — before lifting
topics.html: Every lift begins before anyone touches the patient. Consider the weight of what you are about to move and decide honestly whether you and your partner can manage it or whether you need to call for help. Consider your own physical limitations and your partner's as well, because a lift is only as safe as the weaker of the two people performing it. Then communicate the plan, so that everyone knows who lifts, who leads the count and where the patient is going before any weight leaves the ground.

topics.heading: Lifting rules
topics.html:
The rules that keep a lift safe are few, and they do not change with the situation. Set your feet shoulder-width apart on a firm, level surface before you take any weight. Lift with the legs rather than the back, and never twist while lifting; a loaded spine that rotates is the classic mechanism for a career-ending back injury. When a lift has to be made with one hand, resist the temptation to lean to the other side to compensate, and keep the back straight and locked instead.

Keep the weight close to the body throughout. The farther a load sits from your center of gravity, the more leverage it exerts on your spine. Carrying a stair chair down stairs applies the same principles in a different shape: keep the back straight, flex at the knees, and lean forward from the hips rather than bending at the waist.

topics.heading: Lifting devices — even numbers of people
topics.html:
A patient-carrying device is meant to be lifted by an even number of rescuers, and the number matters more than it first appears. With 2 rescuers, one takes the head end and one takes the foot end. With 4 rescuers, one takes each corner, which is the best arrangement for rough terrain or a long carry. A device is never lifted by 3 people: an odd number throws the device off balance, and an unbalanced device tips over.

The lift itself is performed with the power lift, also called the squat-lift. Squat down to the load instead of bending at the waist, keep the weight close to you and straddled between your feet, plant the feet flat and apart, carry the weight on the balls of the feet, and keep the back locked from start to finish.

The hands do their share of the work through the power grip, which puts as much skin as possible in contact with the handle. Every finger is bent to the same angle, and the hands are held at least 10 inches apart.

topics.heading: Reaching, pushing & pulling
topics.html:
Reaching obeys the same rules as lifting. Keep the back locked and do not twist. Do not reach more than 20 in. (50 cm) in front of you, and avoid a prolonged reach while under strain, because the muscles that stabilize the spine fatigue quickly in that position.

When a load has to be moved horizontally, push it rather than pull it whenever you have the choice, since pushing lets you put your body weight behind the load instead of relying on the smaller muscles of the arms and back. Keep the back locked and the line of pull running through the center of your body, bending the knees to bring yourself into that line. Keep the weight close to the body. If the weight is below your waist, kneel rather than stoop to it. Never push or pull overhead. Keep the elbows bent and the arms close to the sides.

topics.heading: Speed and safety are usually in tension, and the situation decides which wins
topics.html:
Patient moves are sorted into three kinds, and which one you perform depends on what is threatening the patient at that moment rather than on what would be ideal. The table below sets out when each move applies and what it allows in the way of spinal precautions.

MoveWhenSpinal precaution?
EmergencyImmediate danger to life (fire, collapse, toxic gas, must reach other patients, need a flat surface for CPR/bleeding control)NO time — use a long-axis drag to minimize injury
UrgentImmediate life threat needing treatment (poor breathing, shock, altered mental status, rapid decline from heat/cold)YES — abbreviated, e.g., backboard via log roll
NonurgentNo life threat — normal move after full assessment/treatmentFull precautions as needed

The long axis is the imaginary line running down the center of the body, from the head through the spine. In an emergency move you drag the patient from the shoulders along that line so that the body falls into its natural alignment and the spine is protected as far as the circumstances allow. It is worth remembering that the long backboard is now regarded chiefly as a device for moving and transporting a patient rather than a means of long-term immobilization.

topics.heading: Patient-carrying devices
topics.html:
The ambulance carries a range of devices, and each of them is built for a particular patient, terrain or doorway. The table below sets out what each device is best suited to and where it should not be used.

DeviceBest forAvoid for
Wheeled stretcherStandard transport; lowest level = safestRough/uneven terrain (tips easily)
Power stretcherBattery/hydraulic lift, up to ~700 lb—
Bariatric stretcherObese patients (800+ lb rated)—
Stair chairStairs, narrow corners, breathing-difficulty patients (sit-up position)Spine injury, unresponsive, altered mental status, airway care needed
Long backboardSpinal immobilization/transport—
Portable/folding stretcherMCIs—
Scoop stretcherGeneral lifting; splits to slide under a patient without a log roll, and is an accepted device for spinal motion restriction—
Basket/Stokes stretcherRough terrain, multi-level moves—
Flexible/Reeves stretcherNarrow hallways/tight spaces—
Vacuum mattressRigid, conforming, more comfortable than a backboard—

Whichever device you choose, check its weight rating before you commit to the lift. Secure the patient to the device first, and then secure the device to the ambulance.

topics.heading: Moving a patient onto a device
topics.html:
How a patient is moved onto a carrying device depends first on whether you suspect an injury to the spine.

When you do, begin with manual stabilization of the head and neck, apply a cervical collar, and then restrict motion of the neck and spine for the move itself. If the patient is able to move under their own power, assist them rather than lifting or rolling them, because a patient who moves themselves puts less strain on the spine than any technique you can perform for them. A patient found seated in a vehicle is stabilized first and then either assisted out or transferred onto a long backboard, and from there moved to the stretcher.

When no spinal injury is suspected, 4 transfer methods are available. All of them require that a spine injury has been ruled out first.

  • Extremity lift: one rescuer supports the patient at the armpits and wrists while the other supports the knees.
  • Direct ground lift: used to bring a patient from the ground onto the stretcher.
  • Draw-sheet method: the bottom sheet is loosened and the patient is pulled across on it, which makes it the method of choice for bed transfers.
  • Direct carry: used from a bed or another bed-level surface to the stretcher, with the rescuers curling the patient in against their own chests.

topics.heading: Patient positioning
topics.html:
The position a patient rides in is a clinical decision rather than a matter of convenience, and the right one follows from the complaint. The table below sets out the position that suits each of the common presentations.

ConditionPosition
Unresponsive, no spine injuryRecovery position (on side — aids drainage, prevents aspiration)
Comfort (chest pain, nausea, breathing difficulty)Position of comfort, often semi-Fowler/Fowler — monitor airway, switch to recovery if responsiveness drops
ShockSupine (maximizes perfusion)
Trauma/spine injuryDo NOT lower the head (breathing) or raise the legs (no proven benefit, may worsen injury)

Transferring the patient onto the hospital bed at the end of the call is usually done with a modified draw-sheet method.

takeaways: Body mechanics – proper body use to lift/move safely.
Bariatric – significantly overweight/obese patients.
Power lift / power grip – squat-lift technique; max-skin-contact grip.
Direct ground lift / direct carry / draw-sheet method / extremity lift – patient transfer methods used only when no spine injury is suspected.
Long-axis drag = the preferred emergency-move technique.
Never use 3 people on a lifting device — always an even number.

chapters.title: Medical, Legal, and Ethical Issues
chapters.intro: Every call carries legal weight: the patient's right to consent or refuse, the EMT's duty to act, the limits of scope of practice and the standard of care you will be measured against. This chapter works through consent and refusal, advance directives such as DNR orders and POLST forms, a framework for ethical dilemmas, and the legal concepts of negligence, abandonment, confidentiality and Good Samaritan protection.

topics.heading: Scope of practice vs. standard of care
topics.html:
Two ideas are easy to confuse and are tested precisely because of it. Scope of practice is the legal boundary of what an EMT may do. It is defined by state and regional legislation and varies from one location to another, so the same skill may be within scope in one state and outside it in the next. Standard of care is what a reasonably trained EMT would do in a similar situation, and it is the benchmark used in negligence claims. The distinction is worth fixing in your mind now: scope of practice is what you are allowed to do, while standard of care is what you should do, and how well you should do it.

Both have to be maintained after certification. You keep your skills by practicing them to mastery, and you keep your knowledge current through continuing education and recertification. Quality improvement is the other half of that work. After a call, critique your own performance and your crew's, and accept feedback as a way to improve the care you give. The spirit to bring to it is simple: hold yourself to the standard you would want for a member of your own family.

topics.heading: Consent
topics.html:
No competent patient can be treated without permission, and the form that permission takes depends on the patient's condition. The three types you will meet are set out below.

TypeApplies toDescription
Expressed consentCompetent adultPatient directly agrees to care (verbal/gesture), after understanding risks/benefits/alternatives
Implied consentUnresponsive/incapacitated patientLaw assumes a reasonable person would consent to lifesaving care
Consent for minorsChildrenParent/guardian normally consents; in loco parentis = a responsible adult temporarily standing in for the parent (teacher, camp counselor) can consent in an emergency if the parent is unavailable

Capacity to consent, or to refuse, requires that the patient be an adult or an emancipated minor, mentally competent and not impaired by injury, illness or substances, and fully informed of the risks of refusing.

topics.heading: Refusal of care
topics.html:
A competent adult has the right to refuse care, even care you are certain they need. For that refusal to be valid, four conditions must all be met:

  • The patient is a legal adult, or is otherwise legally authorized to refuse.
  • The patient is mentally competent and oriented.
  • The patient has been fully informed of the risks of refusing, in terms they understand.
  • The patient makes the refusal without coercion.

The competence requirement carries a firm consequence: a patient intoxicated by alcohol or drugs cannot give a valid informed refusal.

When a patient does refuse, work through the situation rather than simply leaving. Try again to persuade them to accept transport, explaining the risks clearly, and consult medical direction. Satisfy yourself that the patient genuinely understands the consequences of the decision, then document thoroughly: your assessment findings, the exact risks you explained, and the patient's own words where you can capture them. Have the patient sign a refusal form and obtain a witness signature if one is available. Finally, leave the door open by encouraging them to call back if they change their mind or if their condition worsens.

topics.heading: DNR orders & POLST
topics.html:
A do not resuscitate (DNR) order is a legal document, typically signed by both the patient and a physician, stating that the patient has a terminal illness and does not want resuscitative efforts. It is one form of advance directive, meaning it is written and signed in advance of the event it governs. DNR orders vary in how specific they are. One might direct that resuscitation be attempted only if the arrest is witnessed and not if the patient is found already in arrest, which avoids resuscitating someone who may have sustained brain damage during an unwitnessed period of downtime.

Several related documents serve different purposes. Physician's Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) is broader than a DNR: it covers resuscitation together with other end-of-life preferences, such as artificial feeding and antibiotics, for use if the patient later cannot express their wishes. Some states allow physician assistants and advanced practice registered nurses to validate these forms rather than physicians alone, so check the rules where you work. A living will is a signed statement of preferences about long-term life support and comfort measures, and it typically applies to in-hospital situations rather than prehospital care. A health care proxy is a person the patient has named to make decisions on their behalf should they become unable to.

topics.heading: The critical decision rule
topics.html:
The rule to carry into a resuscitation decision is this: a family member's oral request alone, without a legal DNR document present, is not sufficient grounds to withhold resuscitation. It is better to be criticized or sued for attempting to save a life than for letting a patient die. Without an actual legal document in hand, provide care.

The reverse situation also occurs. If the family is under duress and wants a valid DNR ignored, so that they are asking for resuscitation despite a DNR on file, contact medical direction. The physician may need to speak with the family directly.

topics.heading: Ethical dilemmas — framework
topics.html:
Not every hard call is a clinical one. A colleague who hides a medication error, coming upon a crash after you have been drinking, a patient who confides involvement in a crime: these are genuine tests of judgment, and none of them has a protocol.

The general approach is to identify your options, weigh patient welfare, safety and legal obligation against the competing pressures, and choose the course that best protects the patient and upholds your professional and legal duty, even when that course is uncomfortable. Reporting a colleague's serious medication error is the clearest example. Patient safety, and honesty about the care actually given, supersede loyalty to a colleague.

sections.title: Torts, Negligence & Confidentiality

topics.heading: Torts, negligence & legal concepts
topics.html:
A tort is a civil wrong, as opposed to a criminal act. One party's action causes harm to another, and the matter is resolved through civil liability and a lawsuit rather than criminal prosecution.

Negligence is the tort an EMT is most likely to face, and it has 4 required elements. All of them must be present for a claim to succeed:

  1. Duty to act. You had an obligation to provide care.
  2. Breach of duty. You failed to provide the expected standard of care.
  3. Damages. The patient suffered actual harm.
  4. Causation. Your breach of duty directly caused that harm.

Duty to act exists once you are on duty and dispatched, or in some jurisdictions once you have begun patient contact even while off duty. It varies by state and by employment status.

One doctrine sidesteps that four-part proof. Res ipsa loquitur, meaning "the thing speaks for itself," presumes negligence from the very nature of the injury or circumstance, without each element having to be proved individually. A surgical instrument left inside a patient is the classic example.

Three further terms describe specific wrongs. Abandonment is terminating care without ensuring that an equal or higher level of care continues, and without the patient's consent. Assault is placing a patient in fear of imminent harmful or unwanted contact. Battery is the actual unwanted physical contact, or care performed without consent.

topics.heading: Good Samaritan laws
topics.html: Good Samaritan laws protect providers who voluntarily render emergency care in good faith and without expectation of payment, shielding them from liability for ordinary negligence. That protection does not extend to gross negligence or willful misconduct, and it is not total immunity: you can still be held liable for reckless or grossly negligent care.

topics.heading: Confidentiality & HIPAA
topics.html:
Confidentiality is the protection of patient information from unauthorized disclosure, and EMTs breach it more often by carelessness than by intent. The common ways are discussing patients in public spaces such as elevators, restaurants and social media; sharing patient information with unauthorized bystanders or the media; and leaving patient care reports or other patient information visible or accessible.

The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) governs how patient health information may be shared. Information can generally be shared for treatment, payment and healthcare operations, which is what allows you to hand off to receiving hospital staff, but not for unrelated purposes without authorization.

Two related risks concern what you say about a patient rather than what you disclose. Slander is a spoken false statement that damages someone's reputation, and libel is the same thing in writing. Both are real legal risks if an EMT makes inaccurate, damaging statements about a patient that turn out to be false.

topics.heading: Special situations
topics.html:
Three situations come with their own rules, and each turns up regularly on calls.

  • Medical identification devices. Bracelets, necklaces and wallet cards can inform your treatment decisions by revealing allergies, DNR status or chronic conditions. Use the information when it is present and relevant.
  • Organ donor status. This does not change your resuscitation efforts for a living patient. It becomes relevant only after death has been determined.
  • Safe haven laws. These allow a parent to surrender an unharmed newborn anonymously and legally, usually within a set number of days, at a designated safe location, without facing prosecution for abandonment.

topics.heading: Crime scenes
topics.html:
At a crime scene you have two jobs that can pull against each other, and the order between them is fixed: patient care always takes priority over evidence preservation. Scene safety comes before both, so do not enter until law enforcement confirms the scene is safe.

Within those limits, minimize disturbance to the scene wherever you can do so without compromising care. Avoid unnecessary movement of items, do not cut through bullet or knife holes in clothing but cut around them instead, and preserve footprints and other physical evidence where that is feasible.

Your observations matter as much as your care. Observe and document anything you see or hear, including what patients and bystanders say, because these observations can have real evidentiary value. Do not discuss the case with unauthorized parties such as the media or bystanders, and be prepared to appear as a witness in legal proceedings, where accurate and objective documentation will be what you rely on.

takeaways: Scope of practice = legal boundary of what your certification allows; standard of care = whether you did it the way a reasonably prudent EMT would have.
Expressed / implied / minor consent — each applies to a different patient condition; minors need guardian consent except for emancipated minors and true emergencies.
Valid refusal requires: competent adult + fully informed of risks + demonstrates understanding + thorough documentation + told to call back if anything changes.
A family's oral request alone can't override the need for a real DNR document — without one, provide care.
POLST = signed physician's order for specific life-sustaining treatment; broader than a DNR, unlike a living will.
Negligence = duty to act + breach of duty + damages + causation, all four required together.
Tort = civil wrong (can be sued); crime = offense against the state (prosecuted) — the same act can sometimes be both.
Good Samaritan laws protect good-faith, in-training acts — not gross negligence, not abandonment.
Abandonment = stopping care without an equal-or-higher-trained provider taking over, or without patient consent to stop.
Assault = fear of unwanted contact; battery = actual unwanted contact/care without consent.
Confidentiality/HIPAA allows sharing info with those directly involved in care — not family, bystanders, or the public.
Slander = spoken defamation; libel = written defamation.
Safe haven laws let a parent anonymously surrender an unharmed newborn without prosecution.
At a crime scene: patient care first, minimize disturbance without compromising care, document what you observe.

chapters.title: Medical Terminology
chapters.intro: Medical terms look forbidding until you see that they are assembled from a small set of roots, prefixes and suffixes, and that the directional vocabulary is a handful of paired opposites. This chapter shows how the words are built, lists the pieces worth memorizing, and establishes the anatomical position, body planes and reference lines that every later description of a patient depends on.

sections.title: Word Building & Anatomical Terms

topics.heading: How medical terms are built
topics.html:
Most medical words are assembled from a root together with a prefix, a suffix, or both. The root is the foundation of the word and carries its core meaning, and it usually cannot stand on its own. Cardi means heart and therm means heat, but neither is a word by itself.

To let a root join another word part, a vowel is attached to it, almost always an o. The result is a combining form: therm/o joined to meter gives thermometer. A compound word is a different construction again, two whole words joined together, as small and pox become smallpox.

A prefix is added to the front of a word and modifies its meaning, telling you what kind, where, in which direction or how many. Dys-, meaning difficult, placed in front of pnea, meaning breathing, gives dyspnea. A suffix is added to the end and completes the meaning: arthr, meaning joint, with -itis, meaning inflammation, gives arthritis.

Longer terms come apart the same way, one piece at a time. Cholecystitis is chol/e, meaning bile, plus cyst, meaning a closed sac, plus -itis, meaning inflammation. Put back together, it is inflammation of the closed sac that holds bile, which is the gallbladder.

topics.heading: Key roots / prefixes / suffixes (memorize)
topics.html:
A small stock of word parts accounts for most of the terms an EMT meets, and these are worth committing to memory outright. The roots name the structure, the prefixes qualify or place it, and the suffixes say what is happening to it.

  • Roots: cardi (heart), gastro (stomach), hepat (liver), neur (nerve), nas (nose), or (mouth), and broncho, pulmo and pneumo (all of them lungs).
  • Prefixes: brady- (slow), tachy- (fast), hyper- (above normal), hypo- (below normal), poly- (many), uni- (one), intra- (within), inter- (between), peri- (around), ante- and pre- (before), post- (after), contra- (against), dys- (difficult or painful), sub- (below), and super- and supra- (above).
  • Suffixes: -itis (inflammation), -algia (pain), -emesis (vomiting), -pnea (breathing), -plegia (paralysis), -rrhea (discharge), -spasm (contraction), -ology (study of), -ist (specialist), and -ac and -al (pertaining to).

topics.heading: Abbreviations, acronyms & plain language
topics.html:
An acronym is an abbreviation that can be pronounced as a word, such as CPAP. Convenient as they are, abbreviations and acronyms are a recognized source of communication errors, and the risk is greatest in written documentation and at patient handoff, where the person reading what you wrote cannot stop and ask you what you meant. In those high-risk situations, plain language is the better practice. The common ones, such as CPR and EMS, are understood everywhere and remain fine to use.

The same caution applies with more force still when you are speaking with patients, with families and with children. Jargon they do not understand leaves them unable to answer your questions correctly: a patient asked whether they have ever had an MI may not recognize the term, while the same patient asked about a heart attack will answer at once. Whenever there is any potential for ambiguity or misunderstanding, use simple terms.

topics.heading: Anatomic position is the reference point everything else depends on
topics.html: Anatomy is the study of the structure of the body, and physiology is the study of its function. Diffusion, the movement of a substance from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, is an example of physiology at work. Every directional term in medicine assumes a single starting point. In the anatomic position the body stands upright, faces forward and holds the palms forward, and that fixed frame of reference is what allows a word such as medial or anterior to mean the same thing every time, regardless of how the patient is actually positioned when you find them. Left and right always mean the patient's left and right.

topics.heading: Body planes
topics.html:
A plane is the flat surface produced by an imaginary slice through the body, and three of them are used to describe where something lies. The table below sets out each plane and the halves it divides the body into.

PlaneCuts body into
Sagittal/medianRight & left halves
Frontal/coronalFront & back halves
Transverse/horizontalTop & bottom halves

topics.heading: The directional vocabulary is really just a handful of paired opposites
topics.html:
Directional terms come in pairs of opposites, and they are far easier to learn as pairs than one at a time. The table below gives each term and what it means.

TermMeaning
MedialToward midline
LateralAway from midline
Bilateral / unilateralBoth sides / one side
Anterior (= ventral)Front
Posterior (= dorsal)Back
SuperiorToward head/above
InferiorToward feet/below
ProximalCloser to torso
DistalFarther from torso
Palmar / plantarPalm of hand / sole of foot

topics.heading: Reference lines exist because "the middle" needs a precise definition
topics.html: The midline is an imaginary vertical line running down the center of the body, from between the eyes down to the navel, and it divides the body into right and left halves. The midaxillary line runs vertically down from the middle of the armpit, over the side of the chest and on down the flank of the abdomen, dividing the body front from back; it is the landmark used for assessing lung sounds and for needle decompression. The midclavicular line runs through the center of each collarbone and serves the same sort of precise, chest-based assessment. Lines drawn through the navel divide the abdomen into its four quadrants: right upper (RUQ), left upper (LUQ), right lower (RLQ) and left lower (LLQ).

topics.heading: Positional terms describe how the patient is actually lying, not directional relationships
topics.html:
One last group of terms describes the position the patient is actually lying in rather than the relationship of one body part to another. The table below sets out the positions you will describe most often.

PositionDescription
SupineOn the back
ProneOn the abdomen (facedown)
Recovery (lateral recumbent)On side — preferred for unconscious non-trauma patients (drainage/aspiration prevention)
FowlerSitting, head of stretcher raised 45–60°
Semi-FowlerLeaning back, semi-sitting

takeaways: Anatomic position – standing, facing forward, palms forward (universal reference).
Torso – trunk of the body (no head/limbs).
Plane – a flat surface from slicing through the body.
Dorsal/ventral – synonyms for posterior/anterior.
Acronym = pronounceable abbreviation; avoid jargon with patients/families.
Midline, midaxillary line, and midclavicular line are the three key reference lines used for localization and procedures.

chapters.title: Anatomy and Physiology
chapters.intro: Assessment is only as good as your picture of what lies beneath the skin. This chapter surveys the body systems an EMT works with most: the musculoskeletal system that shapes and moves the body, the respiratory system that moves air, the cardiovascular system that moves blood, and the nervous, lymphatic and other systems that regulate the rest.

sections.title: Musculoskeletal, Respiratory & Cardiovascular Systems

topics.heading: Musculoskeletal system
topics.html:
The musculoskeletal system has 3 functions: it gives the body its shape, it protects the vital organs, and it makes movement possible. The bones do more than provide structure, however. Bone marrow also produces blood cells and stores nutrients.

The skull has two parts. The cranium forms the top, back and sides of the head, and the face is made up of the mandible, the maxillae, the nasal bones, the orbits and the zygomatic arches.

The spine consists of 33 vertebrae, and its hollow center houses the spinal cord. From the top down, the vertebrae fall into five regions: 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck, 12 thoracic vertebrae in the upper back where the ribs attach, 5 lumbar vertebrae in the lower back, 5 sacral vertebrae that form the back wall of the pelvis, and 4 vertebrae in the coccyx, or tailbone. The cervical spine is injured easily, because a heavy head sits on a slender neck, and a cervical injury can be fatal because this part of the cord controls the muscles of breathing. The lumbar spine is also vulnerable, since it is not supported by any other part of the skeleton.

The thorax is formed by 12 pairs of ribs and the 12 thoracic vertebrae. 10 pairs of ribs attach to the sternum; the remaining 2 pairs do not, and these are the "floating ribs." The sternum itself has three parts: the manubrium at the top, the body in the center, and the xiphoid process at the bottom tip.

The pelvis is made up of three bones: the ilium, which is superior and whose upper rim is the iliac crest; the ischium, which is inferior and posterior; and the pubis, which is anterior. The hip joint is formed where the head of the femur, the ball, sits in the acetabulum, the socket.

In the lower extremity, the femur is the largest bone in the body, and a fracture of the femur near the pelvis is what is commonly called a "broken hip." Below the femur lies the patella, or kneecap, and then the two bones of the lower leg: the tibia, the larger, medial bone that forms the shin, and the fibula, the smaller, lateral bone. Each of these ends at the ankle in a bony knob called a malleolus; the lateral malleolus belongs to the fibula and the medial malleolus to the tibia. The foot is built from the tarsals at the ankle, the metatarsals in the foot itself, the calcaneus at the heel, and the phalanges of the toes.

The upper extremity begins at the shoulder, where the clavicle, or collarbone, lies anteriorly and the scapula, or shoulder blade, lies posteriorly; the acromion process forms the top of the shoulder. The humerus is the bone of the upper arm. The forearm has two bones: the radius on the lateral, thumb side, where the radial pulse is felt, and the ulna on the medial side. The wrist is made up of the carpals, the hand of the metacarpals, and the fingers of the phalanges.

Joints are classified by the kind of movement they allow. The hip is a ball-and-socket joint, while the elbow is a hinge joint.

Muscle comes in three types, which differ in how they are controlled and where they are found. The table below sets them out.

Muscle typeControlLocation
Voluntary (skeletal)ConsciousAttached to bones, movement
Involuntary (smooth)AutomaticGI tract, lungs, blood vessels, urinary system
CardiacAutomatic, has automaticityHeart only; very O2-sensitive

topics.heading: Respiratory system
topics.html:
Air follows a fixed path into the lungs. It enters through the mouth or nose and passes into the pharynx, which has two parts, the oropharynx behind the mouth and the nasopharynx behind the nose. At the bottom of the pharynx sits the epiglottis, a flap that blocks food from entering the trachea. Below it lies the larynx, or voice box, which contains the vocal cords, and beneath that the cricoid cartilage. Air then travels down the trachea, which is held open by 16 C-shaped rings of cartilage, and divides into two bronchi, one for each lung. The bronchi branch into progressively smaller bronchioles, which end in the alveoli, the tiny sacs where gas exchange takes place.

The diaphragm is the muscle that divides the chest from the abdomen, and it is the main muscle of breathing; it is driven by the phrenic nerve. Inhalation is an active process. The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles contract, the chest expands, and the negative pressure this creates inside the chest pulls air in. Exhalation, by contrast, is passive. The muscles relax, the chest shrinks, and the resulting positive pressure pushes air out. Two terms that are easily confused describe different parts of this process: ventilation is the movement of gas into and out of the alveoli, while respiration is the exchange of gases between the blood and the cells.

Children differ from adults in ways that matter for airway management. A child's tongue is larger relative to the mouth, and the trachea and cricoid cartilage are narrower and softer, so the airway is more easily obstructed and more easily injured. The rib cage is flatter, and a child in respiratory distress may show a "seesaw" breathing pattern.

topics.heading: Cardiovascular system
topics.html:
The heart has four chambers: 2 atria on top and 2 ventricles below. Blood returns from the body through the venae cavae into the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonary artery to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place. Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, moves into the left ventricle, the strongest of the four chambers, and is pumped out through the aorta to the body. One-way valves prevent blood from flowing backward. The heart also has its own electrical system, the cardiac conduction system, which acts as a built-in pacemaker; this ability to generate its own impulses is called automaticity.

The arteries an EMT needs to know, and where each is found or used, are listed in the table below.

ArteryLocation/Use
CoronarySupplies heart muscle itself
AortaLargest artery, body
PulmonaryException — carries O2-poor blood to the lungs
CarotidNeck — CPR pulse check (adult/child); never palpate both sides at once
FemoralThigh/groin crease
BrachialUpper arm — infant CPR pulse, BP measurement
RadialWrist (thumb side)
Posterior tibialBehind medial ankle
Dorsalis pedisTop of foot

Blood leaves the heart through the arteries, which branch into smaller arterioles and then into the capillaries, where the exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste with the cells takes place. From the capillaries, blood collects into venules, then veins, and finally the venae cavae that return it to the heart. Just as the pulmonary artery is the one artery that carries oxygen-poor blood, the pulmonary vein is the one vein that carries oxygen-rich blood. The carotid and femoral pulses are the central pulses, and they remain palpable even when the peripheral pulses have weakened.

Blood itself has four components, each with its own function, as the table below shows.

Blood componentFunction
PlasmaWatery fluid, carries cells/CO2
RBCs (erythrocytes)Carry O2 (hemoglobin)
WBCs (leukocytes)Fight infection
PlateletsClotting

Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers. The systolic pressure is the pressure in the arteries while the ventricle contracts and pumps; the diastolic pressure is the pressure while the ventricle refills. A reading is written with the systolic over the diastolic, as in "120/80." Perfusion is the adequate delivery of oxygen and nutrients to the cells, together with the removal of their wastes. Hypoperfusion, or shock, is perfusion that is inadequate to meet the cells' needs, and it is life-threatening.

The cells produce their energy through metabolism, which takes one of two forms depending on whether oxygen is available. Aerobic metabolism, which takes place when oxygen is present, is efficient and produces little waste, only carbon dioxide (CO2) and water. Anaerobic metabolism, which the cells fall back on when oxygen is lacking, is inefficient and produces lactic acid. The lactic acid leads to acidosis, which injures cells and impairs the blood's ability to carry oxygen. For gas exchange to work at all, there must be both enough air and enough blood at the alveoli at the same time; this is called V/Q match.

topics.heading: Lymphatic, nervous & other systems
topics.html:
The lymphatic system captures fluid that has escaped from the bloodstream, called lymph, and returns it to the circulation. It also has an immune function, producing the lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. Its organs are the tonsils and adenoids, the spleen, the thymus and, by some accounts, the appendix. One clinical rule follows directly from this anatomy: never take a blood pressure (BP) on the affected arm of a patient who has had a mastectomy, because lymphatic tissue has been removed from the armpit and the pressure of the cuff is a risk.

The nervous system has two divisions. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is made up of the sensory nerves, which carry information from the body to the brain, and the motor nerves, which carry commands from the brain to the body. Within the PNS, the autonomic nervous system (ANS) controls involuntary functions, and it in turn has two branches. The sympathetic branch produces the fight-or-flight response: heart rate rises, breathing deepens and the blood vessels constrict. The parasympathetic branch, sometimes called feed-or-breed or rest, does the opposite: it increases blood flow to the digestive and reproductive organs, slows the heart rate and dilates the vessels. A separate structure, the reticular activating system, keeps a person awake and conscious.

Recognizing sympathetic discharge is a useful assessment skill. A patient who is pale and diaphoretic with an elevated heart rate (HR) and respiratory rate (RR) is showing the body's response to a serious problem, and this can flag serious illness even when the classic symptoms are absent, as in the "silent" myocardial infarction (MI) that older women sometimes experience.

The digestive system is a single passage with supporting organs along it. Food travels from the mouth down the esophagus to the stomach, where acid begins breaking it down, then into the small intestine, whose three parts are the duodenum, jejunum and ileum and where nutrients are absorbed, and finally into the large intestine, or colon, which removes water and forms waste. The liver produces bile, detoxifies the blood, stores sugar and synthesizes blood products. The gallbladder stores bile. The pancreas produces insulin and digestive enzymes. The spleen filters old blood cells and serves as a reservoir of blood; it lies in the left upper quadrant (LUQ) and is at risk in trauma. The appendix, in the right lower quadrant (RLQ), is lymphatic tissue whose function is unclear.

The integumentary system, the skin, provides protection, maintains water balance, regulates temperature, excretes wastes and absorbs shock. It has three layers. The outer layer, the epidermis, contains no blood vessels or nerves. Beneath it, the dermis holds the blood vessels, nerves, glands and hair follicles, which is why an injury that reaches the dermis bleeds, hurts and carries a risk of infection. The deepest layer, the subcutaneous tissue, is fat and soft tissue that insulates the body and absorbs shock.

The endocrine system produces hormones. The pancreas secretes insulin, which regulates glucose. The adrenal glands secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine, the hormones of sympathetic activation; acting on beta-2 receptors they dilate the bronchioles, and acting on beta-1 receptors they increase the rate and force of the heartbeat.

The renal system, or urinary system, regulates fluid balance, filters the blood and adjusts its pH. The kidneys filter urea from the blood, regulate sodium and fluid, and produce bicarbonate. Urine passes from the kidneys through the ureters to the bladder, which serves as a reservoir, and leaves the body through the urethra.

The reproductive system differs by sex. In the male, the testes produce sperm and are connected to the urethra by way of the epididymis and vas deferens. In the female, the ovaries, which lie on either side of the lower abdomen, release eggs into the fallopian tubes, where fertilization takes place. A fertilized egg passes to the uterus, a highly vascular organ in the midline of the lower abdomen that houses the fetus, and the vagina serves as the birth canal.

takeaways: Perfusion / hypoperfusion (shock) – adequate vs. inadequate cellular O2/waste exchange.
Automaticity – the heart's self-generated electrical impulses.
Buffer system – the body's pH regulation.
Central vs. peripheral pulses – carotid/femoral vs. radial/brachial/posterior tibial/dorsalis pedis.
Arteriole/venule – smallest artery/vein branches.
Never take a BP on a mastectomy patient's affected arm.
Cervical spine injury can be fatal because it can affect the muscles that control breathing.

chapters.title: Principles of Pathophysiology
chapters.intro: Pathophysiology is the study of what goes wrong when the body's compensating mechanisms fail. This chapter starts at the cell and its need for oxygen and glucose, builds up through the cardiopulmonary system and the volumes and pressures that keep it working, and arrives at shock, the common endpoint of many emergencies, where the supply of oxygenated blood no longer meets demand.

sections.title: Cellular Metabolism, the Cardiopulmonary System & Shock

topics.heading: Pathophysiology is the study of what happens when compensation fails
topics.html: The body maintains a stable internal state, called homeostasis, through constant small adjustments known as compensation. Pathophysiology is what you are studying whenever a disease process pushes hard enough that those adjustments are no longer enough.

topics.heading: The cell
topics.html:
The cell is the basic building block of the body. Its membrane is selective, controlling what enters and what leaves. Inside, the nucleus holds the cell's DNA, the endoplasmic reticulum synthesizes proteins, and the mitochondria convert glucose into adenosine triphosphate (ATP). ATP is the cell's fuel; it powers every cellular function, including the sodium-potassium pump that moves ions across the membrane. That ion movement creates the electrical charge that allows muscle, including the heart muscle, to contract. To do all this, a cell has three core requirements: water, glucose and oxygen.

Water must be present in the right amount. Too little and the cell dehydrates and dies; too much and its function is disrupted. Dissolved in the water are the electrolytes, among them potassium, sodium and magnesium, which make the cell's electrical functions possible, from nerve transmission to the depolarization of the heart. Glucose is the raw fuel that is broken down to produce ATP, but most cells cannot take it up on their own: they need insulin to move glucose from the blood into the cell.

topics.heading: Oxygen & metabolism
topics.html:
Cells can produce energy with oxygen or without it, and the difference between the two is enormous. The table below compares the two forms of metabolism.

TypeConditionEnergy outputWaste products
AerobicO2 presentHigh (~16× more efficient)CO2, water (manageable)
AnaerobicO2 absent/insufficientLowCO2, lactic acid → acidosis

Anaerobic metabolism sets off a downward spiral. The lactic acid it produces causes acidosis, and in an acidotic environment hemoglobin carries less oxygen. Less oxygen means worsening hypoxia, and the spiral continues downward.

topics.heading: Homeostasis & the fight-or-flight response
topics.html:
Homeostasis is regulated by the hypothalamus and the medulla oblongata. When the body is threatened, the sympathetic nervous system produces the fight-or-flight response. The adrenal glands release epinephrine and norepinephrine, which act on beta-2 receptors to dilate the bronchioles and on beta-1 receptors to increase the heart rate and the force of contraction; at the same time the blood vessels constrict, and blood pressure (BP) rises. At rest the parasympathetic nervous system, the feed-or-breed system, dominates instead.

Two situations blunt this response. Beta blockers reduce the effects of epinephrine and norepinephrine, so a patient who takes them may be unable to compensate normally during an emergency. In adrenal insufficiency, as in Addison's disease, the stress hormones the body needs to maintain blood volume and vessel tone are missing, so the normal compensatory response fails; the vessels dilate and the patient goes into shock.

topics.heading: The cardiopulmonary system
topics.html: The lungs and the heart work as one system, with three jobs: to move oxygen (O2) in, to move carbon dioxide (CO2) out, and to deliver oxygen to the cells. The air we inhale is roughly 79% nitrogen and 21% oxygen; the proportion of oxygen in inhaled air is called the fraction of inspired oxygen, or FiO2. None of this works unless the airway is patent, that is, open and unobstructed.

topics.heading: Lung volumes & respiratory dysfunction
topics.html:
Two measurements describe how much air a patient is moving. Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in one breath, and minute volume is the tidal volume multiplied by the respiratory rate. Not all of each breath reaches the alveoli: about 150 mL of every breath, the dead air space, fills the airway and never takes part in gas exchange. Because minute volume depends on both rate and depth, it can fall in two ways. A heroin overdose (OD) lowers the rate, while an asthma attack lowers the tidal volume; either one reduces the minute volume.

Respiratory dysfunction takes 3 forms:

  1. Disruption of respiratory control. Stroke, drugs such as narcotics, brain trauma and spinal cord injury can all impair the control of breathing.
  2. Disruption of pressure. A hole in the chest wall or the pleural space lets air or blood accumulate, and the lung collapses.
  3. Disruption of lung tissue. Trauma, congestive heart failure (CHF) and sepsis damage the alveoli so that they can no longer exchange gas.

The body has sensors that trigger compensation. Chemoreceptors detect rising CO2 and falling O2 and prompt the brain to increase both the rate and the depth of breathing. Stretch receptors in the blood vessels detect falling pressure and trigger sympathetic activation.

topics.heading: The blood & blood vessels
topics.html:
Two opposing pressures govern the movement of water across the walls of the blood vessels. Plasma oncotic pressure is the pull exerted by large proteins in the plasma, which draws water into the bloodstream. Hydrostatic pressure is the pumping force of the heart, which pushes water out of the vessels. If either pressure is disrupted, the result is edema or dehydration. Liver failure is one example: the failing liver produces too little albumin, oncotic pressure falls, fluid leaks out of the vessels, and the patient develops edema while the blood itself becomes dehydrated. The blood can also fail in its oxygen-carrying role. Anemia, too few red blood cells, reduces the blood's capacity to carry oxygen.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and that blood is oxygenated, except in the pulmonary artery. Veins carry blood toward the heart, and that blood is deoxygenated, except in the pulmonary vein. The capillaries between them are the site of exchange.

The vessels themselves can fail in several ways. The table below sets out the main problems, their causes and their results.

ProblemCauseResult
Loss of tone (vasodilation)Spinal injury, sepsis, anaphylaxis↓pressure → ↓perfusion
Excessive permeability ("leaky" capillaries)Sepsis, high altitude, diseaseFluid leaks out → volume loss, pulmonary edema
Hypertension (high SVR)Smoking, cocaine, geneticsAbnormal constriction → ↑pressure → heart disease/stroke risk
Loss of regulationSpinal injuryBlocked compensation signals → vasodilation + shock

Children vasoconstrict powerfully, so a child's blood pressure can remain normal even after massive volume loss. Capillary refill is a better indicator in a child; a refill time of less than 2 seconds is normal.

topics.heading: The heart
topics.html:
Stroke volume is the amount of blood the heart ejects with each beat, about 70 mL. It rises when preload or contractility increases and falls when afterload increases. Cardiac output is the stroke volume multiplied by the heart rate, and it can fall for three reasons: bradycardia, a low stroke volume as in blood loss, or a rate so fast that the ventricles do not have time to fill, which happens above 180 beats per minute (bpm).

A young heart cannot increase its contractility much, so a child compensates mainly by raising the heart rate (HR). Tachycardia in a child is therefore a serious red flag.

The heart can fail mechanically or electrically. Mechanical dysfunction, from trauma, compression of the heart by the pericardium, or a myocardial infarction (MI), can occur even while the electrical system remains intact. Electrical dysfunction takes the form of dysrhythmias, such as ventricular fibrillation (V-fib), bradycardia and tachycardia, and it results from hypoxia, toxins or medications. In infants, bradycardia is often a sign of hypoxia, a ventilation problem, rather than a cardiac problem.

topics.heading: Shock is fundamentally a supply problem, but the cause varies
topics.html:
Shock is defined as inadequate perfusion. The cells do not receive enough oxygen (O2) and nutrients and cannot get rid of their waste, so they shift to anaerobic metabolism, acidosis develops, and cells and then organs die. Whatever its cause, shock is fundamentally a problem of supply. The cause itself varies, however, and the table below sets out the four types of shock by mechanism.

TypeMechanismCommon cause
HypovolemicToo little blood volume → ↓pressureHemorrhage, dehydration
DistributiveVessels dilate → ↓pressure despite normal volumeAnaphylaxis, sepsis
CardiogenicHeart pump fails → ↓cardiac outputMI, dysrhythmia, trauma
ObstructiveBlood physically blockedTension pneumothorax, pericardial tamponade, pulmonary embolism

Shock progresses through stages. In compensated shock the body is still managing: the heart rate and respiratory rate rise, the vessels constrict, the skin becomes pale, cool and diaphoretic, the patient is mildly anxious and capillary refill is delayed, but the blood pressure may still be normal. In decompensated shock compensation has failed: the blood pressure falls and the mental status is altered. If decompensated shock is not reversed, it becomes irreversible shock, and the patient dies. Two exceptions are worth remembering. A patient in cardiogenic shock may not be able to raise the heart rate, and a patient in septic shock may not be able to vasoconstrict, so the usual compensatory signs can be missing.

topics.heading: Fluid balance
topics.html: About 60% of the body is water, distributed among 3 spaces. Roughly 70% of it is intracellular, inside the cells; 25% is interstitial, between the cells and the vessels; and 5% is intravascular, in the bloodstream. Three mechanisms regulate this balance: the brain and the kidneys, through thirst and urine output; the plasma proteins, through their oncotic pull; and the permeability of the cell and capillary membranes. Dehydration is a loss of fluid, whether from reduced intake, vomiting, diarrhea, rapid breathing, sweating or burns. Edema is a shift of fluid into the interstitial space, as occurs in liver failure, sepsis, high blood pressure (BP) and injury.

topics.heading: Other system dysfunction
topics.html:
The other body systems fail in their own characteristic ways. The brain is protected by the skull, the meninges and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), but that protection has a cost: when trauma causes bleeding or swelling inside a closed skull, there is nowhere for the extra volume to go, and intracranial pressure rises. Medical causes of nervous system dysfunction include stroke, meningitis, encephalitis, multiple sclerosis (MS) and hypoglycemia.

The endocrine system fails when a gland produces too much of a hormone, as in Graves' disease, or too little, as in Type 1 diabetes, where the absence of insulin leaves the cells unable to take up glucose and starving.
