Adrenal insufficiency, with too little cortisol and aldosterone to support the stress response, leads to shock.

Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding may be chronic or acute; an acute, massive bleed leads to hypovolemic shock. Dark or black stools indicate blood from the upper GI tract. Vomiting and diarrhea, whether viral or bacterial in origin, have dehydration, malnutrition and shock as their complications.

Finally, the immune system can overreact. In hypersensitivity, an exaggerated immune response releases excess histamine. Histamine increases capillary permeability, producing edema and narrowing of the airway, and dilates the blood vessels, so the blood pressure falls. The result is the distributive shock of anaphylaxis.

takeaways: Metabolism – converting nutrients into energy; aerobic/anaerobic = with/without O2.
Tidal volume – air per breath; minute volume – tidal × rate; dead air space – ~150 mL that never reaches alveoli.
FiO2 – fraction of inspired oxygen (~21% in room air). Patent – open/unobstructed (airway).
Stroke volume – blood per heartbeat; cardiac output – stroke volume × HR.
Chemoreceptors sense O2/CO2 changes; stretch receptors sense vessel pressure.
SVR (systemic vascular resistance) – pressure the heart pumps against.
V/Q match – alveolar air matched with pulmonary capillary blood.
Diaphoresis – profuse sweating (in shock, typically with cool, pale skin).
Edema – swelling from fluid moving into the interstitial space; dehydration – abnormally low total body water.
Electrolyte – charged particles dissolved in water.
Plasma oncotic pressure – proteins pull water into the bloodstream; hydrostatic pressure – heart's force pushes water out.
Hypersensitivity – an exaggerated immune/allergic response.

chapters.title: Life Span Development
chapters.intro: A newborn, a school-age child and an eighty-year-old are physiologically different patients, and their normal vital signs, airway anatomy and psychological needs change with age. This chapter walks through each stage of life, from infancy through late adulthood, and draws out what each means for assessment and care in the field.

sections.title: Development Across Age Groups

topics.heading: Two separate dimensions change with age
topics.html: Two separate dimensions of a person change with age. Physiologic development is the physical change in the body: the maturing of the organs, the shifting ranges of normal vital signs, and the growth of motor ability. Psychosocial development is mental and social change: the growth of trust, of independence and of identity. Development is divided into 8 stages of life, which follow one another in order: infancy, the toddler years, the preschool years, school age, adolescence, early adulthood, middle adulthood and late adulthood.

topics.heading: Infancy (birth – 1 year)
topics.html:
Infancy runs from birth to 1 year, and the newborn's vital signs differ from those of the older infant. The table below gives the normal ranges.

MeasureNewbornInfant (up to 1 yr)
HR100–17090–160
RR30–6030–60 (0–6mo), 24–30 (6–12mo)
Systolic BP50–70 mmHg~90 mmHg

A newborn weighs 6.6 to 7.7 lbs at birth. That weight doubles by 6 months and triples by 12 months, and the head alone accounts for 25% of total body weight. The infant airway is shorter, narrower, less stable and more easily obstructed than at any other stage of life. Infants breathe through the nose until they are at least 4 weeks old, and they breathe with the diaphragm, so the abdomen moves more than the chest. Because the accessory muscles of breathing are less mature, an infant in respiratory distress tires easily.

The bones of the skull have not yet fused, leaving soft spots called fontanelles. The posterior fontanelle closes by 2 to 3 months and the anterior fontanelle by 9 to 18 months. Until then they are a useful window: a sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration, and a bulging fontanelle in an infant who is not crying suggests increased intracranial pressure (ICP). Infants are also protected during their first months by passive immunity, acquired from the mother during pregnancy and through breast milk.

Newborns arrive with a set of reflexes, which the table below describes.

ReflexStimulusResponse
MoroStartledThrows arms out, spreads fingers, then grabs
PalmarFinger placed in palmGrasps finger
RootingCheek touched (when hungry)Turns head toward stimulus
SuckingLips strokedBegins sucking

Psychosocially, the infant's primary means of communication is crying. Bonding is the infant's sense that its needs will be met, and it is the foundation of the balance between trust and mistrust: a consistent, responsive environment builds trust. Scaffolding is learning by building on what is already known, and temperament is the infant's characteristic reaction to its environment.

topics.heading: Toddler (12–36 months) & preschool (3–5 years)
topics.html:
The toddler stage runs from 12 to 36 months. A toddler's heart rate (HR) is 80 to 140, the respiratory rate (RR) is 24 to 40, and the temperature is 96.8 to 99.5°F. Toddlers gain about 4.4 lbs per year. The terminal airways branch and grow, the brain reaches 90% of its adult weight, muscle mass and bone density increase, and all the primary teeth are in by 36 months. Toilet training illustrates the gap between physical and psychological readiness: it is physiologically possible at 12 to 15 months, but the child is not psychologically ready until 18 to 30 months, and completion averages about 28 months. Separation anxiety between 18 and 24 months, and magical thinking and play-acting between 24 and 36 months, are normal features of this stage.

The preschool years span ages 3 to 5. The HR is 70 to 120 and the RR is 22 to 34. Peer groups become a major influence, and a sense of belonging and group identity develops. Preschoolers may still engage in magical thinking, and one consequence is that they may believe an illness or injury is a punishment. Be reassuring, and keep explanations simple.

topics.heading: School age (6–12) & adolescence (13–18)
topics.html:
School age covers ages 6 to 12. The HR is 65 to 120 and the RR is 18 to 30. The primary teeth are lost and replaced by permanent teeth. Self-esteem develops during these years, shaped by popularity or rejection among peers and by support or neglect. Moral development also begins, as control of behavior shifts from external sources, chiefly the parents, to internal self-control. School-age children can understand explanations, so involve them in their own care.

Adolescence covers ages 13 to 18. Vital signs approach adult values: the HR is 60 to 100, the RR is 12 to 20, and the systolic blood pressure (BP) is about 107 to 117. A rapid growth spurt lasting 2 to 3 years proceeds in a set order, the feet and hands first, then the arms and legs, then the chest and trunk. Reproductive maturity and secondary sexual development arrive, and puberty is the point at which American Heart Association (AHA) cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) guidelines switch from pediatric to adult protocols. Psychosocially, adolescents strive for independence. Concern with body image can lead to eating disorders, self-destructive behaviors are possible, and there is a risk of depression and suicide. Privacy is critical: an adolescent may not want to answer questions in front of friends or parents.

topics.heading: Adulthood — early, middle & late
topics.html:
Early adulthood spans ages 19 to 40. Heart rate, respiratory rate and blood pressure are near the standard adult norms, and physical condition peaks between ages 19 and 26. These are the years of the highest job stress and the years in which childbirth is most common, and accidents are the leading cause of death.

Middle adulthood spans ages 41 to 60. Vision problems appear, chiefly presbyopia; cholesterol becomes a concern; the risk of cancer rises; and women reach menopause in the late 40s to early 50s. Heart disease is the major killer after age 40. Psychosocially, this is the period of the so-called "midlife crisis," of empty-nest syndrome when the last child leaves home, and of concern for aging parents.

Late adulthood begins at 61. The cardiovascular system becomes less efficient and tolerates tachycardia less well, the respiratory system deteriorates, metabolism slows, and the sleep-wake cycle is disrupted. The psychosocial challenges of this stage include the living environment, self-worth, financial burden, and death and dying.

topics.heading: EMS application notes
topics.html:
You do not need to memorize every vital sign range in this chapter. What you need is a general sense of what is normal and what is abnormal at the key ages, and a feel for how each stage changes the way you approach a patient. With infants and toddlers, keep the parent close, because separation anxiety interferes with assessment. Preschoolers may think their illness is a punishment, so use simple, reassuring language. With adolescents, privacy is critical, and you should watch for signs of eating disorders and self-harm. In the elderly, do not assume that confusion is normal, remember that tachycardia is less well tolerated, and keep in mind that the risk of falls is high.

Across the whole life span, one general trend holds: as age increases, the heart rate decreases, the respiratory rate decreases, and the blood pressure increases.

takeaways: Bonding – sense that needs will be met. Trust vs. mistrust – orderly environment builds trust; chaotic environment builds anxiety.
Scaffolding – learning by building on prior knowledge. Temperament – an infant's reaction to their environment.
Moro reflex – startle → arms out, fingers spread, then grab. Palmar reflex – finger in palm → grasps.
Rooting reflex – cheek touched → turns toward stimulus. Sucking reflex – lips stroked → begins sucking.
Empty-nest syndrome – the period after the last child leaves home.
General rule: as age increases, HR and RR decrease while BP increases — there's no single universal normal range.

chapters.title: Airway Management
chapters.intro: No intervention matters if air cannot reach the lungs, which is why the airway comes first in every assessment. This chapter traces the path a breath follows from the nose and mouth to the lungs, explains why one small structure, the epiglottis, accounts for so much airway trouble, and then works through what you actually do about a threatened airway: the two manual maneuvers and when each one applies, sizing and inserting the oral and nasal airways, suctioning within the limits that keep it from doing harm, reading the four sounds an obstructed airway makes, and the technique that makes a bag-valve mask work rather than merely look like it is working.

sections.title: Airway Anatomy & the Manual Maneuvers

topics.heading: Every breath follows the same physical path, and airway management is entirely about keeping that path open
topics.html: Air enters through the nose or mouth, travels through the throat and down the windpipe, and reaches the lungs, where the actual exchange of gases takes place. The nose does something the mouth does not: as air passes through its curved internal passages, the nose warms and humidifies it. The whole path is divided into two regions with a specific dividing line. The upper airway runs from the mouth and nose down to the vocal cords, and the lower airway is everything below that.

topics.heading: The epiglottis is a single small structure doing a genuinely critical job
topics.html: Right where the throat meets the windpipe sits the epiglottis, a flap that flips downward every time you swallow, sealing off the airway so that food and liquid go toward the esophagus instead of the lungs. Just below it is the glottic opening, at the level of the vocal cords, which marks the actual boundary between the upper and lower airway. This one structure explains a great deal of airway pathology. Swelling here, injury here, or failure of the mechanism itself, as in a patient with a depressed level of consciousness who can no longer protect their own airway, is why airway problems are addressed before almost anything else in patient care.

topics.heading: In an unresponsive patient the tongue is the most common obstruction, and it is an obstruction you can fix with your hands
topics.html:
The tongue is anchored to the lower jaw. When a patient loses consciousness, the muscles that hold the jaw forward relax, the jaw falls back toward the spine, and the tongue falls back with it against the posterior wall of the throat. Nothing is stuck in the airway and nothing is swollen; the airway has simply folded shut. This is the single most common cause of airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient, and the reason the first thing you do for such a patient costs nothing and takes two seconds.

Both manual maneuvers work by the same mechanism: they move the lower jaw forward, and the tongue, being attached to it, comes forward off the back of the throat. Neither one opens anything. They un-fold something.

topics.heading: Head-tilt/chin-lift is the default; jaw-thrust is the one you use when the spine is in question
topics.html:
The head-tilt/chin-lift is the standard maneuver for a patient with no suspected spinal injury. One hand on the forehead tilts the head back; the fingertips of the other hand under the bony part of the chin lift it upward. Keep your fingers on bone. Pressing into the soft tissue under the chin pushes the base of the tongue up into the airway, which is the opposite of what you are trying to do.

The jaw-thrust is the maneuver for a patient in whom you suspect a spinal injury, because it opens the airway without moving the neck. You position yourself at the patient's head, place your fingers behind the angles of the jaw on both sides, and displace the jaw forward while keeping the head in a neutral, in-line position. It is harder to hold and it ties up both of your hands, which is why it is not the default.

There is an order of priority worth being explicit about, because scenarios are written to test it. A patient with a suspected spinal injury who has no airway gets the jaw-thrust first. If the jaw-thrust does not open the airway, you use the maneuver that does. An open airway is the higher priority, because a protected spine in a patient who is not breathing is not a good outcome.

topics.heading: A child's airway is not a small adult airway, and the differences change what you do
topics.html:
Several differences matter at the bedside. A child's tongue is proportionally larger relative to the mouth, so tongue obstruction is more likely and more complete. The airway structures themselves are smaller and softer, so a given amount of swelling narrows the airway far more, and so the trachea can be collapsed by pressure from outside. The back of an infant's head is proportionally large, so when an infant is laid flat on a hard surface the head is pushed forward into flexion and the airway closes.

The practical consequence is that the neutral position for an infant or small child is not the same as for an adult. You may need a folded towel under the shoulders to bring the airway back into line, and over-extending the neck, tilting the head back as far as it will go, will kink a soft trachea shut rather than open it.

takeaways: Airway path: nose/mouth → throat → windpipe → lungs (gas exchange).
The nose warms and humidifies incoming air; the mouth does not.
Upper airway: mouth/nose down to the vocal cords. Lower airway: everything below the vocal cords.
Epiglottis: flap that seals the airway during swallowing, directing food/liquid to the esophagus instead of the lungs.
Glottic opening (at the vocal cords) marks the boundary between upper and lower airway.
A patient with depressed LOC may lose the ability to protect their own airway via this mechanism — why airway comes first in patient care.
The tongue is the most common airway obstruction in an unresponsive patient; it is attached to the jaw, so moving the jaw forward moves the tongue forward.
Head-tilt/chin-lift: the default maneuver, no suspected spinal injury. Lift the bony chin, not the soft tissue under it.
Jaw-thrust: the maneuver for suspected spinal injury — opens the airway without moving the neck.
If a jaw-thrust does not open the airway, use the maneuver that does. An open airway outranks spinal precautions.
Pediatric airway: larger tongue, smaller and softer structures, large occiput. Padding under the shoulders keeps an infant's airway in line; over-extension kinks it shut.

sections.title: Airway Adjuncts — OPA and NPA

topics.heading: An adjunct holds the tongue off the back of the throat so your hands do not have to
topics.html:
A manual maneuver works only while you are doing it. The moment you let go to do something else, the jaw falls back and the airway closes again. An airway adjunct is a device that holds the tongue away from the posterior pharynx mechanically, so the airway stays open without a rescuer permanently committed to holding it.

Neither adjunct is a definitive airway. Neither one seals the trachea, and neither protects the lungs from vomit. A patient with an adjunct in place can still aspirate, and you still need suction within reach.

topics.heading: The oropharyngeal airway: no gag reflex, sized from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe
topics.html:
The oropharyngeal airway (OPA) is a rigid curved plastic device that sits in the mouth with its tip in the posterior pharynx. Its one absolute requirement is that the patient has no gag reflex. In a patient who retains a gag, an OPA will provoke gagging and vomiting, and in a patient who cannot protect their airway that vomit goes into the lungs. If the patient tolerates it, the adjunct was appropriate; if the patient gags on it, remove it.

Sizing: measure from the corner of the patient's mouth to the tip of the earlobe, or from the center of the mouth to the angle of the jaw. Both landmarks are taught and both give a workable length. Size matters in both directions: an OPA that is too long can push the epiglottis down over the glottic opening and obstruct the airway you were trying to open, and one that is too short leaves the tongue exactly where it was.

Insertion, adult: open the mouth, insert the airway with the tip pointed toward the roof of the mouth, and as it reaches the back of the mouth rotate it 180 degrees so the curve follows the curve of the tongue. The flange should rest against the lips.

Insertion, pediatric: do not use the rotation technique. A child's palate is soft and the rotation tears it. Insert the airway right side up, following the curve of the tongue, using a tongue depressor to hold the tongue down and out of the way.

topics.heading: The nasopharyngeal airway: tolerated by a patient with a gag, sized nose to earlobe
topics.html:
The nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) is a soft flexible tube that passes through the nostril into the posterior pharynx. Its advantage is the one the OPA lacks: most patients with an intact gag reflex will tolerate it. That makes it the adjunct for the patient whose level of consciousness is depressed but not absent, the semi-conscious patient who keeps losing their airway but gags on anything in their mouth.

Sizing: length is measured from the tip of the nose to the tip of the earlobe. Diameter should be the largest that fits the nostril without blanching it, roughly the diameter of the patient's own little finger.

Insertion: lubricate the tube generously with a water-soluble lubricant. Position the bevel toward the septum, the wall dividing the nostrils, and advance the tube straight back, along the floor of the nasal cavity, not upward. The nasal passage runs backward, not up toward the eyes; advancing upward drives the tube into the roof of the nasal cavity and causes bleeding. If you meet resistance, do not force it. Withdraw and try the other nostril.

The contraindication to know: an NPA is avoided in a patient with signs of a basilar skull fracture or significant mid-face trauma — raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, fluid from the nose or ears. The concern is a tube passing through a fracture at the base of the skull rather than into the pharynx.

takeaways: An adjunct holds the tongue off the posterior pharynx mechanically; a manual maneuver only works while you hold it.
Neither adjunct protects against aspiration. Keep suction within reach.
OPA requires NO gag reflex. If the patient gags, remove it.
OPA sizing: corner of the mouth to the tip of the earlobe, or center of the mouth to the angle of the jaw.
Too long an OPA can push the epiglottis over the glottic opening and obstruct; too short leaves the tongue in place.
OPA insertion, adult: tip toward the roof of the mouth, rotate 180° at the back of the mouth. Flange rests at the lips.
OPA insertion, pediatric: right side up with a tongue depressor. Do NOT rotate — it tears the soft palate.
NPA is tolerated by most patients WITH a gag reflex — the adjunct for a semi-conscious patient.
NPA sizing: tip of the nose to the tip of the earlobe; diameter roughly the patient's little finger.
NPA insertion: lubricate, bevel toward the septum, advance straight back along the floor of the nose — never upward. Resistance means try the other nostril, not more force.
Avoid an NPA with signs of basilar skull fracture or major mid-face trauma (raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, drainage from nose or ears).

sections.title: Suctioning & the Sounds of an Obstructed Airway

topics.heading: Suctioning removes what you can hear; it is a time-limited procedure because it removes oxygen too
topics.html:
Suction clears blood, vomit, and secretions from the airway. The reason it is limited in time is that a suction catheter in the pharynx removes air along with fluid, and for the duration of the procedure the patient is neither breathing nor being ventilated. Suctioning a hypoxic patient makes them more hypoxic before it makes them better, so you pre-oxygenate when you can, suction for a defined interval, and ventilate again.

The limit taught for an adult is no more than about 15 seconds per attempt, and shorter in a child or infant — about 10 seconds or less, with a lower suction pressure. Some texts teach 10 seconds for an adult rather than 15; local protocol governs the number you are held to. The principle behind whichever number your system uses does not vary: suction, then ventilate, then suction again, rather than staying in the airway until it is perfectly clear.

topics.heading: The technique details are the ones that separate suctioning that helps from suctioning that injures
topics.html:
Measure the catheter before you insert it: from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw or earlobe, the same landmark as an OPA. Insert it without suction applied, to the measured depth only, and apply suction while withdrawing in a sweeping motion. Suctioning on the way in pulls the soft tissue of the pharynx into the catheter tip and removes oxygen for the whole insertion rather than the withdrawal. Never insert past the point you can see.

The rigid (Yankauer) catheter is the one for thick secretions and vomit in the mouth of an adult, because its bore is wide enough not to clog. A soft (French) catheter is for the nose, for a stoma, or for going through an adjunct. If vomit is thick enough to clog even a rigid catheter, log-roll the patient onto their side and let gravity do it.

Stimulating the back of the throat can trigger a vagal response and slow the heart rate, which matters most in infants and children. If the heart rate falls during suctioning, stop and ventilate.

topics.heading: Four sounds, four different problems, four different responses
topics.html:
An airway in trouble usually announces itself, and the sound tells you where the problem is and what to do about it. This is high-yield because each sound has a distinct and non-interchangeable response.

Snoring is the tongue against the posterior pharynx — a partially obstructed upper airway in a patient with depressed consciousness. The response is positional: a manual maneuver, then an adjunct. Suction does nothing for it.

Gurgling is fluid in the airway — blood, vomit, or secretions. The response is suction. Repositioning does nothing for it.

Stridor is a high-pitched sound, heard on inspiration, produced by narrowing at or above the level of the larynx: swelling from anaphylaxis or burns, infection, or a foreign body. It is an upper-airway emergency, and it is the sound that should make you think about rapid transport rather than another adjunct, because nothing in an EMT's hands opens a swollen larynx.

Wheezing is a whistling sound from narrowed lower airways, classically on expiration, and it points to bronchoconstriction — asthma, COPD, and also the lower-airway component of anaphylaxis. It is treated pharmacologically, not mechanically.

And the sound that is not a sound: a patient making obvious respiratory effort with no air movement at all has a complete obstruction. Silence with effort is worse than any noise on this list.

takeaways: Suction removes oxygen along with fluid; pre-oxygenate, suction, then ventilate.
Limit a single attempt to about 15 seconds in an adult and about 10 seconds or less in a child or infant, at a lower pressure. Some texts teach 10 seconds for adults; local protocol governs.
Measure the catheter corner-of-mouth to earlobe/angle of jaw; insert to that depth only, never past what you can see.
Insert WITHOUT suction; apply suction while withdrawing, sweeping.
Rigid (Yankauer): thick secretions and vomit in an adult's mouth. Soft (French): nose, stoma, or through an adjunct.
Thick vomit that clogs the catheter: log-roll the patient and let gravity clear it.
Suctioning can trigger a vagal response and bradycardia, especially in children. If the heart rate falls, stop and ventilate.
Snoring = tongue = reposition and place an adjunct.
Gurgling = fluid = suction.
Stridor = upper airway narrowing (inspiratory, high-pitched) = an emergency you transport rather than fix.
Wheezing = lower airway constriction (expiratory) = treated with medication, not with an adjunct.
Respiratory effort with no air movement = complete obstruction. Silence with effort is the worst sign here.

sections.title: Choking — Foreign Body Airway Obstruction

topics.heading: Mild or severe is the only question, and the answer is how much air is moving
topics.html:
A foreign body in the airway produces one of two problems, and telling them apart decides everything that follows. The deciding evidence is air movement, not whether the patient looks distressed.

A mild obstruction leaves enough of the airway open for effective air exchange. The patient can cough forcefully, can speak, and can move air you can hear. Do not intervene. A forceful cough generates more airflow, and more sudden pressure, than any thrust a rescuer can deliver by hand, and the patient is already doing the most effective thing available. Stay with them, encourage the coughing, and watch. Reaching in with thrusts or a finger on a patient who is still clearing the airway themselves can drive the object further in and convert a mild obstruction into a severe one.

A severe obstruction means air exchange has become inadequate. The cough is weak or absent, the patient cannot speak, there is high-pitched stridor or no sound at all, and cyanosis follows. Many patients clutch the throat — the universal choking sign. Note the trap here: a patient with a weak, ineffective cough is still technically coughing, and still counts as severe. The question is never whether something is happening but whether enough air is moving to sustain the patient.

Silence with visible effort is the worst finding in the whole chapter: the patient is trying to breathe and nothing is moving.

topics.heading: The 2025 sequence: five back blows first, at every age
topics.html:
The 2025 AHA guidelines settled on one shape for the maneuver across every age group: five back blows, then five thrusts, repeated. Only the second half changes with age.

AdultChild (1 year to puberty)Infant (under 1 year)
First5 back blows between the shoulder blades, with the heel of the hand
Then5 abdominal thrusts5 abdominal thrusts5 chest thrusts, heel of one hand on the lower sternum
Repeat untilThe object is expelled, or the patient becomes unresponsive
If you cannot reach around the abdomen5 chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts — late pregnancy, or significant obesityAbdominal thrusts are not used at this age at all

For a responsive adult or child, position yourself behind the patient, place a fist thumb-side in just above the navel and below the xiphoid, grasp it with the other hand, and deliver each thrust inward and upward as a distinct movement rather than a squeeze. For an infant, support the head and jaw, lay the infant face down along your forearm with the head lower than the chest for the back blows, then turn the infant as a unit and deliver chest thrusts on the lower sternum.

Abdominal thrusts are never used on an infant. An infant's liver is proportionally large and sits low, largely below the protection of the rib cage, and an abdominal thrust can tear it.

topics.heading: What changed in 2025, and why it changed
topics.html:
Two pieces of this are new, and both are the kind of detail a question is built on.

Back blows were added to the adult and child sequences. An adult used to receive abdominal thrusts alone, and a child the same. A cohort study of 709 people with a foreign body airway obstruction found that back blows relieved more obstructions, and caused fewer injuries, than abdominal thrusts did. The AHA also wanted one sequence a rescuer could remember under stress rather than three, and infants were already receiving back blows first — so the adult and child sequences moved to match, rather than the other way round.

Infant chest thrusts are delivered with the heel of one hand. They used to be delivered with two fingers, the same landmark as infant compressions. Two fingers turned out not to reach a useful depth reliably, and the technique was dropped from infant chest compressions for the same reason. Note the AHA's own care with the words: these are chest thrusts, not chest compressions, because nothing about rate or recoil applies — you are trying to expel an object, not perfuse a brain.

topics.heading: When the patient goes unresponsive, it stops being a choking call
topics.html:
Once the patient loses consciousness, the maneuver changes completely. Lower them to the ground and begin CPR, starting with chest compressions. Compressions generate higher airway pressures than an abdominal thrust does, so they are both the resuscitation and the best remaining attempt at clearing the object.

The one modification is that before each set of rescue breaths you look in the mouth, and remove an object only if you can actually see it. If the chest does not rise on the first breath, reposition the head and try once more before returning to compressions. Do not stop to check for a pulse between cycles the way you would in an ordinary arrest.

Blind finger sweeps are not done, at any age. A finger you cannot see with can push a partially dislodged object back past the vocal cords, and in a child or infant the airway structures are small and soft enough to injure on the way.

topics.heading: After it clears, and the obstructions this does not fix
topics.html:
A patient whose obstruction is relieved still goes to the hospital. Abdominal thrusts can injure the liver, spleen or stomach; a fragment of the object may remain; and aspiration of what did go down shows up hours later as pneumonia. Reassess the airway and breathing, give oxygen if it is indicated, and transport.

Finally, know what this sequence is for. Back blows and thrusts relieve a mechanical obstruction sitting in the airway. They do nothing at all for an airway narrowed by swollen tissue — anaphylaxis, an inhalation burn, epiglottitis, angioedema. Those patients are also stridorous and also in trouble, but nothing in an EMT's hands opens a swollen larynx, and the answer is oxygen, minimal agitation, and rapid transport toward a provider who can secure the airway. Thrusting on them wastes the time they have.

takeaways: Mild vs. severe turns on air exchange, not on distress. Forceful cough and speech = mild = encourage coughing and do nothing else.
A weak or ineffective cough, stridor, inability to speak, or cyanosis = severe, even though the patient is still 'doing something.'
2025 AHA sequence, every age: 5 back blows, then 5 thrusts, repeated until the object clears or the patient goes unresponsive.
Adult and child: the thrusts are abdominal. Infant under 1 year: the thrusts are chest thrusts, with the heel of one hand.
Back blows are new for adults and children — it used to be abdominal thrusts alone. A cohort of 709 patients showed back blows relieved more obstructions with fewer injuries.
Infant chest thrusts use the heel of one hand, not two fingers. Two fingers did not reach adequate depth, and were dropped from infant compressions too.
Abdominal thrusts are not used under 1 year: the infant liver is large, low, and poorly protected.
Cannot get your arms around the abdomen (late pregnancy, significant obesity)? 5 chest thrusts replace the abdominal thrusts.
Patient goes unresponsive: lower them and start CPR with compressions. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths, remove only what you can see.
No blind finger sweeps at any age — they push the object deeper.
Every patient whose obstruction is relieved is still transported: thrust injuries, retained fragments, and later aspiration pneumonia.
Thrusts relieve a foreign body. They do nothing for a swollen airway (anaphylaxis, burns, epiglottitis) — that is oxygen, calm, and rapid transport.

sections.title: Bag-Valve-Mask Ventilation

topics.heading: The bag-valve mask is the skill most often performed badly, and the failure is almost always the seal
topics.html:
A bag-valve mask (BVM) delivers positive-pressure ventilation to a patient who is not breathing adequately on their own. The adult bag holds roughly 1,200 to 1,600 mL. Connected to oxygen at 15 L/min with a reservoir attached, it delivers close to 100 percent oxygen; without oxygen connected it delivers room air, about 21 percent, which is still worth doing while someone sets up the tank.

The device fails in a specific and predictable way. Squeezing the bag is easy; maintaining a seal on the face with one hand while holding the jaw forward with the same hand is hard, and when the seal leaks the volume goes into the room instead of the patient. This is why two-rescuer BVM is preferred whenever a second pair of hands exists: one rescuer uses both hands to hold the mask and the jaw, the other squeezes the bag. It is not a matter of preference or staffing convenience. Two-rescuer technique delivers measurably more volume.

topics.heading: The mechanics: E-C clamp, chest rise, one second, and no faster than the rate calls for
topics.html:
For a single rescuer, the E-C clamp is the hand position: thumb and index finger form a C over the mask pressing it to the face, while the remaining three fingers form an E along the bony ridge of the jaw, lifting the jaw up into the mask rather than pressing the mask down into the face. Lifting the jaw into the mask both seals and opens; pressing the mask down pushes the jaw back and closes the airway.

Position the mask with the narrow end over the bridge of the nose and the wide end in the groove between the lower lip and the chin. Squeeze over about one second, and squeeze only until the chest visibly rises. Visible chest rise is the endpoint, not a full squeeze of the bag.

Rate, for a patient who has a pulse but is not breathing adequately: about 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute) in an adult, and 1 every 2 to 3 seconds (20 to 30 per minute) in an infant or child. During CPR with an advanced airway in place, ventilations run about 10 per minute without pausing compressions. Note that older references teach 10 to 12 per minute for an adult; the current AHA figure is 10.

topics.heading: Too much ventilation is its own injury, and the troubleshooting order is fixed
topics.html:
Ventilating too fast or with too much volume is actively harmful, not merely wasteful. Excess pressure opens the esophagus and forces air into the stomach. Gastric distention pushes the diaphragm up, reducing the volume the lungs can hold, and it makes vomiting and aspiration far more likely. Beyond that, sustained positive pressure in the chest raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces the blood returning to the heart, which lowers cardiac output at the exact moment the patient can least afford it.

When the chest does not rise, work through the causes in this order, because the common ones come first: re-seal the mask (the most common failure by a wide margin), reposition the head and jaw, suction if there is fluid, and check for an obstruction. Squeezing harder is not on the list. If the seal is leaking, more force makes a louder leak.

takeaways: Adult BVM volume is roughly 1,200–1,600 mL; with 15 L/min oxygen and a reservoir it delivers close to 100% oxygen.
Two-rescuer BVM is preferred whenever a second rescuer is available — one holds the mask with both hands, one ventilates. It delivers more volume than one-rescuer technique.
One-rescuer hand position: E-C clamp. Thumb and index finger seal the mask (C); three fingers lift the jaw into the mask (E).
Lift the jaw up into the mask; do not press the mask down into the face.
Mask position: narrow end over the bridge of the nose, wide end between the lower lip and chin.
Squeeze over about one second, and only until the chest visibly rises. Chest rise is the endpoint, not an emptied bag.
Rate with a pulse: adult about 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min); infant or child 1 every 2–3 seconds (20–30/min). Older texts say 10–12/min for adults; current AHA is 10.
With an advanced airway during CPR: about 10 ventilations per minute, without pausing compressions.
Over-ventilation causes gastric distention (raising the diaphragm, inviting vomiting) and raises intrathoracic pressure, reducing venous return and cardiac output.
No chest rise? Re-seal, reposition, suction, check for obstruction — in that order. Squeezing harder is never the fix.

chapters.title: Ventilation & Oxygen Equipment
chapters.intro: Oxygen is a drug, delivered by equipment that has to match the patient's need and be handled with respect for the pressure it holds. This chapter covers the decision that comes first — whether this patient needs oxygen or needs someone to breathe for them — then fits the delivery device to the patient, uses the Venturi mask and the COPD patient as the case that proves more oxygen is not always better, and finishes with the cylinders, regulators, flowmeters, pin-index system and fire hazards that make oxygen equipment safe or dangerous.

sections.title: Oxygen or Ventilation? Making the Call

topics.heading: Oxygen and ventilation solve different problems, and giving the wrong one is a recognizable exam trap
topics.html:
Supplemental oxygen enriches the air a patient is moving. It assumes the patient is moving air. Ventilation — a bag-valve mask — moves air for a patient who is not moving enough of it themselves. A patient breathing 6 times a minute with shallow chest movement does not have an oxygen-concentration problem; they have a volume problem, and a non-rebreather at 15 L/min enriches a tidal volume that is too small to matter. The reverse error is rarer but real: bagging a patient who is breathing adequately and merely hypoxic adds nothing and risks gastric distention.

So the question is not "how sick does this patient look" but "is air actually moving in adequate volume at an adequate rate?" If yes, and the patient is hypoxic, give oxygen. If no, ventilate — and give oxygen through the bag while you do.

topics.heading: The findings that say ventilation, not a mask
topics.html:
Inadequate breathing has a consistent picture, and any of it should push you toward the bag: a rate that is too slow or too fast to move useful volume, chest rise that is shallow or absent, breath sounds that are diminished or absent, cyanosis, altered mental status, an inability to speak more than a word or two at a time, and in a child, the specific signs that the work of breathing has become unsustainable — nasal flaring, retractions between and below the ribs, grunting, and head bobbing.

One pattern deserves naming because it is regularly misread. A patient in severe respiratory distress who suddenly becomes quiet and sleepy is usually not improving. Falling respiratory effort and a falling level of consciousness in a patient who was working hard a minute ago are signs of exhaustion and rising carbon dioxide, and that patient is about to need ventilation rather than reassurance.

When you assist ventilations in a patient who still has some respiratory drive of their own, time your squeezes to the beginning of their own inspiratory effort. Bagging against a patient who is trying to exhale forces air into the stomach and fights the patient rather than helping them.

takeaways: Supplemental oxygen enriches the air a patient moves; ventilation moves air for a patient who cannot move enough of it.
A slow, shallow breather has a volume problem — a non-rebreather enriches a tidal volume too small to help. Ventilate.
Signs pointing to ventilation: rate too slow or too fast, shallow or absent chest rise, diminished breath sounds, cyanosis, altered mental status, one- or two-word sentences.
Pediatric signs of unsustainable work of breathing: nasal flaring, retractions, grunting, head bobbing.
A patient in severe distress who goes quiet and sleepy is tiring, not improving. Rising CO2 and falling effort mean ventilation is next.
When assisting a patient with some drive of their own, time squeezes to the start of their own inspiration — bagging against exhalation inflates the stomach.

sections.title: Delivery Devices, Flow Rates & Targets

topics.heading: Four devices, and the flow rate is part of the device
topics.html:
Each delivery device has a flow range it is designed for, and running it outside that range either fails to work or actively harms. The numbers below are the commonly taught EMT figures; the delivered concentration is always approximate, because it depends on how much room air the patient entrains around the device with each breath.

DeviceFlowApprox. O₂Use it for
Nasal cannula1–6 L/min~24–44%Mild hypoxia; a patient who will not tolerate a mask
Simple face mask6–10 L/min~35–60%Moderate need; less often carried
Non-rebreather mask10–15 L/min~80–90%Significant hypoxia in a patient breathing adequately
Bag-valve mask with reservoir15 L/min~100%Inadequate breathing or apnea — you are moving the air

Two floor values are worth holding onto. A nasal cannula below 1 L/min delivers essentially nothing, and above 6 L/min it dries and irritates the nasal mucosa without meaningfully raising the delivered concentration. A non-rebreather below about 10 L/min cannot keep its reservoir bag inflated, and a non-rebreather whose bag collapses on inspiration is not delivering what the label claims — inflate the reservoir before you put the mask on the patient, and turn the flow up if the bag deflates as they breathe.

topics.heading: Titrate to a target, and know the one population with a lower target
topics.html:
The modern practice is to treat hypoxia rather than to reflexively apply high-flow oxygen to everyone who looks unwell. For most patients the target saturation is roughly 94% or above, and reaching it on a nasal cannula is a better outcome than overshooting it on a non-rebreather. For a patient with known COPD, the commonly taught target is lower, around 88–92%, which is closer to their own chronic baseline.

The important qualifier, repeated because it is the thing candidates get wrong in both directions: a lower target is a reason to titrate, never a reason to withhold. A hypoxic COPD patient gets oxygen. Local protocol sets the actual numbers.

takeaways: Nasal cannula: 1–6 L/min, ~24–44%. Below 1 L/min does nothing; above 6 L/min dries the mucosa without adding much.
Simple face mask: 6–10 L/min, ~35–60%.
Non-rebreather: 10–15 L/min, ~80–90%. Inflate the reservoir before applying; a bag that collapses on inspiration means the flow is too low.
BVM with reservoir at 15 L/min: ~100% — and it is for patients whose own breathing is inadequate.
Delivered concentration is always approximate; it depends on room air entrained around the device.
General target: SpO₂ about 94% or above. Known COPD: about 88–92%. Local protocol governs.
A lower target means titrate, never withhold. A hypoxic COPD patient gets oxygen.

sections.title: Oxygen Delivery & Equipment Safety

topics.heading: Oxygen delivery isn't one-size-fits-all — the device has to match the patient's actual need
topics.html: A Venturi mask is a specific tool for a specific problem. It delivers a precisely controlled percentage of oxygen, rather than the more variable concentration of a standard mask. That precision is useful in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), where the goal is enough oxygen and not more. A small number of COPD patients retain carbon dioxide (CO2) chronically and depend more on low oxygen levels than on rising CO2 as their trigger to breathe, and in those patients a large excess of oxygen can worsen ventilation. That is a reason to titrate, not a reason to withhold. The clinical rule has changed and the exam follows it: a hypoxic COPD patient gets oxygen. Aim for a saturation near the patient's own baseline, commonly the low 90s rather than 100%, and watch mental status and respiratory effort as you go. Leaving a hypoxic patient hypoxic is the larger and more immediate danger, and the old teaching that COPD patients should be denied oxygen out of fear of removing their drive to breathe is no longer taught.

topics.heading: Oxygen equipment has safety features that exist because oxygen systems are genuinely dangerous if mishandled
topics.html: Oxygen systems are genuinely dangerous if they are mishandled, and the safety features of the equipment exist for that reason. The pin-index safety system on oxygen cylinders exists specifically to prevent the wrong regulator from being connected to the wrong gas cylinder, a real hazard given how many medical gases look similar but behave very differently under pressure. Two pieces of equipment are easily confused. The regulator steps the cylinder's very high internal pressure down to a usable level, while the flowmeter is what actually controls and displays how many liters per minute are being delivered to the patient. One small but real hazard is also worth knowing: adhesive tape or petroleum-based products near oxygen equipment pose a genuine fire risk, because oxygen dramatically accelerates combustion.

topics.heading: Cylinder pressure, safe residual, and not running out on the way in
topics.html:
A full portable oxygen cylinder reads roughly 2,000 psi. The number that matters operationally is the safe residual pressure of about 200 psi: at or below that, the cylinder is treated as empty and changed out, because the last of the pressure does not deliver a reliable flow and because a cylinder emptied completely can draw in contaminants. A gauge reading 300 psi at the start of a long transport is a problem to solve at the scene, not in the back of a moving ambulance.

Handling rules follow from the pressure involved. Secure cylinders so they cannot fall — a cylinder whose valve stem snaps off becomes a projectile driven by 2,000 psi. Open the valve fully, then back it off slightly. Keep the cylinder away from heat, and keep oil, grease, and petroleum products away from every fitting.

takeaways: Venturi mask delivers a precisely controlled oxygen percentage, unlike the more variable concentration of a standard mask.
A hypoxic COPD patient still gets oxygen — titrate toward their own baseline (often the low 90s) rather than withholding it. Never deny oxygen to a hypoxic patient.
Pin-index safety system prevents the wrong regulator from connecting to the wrong gas cylinder.
Regulator: steps the cylinder's high internal pressure down to a usable level.
Flowmeter: controls and displays liters per minute delivered to the patient.
Adhesive tape and petroleum-based products near oxygen equipment are a fire risk — oxygen dramatically accelerates combustion.
A full portable cylinder reads about 2,000 psi; safe residual pressure is about 200 psi, at which point it is treated as empty and swapped.
Secure cylinders against falling — a snapped valve stem at 2,000 psi makes the cylinder a projectile. Keep oil and grease away from all fittings.

chapters.title: Scene Size-Up
chapters.intro: Scene size-up begins before the ambulance stops and never really ends. This chapter lays out its four components, the danger-zone distances to keep at a collision, the standard precautions to take before patient contact, how the mechanism of injury or the nature of the illness predicts what you will find, and how to decide early whether the patients on scene exceed the resources you have.

sections.title: Scene Safety, Nature of the Call & Resources

topics.heading: Scene size-up — 4 components
topics.html:
The scene size-up is the first part of patient assessment, but it does not end when you reach the patient. Scenes are dynamic, so the size-up continues throughout the call. It has four components: scene safety, Standard Precautions, the nature of the call (the mechanism of injury (MOI) or the nature of the illness), and the number of patients together with the resources they will need.

Never assume a scene is safe, even when police, fire, or other units are already there. Always do your own size-up. It begins before the ambulance stops, and you keep observing as you approach and again before you exit the vehicle.

topics.heading: Approaching a collision — danger zone distances
topics.html:
When you approach a motor vehicle collision, the hazards present determine how far from the wreck you park. The table below sets out the danger-zone distance for each hazard.

HazardDistance
No apparent hazard≥50 ft (15.2 m) all directions
Fuel spilled≥100 ft (30.4 m); park upwind, uphill if fuel flowing; avoid gutters/ditches; no flares
Vehicle on fire≥100 ft (30.4 m), even if the fire looks small
Wires downPark at least one full span of wire away from poles
HazMatCheck ERG or call CHEMTREC (800-424-9300); park upwind, 50 ft–2000+ ft depending on substance

Violence and crime scenes are a hazard of a different kind. Never enter a violent scene to provide care. The warning signs are fighting or loud voices, weapons that are visible or have been used, signs of alcohol or drug use, an unusual silence, and a known history of prior violence at that address.

topics.heading: Standard Precautions (BSI)
topics.html:
Standard Precautions, also called body substance isolation (BSI), are the measures you take to keep a patient's body substances from reaching you. Body substances include blood, saliva, and all other body fluids, and they enter the body through cuts and other openings in the skin or through the eyes, nose, and mouth. The high-risk situations are bleeding, coughing, sneezing, and direct contact such as mouth-to-mouth. The infection risk runs both ways: the patient can infect you, and you can infect the patient.

The protection you choose depends on the situation. Gloves and eyewear are appropriate for trauma with suspected bleeding. A mask and eyewear are added when you are suctioning or the patient is spitting blood. An N-95 or HEPA respirator is worn when tuberculosis (TB) or another airborne disease is suspected.

topics.heading: Nature of the call — mechanism of injury
topics.html:
The mechanism of injury (MOI) is the force or forces that caused an injury. Certain mechanisms are commonly associated with certain injuries: falls and collisions with bone and joint injury, fire and explosion with burns, and gunshots with penetrating soft-tissue injury. Knowing the mechanism therefore tells you what to look for before you have found it.

Maintaining a high index of suspicion means staying aware of possible injury even when there are no obvious signs of it. Never assume there is no injury just because the mechanism seems minor.

topics.heading: Motor vehicle collisions
topics.html:
Every motor vehicle collision (MVC) is really 3 collisions: (1) the vehicle hits an object, (2) the occupant's body hits the interior of the vehicle, and (3) the organs hit the inside of the body. Airbags deploy once only. The powder they release is nontoxic and should not be mistaken for smoke, but the bags themselves can cause abrasions and fractures, and they can turn loose objects into projectiles.

The type of collision predicts the pattern of injury, as the table below shows.

Collision typeInjury pattern
Head-onUp-and-over: head/windshield → head, neck, chest, abdomen. Down-and-under: knees/dash → knee, leg, hip
Rear-endNeck/head injury — head stays still, body pushed forward; whiplash if headrest misplaced
Side-impact (T-bone)Neck injury (head stays still, body pushed laterally); direct injury to head, chest, abdomen, pelvis, thighs
RolloverMost serious — multiple impacts, ejection risk if unbelted, any injury pattern possible
Rotational impactStruck vehicle spins → subsequent impacts, multiple injury patterns

topics.heading: Falls & penetrating/blunt trauma
topics.html:
In a fall, consider the height, the surface struck, the part of the body that hit it, and anything that interrupted the fall. The national field triage guideline sets the adult threshold at more than 10 feet (3 m), and for a child under 15 years old at more than 10 feet (3 m) or 2–3 times the child's height. The adult figure used to be taught as 20 feet, or three times the patient's height, and it came down because injuries were being missed below it. In an older adult there is no useful height at all: a ground-level fall, particularly onto a hip or while on anticoagulants, is a significant mechanism on its own. A patient who has fallen that far should go to a trauma center.

Penetrating trauma is classified by the velocity of the object. Low-velocity wounds, such as those from knives, are localized, although the blade may have moved inside the body. Medium-velocity wounds come from handguns and shotguns. Arrows, like knives, are low-velocity. High-velocity wounds, from rifles, can cause damage almost anywhere. A bullet injures in two ways: along its direct path, and by cavitation, in which the pressure wave creates a temporary cavity larger than the bullet itself.

In blunt-force trauma the energy travels through the body, so organs can rupture or hemorrhage while the external signs stay subtle. The MOI is your main clue that something serious has happened inside.

topics.heading: Number of patients & resources
topics.html: Actively scan the scene for additional patients, such as passengers and pedestrians. If there are more patients than you can handle, call for more ambulances immediately rather than waiting to see how things develop. Call for extra help early: once you are involved in patient care it is easy to forget, and by then it may be too late for help to arrive in time.

takeaways: Blunt-force trauma – injury from a blow that doesn't penetrate skin/tissue.
Danger zone – the area around wreckage requiring special safety precautions.
Index of suspicion – awareness that injuries may be present.
Mechanism of injury (MOI) – force(s) that may have caused injury.
Nature of the illness – what is medically wrong with the patient.
Penetrating trauma – injury from an object passing through skin/tissue.
Scene size-up = safety check, Standard Precautions, MOI/nature of illness, patient count, resource needs.

chapters.title: Primary Assessment
chapters.intro: The primary assessment exists to find and fix whatever will kill the patient in the next few minutes. This chapter sets out its six parts in order: forming a general impression, judging mental status on the AVPU scale, checking airway, breathing and circulation, and deciding transport priority. Everything else in patient assessment waits until this is done.

sections.title: General Impression, Mental Status & ABCs

topics.heading: Primary assessment — 6 parts
topics.html:
The primary assessment, also called the initial assessment, is the first part of patient assessment. Its focus is exclusively on threats to life: the airway, breathing, and circulation. In one sentence, its purpose is to quickly and efficiently identify and treat any threats to the patient's life. The primary assessment has 6 parts, performed in this order:

  1. Form a general impression.
  2. Assess mental status, with manual stabilization of the spine if it is indicated.
  3. Assess the airway.
  4. Assess breathing.
  5. Assess circulation.
  6. Determine the patient's priority.

A-B-C is a guide to interventions, not a mandatory sequence. Do what the patient needs most, in whatever order that requires. C-A-B, with compressions first, is used for a patient who appears lifeless or pulseless; A-B-C is used for a patient who shows signs of life. When several EMTs are present, they can handle several priorities at the same time.

topics.heading: Priority order of concerns
topics.html: Within the primary assessment, some problems must be dealt with before others. The first concern is exsanguinating (severe) bleeding, which must be controlled immediately. The second is vomit or other material in the airway that the patient could aspirate; suction it before you ventilate. The third is a patient who is not breathing or who has only agonal breathing; check the pulse and begin CPR if it is needed. If there is no immediate threat to life, administer oxygen as appropriate and evaluate the patient for shock.

topics.heading: Spinal motion restriction (SMR)
topics.html:
Spinal motion restriction (SMR) restricts movement of the head, neck, and spine whenever a spinal injury is possible or likely, judged from the mechanism of injury (MOI), the history, and the signs and symptoms. Apply it on first contact with the patient and continue it until the physical examination rules a spinal injury out. Manual stabilization means holding the head still in a neutral, in-line position, facing forward; do not pull or twist it.

SMR is not the highest priority when it interferes with the airway, ventilation, or bleeding control. If you are alone, some spinal movement may be necessary to ventilate the patient effectively. With a responsive patient, an alternative is to instruct the patient not to move and to keep the nose in line with the umbilicus.

topics.heading: Forming a general impression
topics.html:
The general impression is formed from the environment, the chief complaint, and the patient's appearance. The chief complaint is the reason EMS was called, usually in the patient's own words, and it may differ from the actual problem; jaw pain, for example, can be a myocardial infarction (MI). The table below lists the signs that shape the general impression and what each one means.

SignSignificance
Lifeless appearanceNo movement/breathing or gasping → begin CPR/defib prep if pulseless
Altered mental statusImpact on the patient matters, not the cause; assess more aggressively
Anxious, pale, sweatyPossible shock — look for rapid pulse/resp rate
Obvious trauma to head/chest/abdomen/pelvisHigh risk of airway compromise, shock, death
Tripod positionSevere difficulty breathing
Levine's sign (fist clenched on chest)Severe chest pain/discomfort

The absence of these red-flag signs does not guarantee that the patient is stable.

topics.heading: Assess mental status — AVPU
topics.html:
Mental status is assessed with the AVPU scale, which the table below sets out.

LevelResponse
AlertAwake, talks/answers sensibly
VerbalResponds to verbal stimuli only
PainfulResponds only to painful stimuli (pinch toe/ear, trapezius squeeze)
UnresponsiveNo response even to pain

If the patient is alert, check orientation to person, then place, then time. A depressed mental status may indicate hypoxia or shock, so administer oxygen (O2) and treat the patient as a high transport priority.

topics.heading: Assess airway, breathing & circulation
topics.html:
A patient who is alert and talking or crying clearly has an open airway. A patient who is not alert, or whose breathing is noisy, has a compromised airway. Open it with a jaw-thrust or a head-tilt/chin-lift, suction as needed, and insert an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway.

Breathing problems range from the most severe to the least. A patient in respiratory arrest who still has a pulse needs rescue breathing. A patient who is not alert and is breathing inadequately needs positive pressure ventilation with O2. A patient with some alertness but inadequate breathing needs assisted ventilations with 100% O2. A patient who is breathing adequately but shows signs of distress or hypoxia receives O2 based on the pulse oximetry reading, the examination, and the complaint.

Circulation is assessed through the pulse, the skin, and any bleeding. In a light-skinned patient, check the pulse and the skin color at the wrist; in a dark-skinned patient, check the lips and nail beds. The pulse check during the primary assessment needs only 3 outcomes: normal, unusually slow, or unusually fast. Control severe bleeding immediately, because it can kill in 1–2 minutes.

topics.heading: Determine priority
topics.html:
The last step of the primary assessment is to determine the patient's priority. Patients fall into one of three categories, described in the table below.

CategoryCriteria
StableVitals normal or only slightly/explainably abnormal; no threat to ABCs
Potentially unstableNo immediate life threat, but could deteriorate; don't delay transport
UnstableActual/imminent threat to ABCs

Priority can change during the call. An unresponsive patient is automatically a high priority. The high-priority conditions are a poor general impression, unresponsiveness, failure to follow commands, difficulty breathing, shock, complicated childbirth, cardiac-type chest pain, uncontrolled bleeding, and severe pain anywhere.

Capillary refill is checked by pressing the nail (or the back of the hand or foot in an infant); the color should return to pink in less than 2 seconds. Prolonged or absent refill indicates a circulation problem, although the test is less reliable in the elderly and in cold environments. An infant's airway is kept in a neutral position, not tilted back like an adult's.

takeaways: A-B-Cs – airway, breathing, circulation. AVPU – alert, verbal, painful, unresponsive.
Chief complaint – reason EMS was called, patient's own words.
General impression – first impression based on environment, chief complaint, appearance.
Manual stabilization – hands used to prevent head/neck movement until a collar is applied.
Primary assessment – find/treat life threats first (6 parts).
Priority – decision on immediate transport vs. further on-scene care.
Spinal motion restriction – limiting head/neck/spine movement when injury is possible.

chapters.title: Vital Signs and Monitoring Devices
chapters.intro: Vital signs turn an impression into numbers you can trend over time. This chapter covers the core set of pulse, respirations, skin, pupils and blood pressure, what counts as normal and how to take each one without introducing the errors that make the number wrong, the methods for measuring blood pressure and what a palpable pulse implies about it, and the monitoring devices — pulse oximetry, capnography and blood glucose — that add information but never replace what you see in the patient.

sections.title: Taking the Core Vitals

topics.heading: Normal adult ranges are the baseline every other number is read against
topics.html:
A vital sign means nothing until you know what it is being compared to. These are the adult figures.

SignNormal adultWorth noting
Pulse60–100/minBelow 60 is bradycardia, above 100 tachycardia — both normal in some people and ominous in others
Respirations12–20/minBelow 12 or above 20 in a sick adult is a finding, not a variation
Blood pressureabout 120/80Systolic below 90 in an adult is the commonly used marker of hypotension
SpO₂94–99%Interpreted with the patient's work of breathing, never alone
Temperatureabout 98.6 °F / 37 °C

Pediatric ranges differ by age and are covered in depth in the reference cards. The single most important difference is directional: children compensate well and then fail suddenly, and bradycardia in a child is usually a late sign of hypoxia rather than a heart problem.

topics.heading: Pulse: rate, rhythm, and strength — and the site depends on the patient
topics.html:
Take the pulse at the radial artery in a responsive adult or child, the carotid in an unresponsive adult or child, and the brachial in an infant, whose neck is too short to find a carotid reliably. Count for 30 seconds and double it; count a full 60 seconds if the rhythm is irregular, because doubling half of an irregular rhythm doubles the error with it.

Report three things, not one. Rate is the number. Rhythm is regular or irregular. Strength is strong, weak, or thready — and a weak thready pulse at a normal rate is a more worrying finding than a strong pulse at 110.

topics.heading: Respirations: count them without telling the patient you are counting
topics.html:
Breathing is the one vital sign under voluntary control, and a patient who knows you are counting their breaths will change them. The standard approach is to keep your fingers on the radial pulse after you have finished counting it and count respirations while the patient believes you are still on the pulse.

As with the pulse, the number is not the whole finding. Note depth (normal or shallow), effort (easy, labored, accessory muscle use, retractions), and any sounds — the wheezing, stridor, snoring and gurgling covered in the airway chapter. A rate of 20 that is shallow and labored is a sicker patient than a rate of 24 that is deep and easy.

topics.heading: Skin and pupils are the two vitals you assess by looking
topics.html:
Skin has three components. Color: pink is normal; pale suggests poor perfusion or blood loss; cyanotic (blue-gray) means poor oxygenation; flushed suggests heat exposure or certain poisonings; jaundiced (yellow) points to liver problems; mottled, a blotchy pattern, is a sign of poor perfusion seen particularly in children. In patients with darker skin, check the color of the nail beds, the inside of the lips, and the conjunctiva rather than the face. Temperature and condition: cool and clammy is the classic shock picture; hot and dry suggests heat stroke.

Capillary refill, measured by pressing a nail bed and releasing, should return within 2 seconds. It is a reliable perfusion indicator in children and less reliable in adults, where cold ambient temperature confounds it.

Pupils are remembered as PEARRL: Pupils Equal And Round, Regular in size, react to Light. Unequal pupils suggest a head injury or stroke; pinpoint pupils suggest opioids; widely dilated pupils suggest stimulants, hypoxia, or a drop in blood flow to the brain; pupils that are fixed and do not react at all are a serious neurological finding.

topics.heading: Trend the numbers, because one set of vitals is a snapshot and two sets are information
topics.html: A single set of vital signs tells you where the patient is. Two sets tell you where they are going, which is the part that changes decisions. Reassess every 5 minutes for an unstable patient and every 15 minutes for a stable one, and document each set with a time, because a pressure that fell from 130 to 100 over ten minutes is a different patient from one who has been 100 all along.

takeaways: Adult normals: pulse 60–100, respirations 12–20, BP about 120/80, SpO₂ 94–99%, temperature about 98.6 °F.
Adult systolic below 90 mmHg is the commonly used marker of hypotension.
Pulse site: radial (responsive adult/child), carotid (unresponsive adult/child), brachial (infant).
Count the pulse 30 seconds and double it — but a full 60 seconds if it is irregular.
Report pulse as rate, rhythm, and strength. A weak thready pulse at a normal rate is worse than a strong fast one.
Count respirations without the patient knowing — keep your fingers on the wrist after taking the pulse.
Respirations: note depth, effort, and sounds as well as rate.
Skin color: pale (poor perfusion/blood loss), cyanotic (poor oxygenation), flushed (heat/poisoning), jaundiced (liver), mottled (poor perfusion, especially children).
In darker-skinned patients assess color at the nail beds, inside of the lips, and conjunctiva.
Capillary refill should return within 2 seconds; most reliable in children, confounded by cold in adults.
PEARRL: Pupils Equal And Round, Regular in size, react to Light. Unequal = head injury or stroke; pinpoint = opioids; dilated = stimulants or hypoxia.
Bradycardia in a child is usually a late sign of hypoxia, not a primary heart problem.
Reassess vitals every 5 minutes if unstable, every 15 minutes if stable. Time-stamp every set — the trend is the information.

sections.title: Blood Pressure, Pulse Oximetry & Glucose

topics.heading: Core vitals & rapid pulse-based BP estimate
topics.html:
The core vital signs are the pulse, respirations, the skin (its color, temperature, and condition), the pupils, and blood pressure (BP). Before a cuff is on the patient, the pulses you can feel give a rough estimate of the systolic blood pressure. A palpable radial pulse implies a systolic pressure of at least roughly 80–90 mmHg. If the radial pulse is absent but the femoral pulse is palpable, the systolic pressure is at least roughly 70 mmHg. If only the carotid pulse can be felt, with the femoral and radial both absent, the systolic pressure is at least roughly 60 mmHg.

This is a rough field-triage estimate, not a substitute for an actual blood pressure reading.

topics.heading: Blood pressure methods & pulse oximetry
topics.html:
Blood pressure can be measured in three ways. By auscultation, you listen with a stethoscope for the Korotkoff sounds: the first sound you hear marks the systolic pressure, and the point at which the sound disappears marks the diastolic. By palpation, you feel for the return of the pulse as the cuff deflates; this gives the systolic pressure only. The third method is an automatic blood pressure monitor.

Pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin that is saturated with oxygen (O2). It cannot tell you how the patient is breathing, only how saturated the blood is. A patient in obvious respiratory distress, with accessory muscle use and cyanosis, can still show 98% on the pulse oximeter, so the number never overrides what you see clinically. The reading is also unreliable with poor perfusion or shock, nail polish, cold extremities, and carbon monoxide poisoning, which produces a falsely high reading.

topics.heading: The technique errors that make a blood pressure reading wrong
topics.html:
A blood pressure is only as good as how it was taken, and the errors are systematic rather than random, which means they mislead in a predictable direction.

Cuff size is the most common. The bladder should cover roughly 80 percent of the circumference of the upper arm and about two-thirds of its length. A cuff that is too small reads falsely high; a cuff that is too large reads falsely low. This is why an adult cuff on a child's arm produces a reassuring number in a child who is not reassuring.

Arm position: the arm should be supported at the level of the heart. An arm held below heart level reads high; above, low. Deflation rate: about 2 mmHg per second. Deflating quickly skips past the true systolic and diastolic points and reads low and narrow.

Where not to take it: avoid an injured extremity, an arm with a dialysis fistula, an arm on the side of a previous mastectomy, and an arm with an IV running. Use the other arm.

topics.heading: Monitoring devices: glucose, and what capnography adds that pulse oximetry cannot
topics.html:
A blood glucose reading is useful only if you know the normal range and interpret the result together with the patient's mental status and history, never in isolation. A normal fasting value runs roughly 70–99 mg/dL, and a value below 70 mg/dL is the commonly used threshold for hypoglycemia. A patient with an altered mental status and no obvious cause has earned a glucose check.

Capnography measures exhaled carbon dioxide, normally about 35–45 mmHg, and it answers a question pulse oximetry cannot: whether the patient is ventilating, not merely whether their blood is saturated. That distinction matters most in exactly the situation where oximetry is most reassuring and most wrong — a patient on high-flow oxygen whose saturation stays high for minutes after their ventilation has become inadequate. Capnography also drops immediately when air stops moving, which is why it detects a displaced airway or a fall in perfusion faster than a saturation reading does.

The same caution applies to every device on this list: vitals and monitors refine a picture built from the patient in front of you, and they never replace it. Circulation in children in particular is assessed with different pulse points and a heavier reliance on capillary refill.

takeaways: Palpable radial ≈ systolic at least 80–90 mmHg; femoral only ≈ at least 70; carotid only ≈ at least 60. A field estimate, not a reading.
Auscultation: first Korotkoff sound = systolic, disappearance = diastolic. Palpation gives systolic only.
Pulse oximetry reports saturation, not ventilation. A distressed cyanotic patient can read 98%.
Oximetry is unreliable with poor perfusion, shock, nail polish, and cold extremities; carbon monoxide poisoning makes it read falsely HIGH.
Cuff too small reads falsely high; cuff too large reads falsely low. An adult cuff on a child gives a falsely reassuring number.
Support the arm at heart level; deflate at about 2 mmHg per second. Deflating too fast reads low.
Do not take a BP on an injured limb, a dialysis fistula arm, a post-mastectomy arm, or an arm with an IV.
Normal fasting glucose is roughly 70–99 mg/dL; below 70 mg/dL is the usual hypoglycemia threshold.
Altered mental status with no obvious cause earns a glucose check.
Capnography (normal 35–45 mmHg) measures ventilation, which oximetry cannot — and it falls immediately when air stops moving.
Monitors refine the assessment; they never replace looking at the patient.

chapters.title: Principles of Assessment
chapters.intro: History taking and the physical examination are skills with a structure, and the structure is what keeps you from missing things. This chapter presents the OPQRST and SAMPLE frameworks, the three examination techniques of observing, auscultating and palpating, how to choose a body-system exam from the chief complaint, and the mental shortcuts that speed clinical decisions and the ways they mislead.

sections.title: History Taking & the Physical Exam

topics.heading: History taking
topics.html:
The patient history has 2 components: the history of present illness (HPI) and the past medical history (PMH). If the patient cannot communicate, gather the history from family members, bystanders, and the medications and medical devices found at the scene. Building rapport makes the history better: get down to the patient's level, show empathy, and listen carefully so that you do not re-ask questions the patient has already answered.

Open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with a simple yes or no, are the default because they draw out more detailed information. Closed-ended questions, which can be answered yes or no, are reserved for serious or urgent situations that need fast answers. Diagnosis is not always definitive; sometimes the goal is simply to establish what this patient needs rather than exactly what is wrong.

topics.heading: OPQRST & SAMPLE
topics.html:
Two mnemonics organize the history. OPQRST guides your questions about the present complaint; the table below gives the meaning of each letter with a sample question.

LetterMeaningSample question
OOnsetWhat were you doing when it began?
PProvocationWhat triggers it? What relieves it?
QQualityDescribe the pain/problem
RRegion/RadiationWhere? Does it spread?
SSeverityScale 0–10
TTimeWhen did it start? Sudden or gradual? Changed since onset?

SAMPLE covers the rest of the patient's history, as the second table shows.

LetterMeaning
SSigns and symptoms
AAllergies
MMedications (Rx, OTC, recreational, supplements, birth control)
PPertinent past history
LLast oral intake
EEvents leading to injury/illness

The medications a patient takes can reveal conditions the patient has not disclosed; a patient who denies diabetes but takes insulin is one example. A good history question tends to yield 2 more good questions.

When taking a history from a child, use simple language, include the parents or caregivers, and remember that children may feel that illness is a "punishment."

topics.heading: Physical examination — 3 techniques
topics.html:
The physical examination uses 3 techniques, which the table below describes.

TechniqueDescription
ObserveLook for overall condition; compare injured vs. uninjured side
AuscultateListen (usually via stethoscope) for abnormal sounds
PalpateFeel for deformities/abnormalities

When examining an alert infant or small child, reverse the usual order and work from toe to head. Explain each step, examine the child on the parent's lap if possible, never lie about whether something will hurt, and protect the child's modesty.

topics.heading: Body system exams (choose by chief complaint)
topics.html:
Which body system you examine in detail is chosen by the chief complaint.

For a respiratory complaint, always assess first whether breathing is adequate. Then observe the motion of the chest wall, auscultate the lung sounds (wheezes indicate narrowing of the airways; rhonchi and rales indicate fluid), obtain a pulse oximetry reading, and look for edema.

The cardiovascular exam covers the skin color, temperature, and condition, the mental status, the pulse, and the blood pressure (BP), which is taken in both arms because a difference of more than 20 mmHg may indicate an aortic aneurysm. Look for jugular vein distention (JVD) and palpate the chest for tenderness.

The nervous system exam includes a stroke scale, peripheral sensation and movement (unequal findings suggest a possible spinal injury), palpation of the spine, grip and foot strength, the pupils, and the gait.

The endocrine exam looks at the mental status and the skin, since cool, moist skin suggests possible hypoglycemia. Measure the blood glucose, check for an insulin pump, and look for medical identification (ID) jewelry.

In the gastrointestinal exam, observe the patient's position, such as a fetal position or guarding. Inspect the abdomen, auscultate for bowel sounds before you palpate, and then palpate the quadrants, leaving the painful area for last.

For a suspected allergic reaction, the immune system exam inspects the point of contact, the skin for rash or hives, and the face, lips, and mouth for swelling. Listen to the patient's voice and auscultate the lungs for wheezing.

The musculoskeletal exam is mostly trauma-related. Inspect for deformity, swelling, and bruising; palpate gently for crepitation; compare the two sides for symmetry; and palpate from head to toe for multiple injuries.

topics.heading: Critical thinking & decision making
