topics.html: EMTs do diagnose; cardiac arrest is a diagnosis. The diagnoses are often general, however, such as "abdominal pain of unknown cause." A field diagnosis, also called a presumptive or working diagnosis, is based on the history, the physical exam, and the vital signs, and the differential diagnosis is the list of possible conditions that could explain the findings. Compared with traditional medicine or emergency medicine, diagnosis in EMS is urgent, focused, and limited in scope: the goal is to rule out life threats, treat according to protocol, and transport. Red flags are signs or symptoms that suggest a serious underlying condition; tearing abdominal pain that radiates to the back, for example, suggests an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).

topics.heading: Diagnostic heuristics & their pitfalls
topics.html:
Clinicians rely on mental shortcuts, or heuristics, to reach a diagnosis quickly, and each one carries a characteristic pitfall. The table below defines the common heuristics and the error each can produce.

HeuristicDefinitionPitfall
RepresentativenessMatch signs/symptoms to a known patternAtypical presentations get missed
AvailabilityRecency bias — a recently-seen condition seems more likelyOverestimating rare-condition frequency
OverconfidenceExcess trust in own knowledgeMissed errors/limitations
Confirmation biasSeeking only supporting evidenceIgnoring contradicting data
Illusory correlationAssuming causation from coincidental associationFalse cause-effect
Anchoring & adjustmentSticking to the initial hypothesis despite new infoMissing an evolving diagnosis
Search satisfyingStopping the search once "an answer" is foundMissing secondary diagnoses

Thinking like an expert means accepting ambiguity as inherent to EMS, knowing the limits of both people and technology, building strong foundational knowledge, learning the conditions that mimic one another, not letting the search for a diagnosis delay needed treatment, and knowing the limits of your own competency.

takeaways: Chief complaint – symptom/concern described by the patient.
Closed-ended question – answerable with yes/no; open-ended question – requires more than yes/no.
Crepitation – grating of broken bone ends.
Diagnosis – a label for the patient's condition guiding care; differential diagnosis – list of potential diagnoses.
HPI – history of present illness; PMH – past medical history.
JVD – jugular vein distention.
OPQRST – onset, provocation, quality, region/radiation, severity, time.
SAMPLE – signs/symptoms, allergies, medications, pertinent history, last oral intake, events.

chapters.title: Secondary Assessment
chapters.intro: Once the primary assessment has found no immediate threat to life, the secondary assessment looks for everything else. Its three components are the same for every patient, but their order changes with the situation. This chapter separates the responsive medical patient from the unresponsive one and the minor trauma patient from the seriously injured, then covers the rapid trauma assessment, the detailed exam and cervical collars.

sections.title: Medical vs. Trauma Patients & Cervical Collars

topics.heading: 3 components, order varies by patient type
topics.html:
The secondary assessment has 3 components: the history, the physical exam, and baseline vital signs. It follows the scene size-up and the primary assessment. For a medical patient the history carries most of the weight; for a trauma patient the physical exam does. With a critical patient the secondary assessment is often done en route, while with a stable patient it is fine to do it on scene. Patients are approached as one of 3 types: medical, trauma, or unknown nature.

The assessment gathers signs and symptoms, and the distinction between them matters. A sign is something you can observe, such as a deformity or edema. A symptom is something the patient reports, such as pain or shortness of breath (SOB).

topics.heading: Medical patient — responsive vs. unresponsive
topics.html:
The order of the secondary assessment for a medical patient depends on whether the patient is responsive, as the table below shows.

ResponsiveUnresponsive
OrderHistory (OPQRST + SAMPLE) → focused exam → vitalsRapid head-to-toe exam → vitals → history from bystanders
PriorityVariesAutomatically high priority

In the unresponsive patient, always check the pupils, which are the finding most often forgotten when the eyes are closed, and look for medical identification (ID) jewelry or a medical tattoo. Ask bystanders for the patient's name, what happened, any prior complaints, known illnesses, and medications; say "medications," not "drugs."

topics.heading: Trauma patient — minor vs. serious injury
topics.html:
For a trauma patient with a minor injury who is a low priority, take the history, perform a focused physical exam, obtain vital signs, and then gather the past medical history (PMH). The findings you look for in the exam are summarized by the mnemonic DCAP-BTLS: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures or penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, and Swelling.

For a patient with serious or multisystem trauma who is a high priority, continue manual stabilization of the spine, consider calling for advanced life support (ALS), perform a rapid trauma assessment covering the whole body from head to toe, obtain vital signs, and, if the patient is unresponsive, take a brief history from bystanders.

A significant mechanism of injury (MOI) puts a patient in the serious category. A significant fall is more than 10 feet (3 m) for an adult under the current national field triage guideline — it was taught as 20 feet for years — and, for a child under 15 years old, more than 10 feet (3 m) or 2–3 times the child's height. In an older adult, any fall can qualify. A high-risk crash is one with intrusion of more than 12 inches at the occupant's site or more than 18 inches at any site, ejection, a death in the same passenger compartment, a pedestrian or cyclist thrown, run over, or struck with significant impact, or a rider separated from a motorcycle or similar vehicle with significant impact.

topics.heading: Rapid trauma assessment (head-to-toe)
topics.html:
The rapid trauma assessment moves from head to toe. At each area you look and feel for wounds, tenderness, and deformities (WTD), plus the specific findings for that area listed in the table below.

AreaAssess (plus)
HeadWounds/tenderness/deformities, crepitation, ear drainage, skull depression, Battle's sign, pupils, mouth
NeckWTD, JVD, crepitation, stoma/tracheostomy, medical ID
ChestWTD, paradoxical motion, crepitation, subcutaneous emphysema, breath sounds present/equal
AbdomenWTD, firmness/distention, colostomy bags (leave in place), pulsating mass = don't press further
PelvisWTD, priapism; stop palpating once pain is reported
ExtremitiesWTD, distal circulation/sensation/motor function
PosteriorLog-roll to assess spine/buttocks — good time to slide in a backboard

topics.heading: Detailed physical exam & cervical collars
topics.html:
The detailed physical exam is done after the critical interventions and the rapid trauma assessment. It is the lowest priority of the assessment steps and is usually performed en route. It is most appropriate for the unresponsive trauma patient, the patient with a significant injury, or the patient with an unknown MOI.

A cervical collar must be rigid and correctly sized; soft collars have no role in prehospital care. The size is determined by the length of the neck, not its width. A collar of the wrong size can obstruct the airway, and you must never compromise the airway for the sake of a collar. Assess the neck before you apply the collar, because once it is on you can no longer inspect or palpate the back of the neck.

topics.heading: Pediatric exam notes
topics.html:
A child's anatomy changes what the examination shows. Never press on the fontanelles. A fontanelle that bulges while the infant is crying is normal, but one that bulges when the infant is not crying suggests meningitis or increased intracranial pressure (ICP), and a sunken fontanelle suggests dehydration. Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears should make you suspect a skull fracture. Because children are nose-breathers, an obstruction of the nose is more dangerous for them than for an adult.

The child's head is proportionally heavier and the neck supports it less well, so the cervical spine is highly vulnerable to injury, and because the bones are incompletely calcified there may be no visible fracture even when the spinal cord has been injured. The ribs are soft and may not fracture despite significant injury inside the chest. The abdominal organs are proportionally larger and less protected, and children 8 years old and younger are abdominal breathers.

In the extremities, capillary refill is checked by squeezing rather than by pressing the nail bed. The bones are pliable and will bend, buckle, or splinter before they fracture.

takeaways: Detailed physical exam – head-to-toe exam adding face/ears/eyes/nose/mouth vs. the rapid assessment.
Distention – stretched/larger than normal. HPI – history of present illness.
Paradoxical motion – a chest segment moving opposite to the rest of the chest.
PMH – past medical history. Priapism – persistent erection (spinal/medical cause).
Rapid trauma assessment – a quick head-to-toe exam for wounds/tenderness/deformities.
Sign – observable evidence; symptom – patient-reported finding.
Stoma – a permanent neck breathing opening; tracheostomy – a surgical airway incision with a tube.

chapters.title: Reassessment
chapters.intro: A patient's condition is a moving target, and reassessment is how you keep watching it. This chapter covers the four components to repeat, how often to repeat them for stable and unstable patients, and how trending vital signs over time reveals a change that any single set would hide.

sections.title: Trending, Intervals & FIRR

topics.heading: Reassessment — 4 components
topics.html:
Reassessment is the last step of patient assessment, and it is the step that turns a single snapshot of the patient into a picture of where the patient is heading. It is built from four components, repeated in order:

  1. Repeat the primary assessment. Recheck mental status, airway patency, the rate and quality of breathing, the rate and quality of the pulse, and the color and temperature of the skin.
  2. Reestablish the patient's priority. A patient who was stable may no longer be, and a patient who was unstable may have improved.
  3. Reassess and record the vital signs, and compare them with the baseline set and with every set taken since.
  4. Repeat the pertinent parts of the history and physical exam, and check every intervention you have made: oxygen (O2) delivery, bleeding control, the cervical collar (C-collar), and any splints.

Reassessment must never be skipped. The one exception is the patient whose lifesaving interventions leave you no hands free to perform it, and in that case your partner performs the reassessment instead.

topics.heading: Reassessment intervals
topics.html:
How often you reassess depends on how sick the patient is. The table below gives the interval for each category of patient.

Patient statusInterval
StableEvery 15 min
Unstable/potentially unstableEvery 5 min

A stable patient is reassessed every 15 minutes, and an unstable or potentially unstable patient every 5 minutes. These intervals are a minimum, not a schedule to wait for. If you suspect any change in the patient's condition, repeat at least the primary assessment immediately rather than waiting for the next scheduled interval.

topics.heading: Trending & FIRR
topics.html:
Trending is the tracking of changes in the patient's condition over time. A single set of vital signs tells you where the patient is at one moment; a series of sets tells you which way the patient is moving. A pulse that rises while the blood pressure (BP) falls, for example, points to a deteriorating patient in shock in a way that neither number would on its own. Because of this, trending is more clinically valuable than any single set of vital signs.

The management of a patient after the assessment can be summarized by the four steps of FIRR: field impression, interventions, reassessments and report. The table below sets out what each step contains.

StepContent
Field ImpressionYour working impression (not a diagnosis) — affected body system + probable cause
InterventionsMeds beyond O2 require medical control permission; document time given
ReassessmentsPer interval above; compare to baseline; document time of each
ReportHandoff to next provider (ED nurse/doctor)

Your field impression is a working impression, not a diagnosis: it names the body system affected and the probable cause. Interventions follow from it, and any medication beyond oxygen requires authorization from medical control, through standing orders or a direct order per local protocol; document the time each intervention is given. Reassessments are carried out at the interval that matches the patient's status, compared against the baseline, and documented with the time of each. The final step is the report, the handoff to the next provider, usually the emergency department (ED) nurse or physician.

The handoff report follows a set order. You give the patient's name, age and gender; then the subjective information, meaning the chief complaint, history of the present illness (HPI), past medical history (PMH), allergies and medications; then the objective information, meaning vital signs, examination findings and scene observations; then the interventions given and their timing; and finally your reassessment findings.

takeaways: Reassessment – repeat primary assessment, repeat/record vitals, repeat physical exam, check interventions.
Trending – changes in patient condition over time indicating improvement or deterioration.

chapters.title: Communication and Documentation
chapters.intro: What you say on the radio and write in the report follows the patient into the hospital and, sometimes, into court. This chapter covers radio systems and the discipline of a clear medical report, the rules for talking to medical direction, therapeutic communication with patients, and the prehospital care report: what it is for, how to write the narrative, and the legal traps in documentation.

topics.heading: Radio systems
topics.html:
An EMS radio system is built from a handful of components, each with a different job and a different reach. The table below describes each one.

ComponentDescription
Base stationFixed two-way radio (hospital/dispatch)
Mobile radioVehicle-mounted, 20–50 watts, 10–15 mi range
Portable radioHandheld, 1–5 watts
RepeaterPicks up low-power signals, retransmits at higher power on a different frequency
Cell phoneCommercial cell tower transmission; some hospitals prefer for privacy
TelemetryWireless data transmission (ECG, vitals)

topics.heading: Principles of radio communication
topics.html:
Good radio communication starts before you key the microphone. Make sure the radio is on and the volume set, reduce the background noise around you, and listen to confirm the frequency is clear before you transmit. Press the push-to-talk (PTT) button and wait 1 second before speaking, so the first word is not cut off, and hold the microphone 2 to 3 inches from your lips.

Identify the unit you are calling first, then yourself, and wait for the "stand by" clearance before continuing. Speak slowly and clearly, and keep each transmission to 30 seconds or less. Use plain English rather than codes. When a number could be misheard, say the number and then its individual digits, as in "fifteen, one-five."

Because radio traffic can be overheard, never give a patient's name over the air, and never use profanity or slander. Keep your language objective and impartial. By convention you say "we" rather than "I," and "affirmative" and "negative" rather than "yes" and "no." Report your assessment findings, not a field diagnosis: the patient "complains of abdominal pain," not "probably has appendicitis."

topics.heading: Radio medical report — 12 parts
topics.html:
The radio medical report tells the receiving hospital what is coming so that it can decide where in the emergency department (ED) the patient belongs and have the right staff ready before you arrive. It has 12 parts, given in this order:

  1. Unit identification and provider level
  2. Estimated time of arrival (ETA)
  3. Patient age and sex
  4. Chief complaint
  5. Brief pertinent history of the present illness (HPI)
  6. Major past illnesses
  7. Mental status
  8. Baseline vital signs
  9. Pertinent physical exam findings
  10. Emergency care given
  11. Response to care
  12. Contact with medical direction, if it is needed or you have questions

Deliver the report in a steady tone even when the patient is critical. A calm, ordered report is easier to act on than an urgent one.

topics.heading: Medical direction communication rules
topics.html:
When you speak with medical direction, the physician's orders are based entirely on what you report, so speak slowly and clearly. After you receive an order, repeat it back word for word, and do the same when a request is denied. If an order is unclear, ask the physician to repeat it, and then repeat it back once you understand it.

If an order seems inappropriate, question it. Questioning may reveal that the physician misunderstood something you reported, or it may bring out an explanation that makes the order clear.

sections.title: Interpersonal Communication & the PCR

topics.heading: Therapeutic communication
topics.html:
Communication with the patient is part of care, not a preliminary to it. Make eye contact, while respecting the cultural norms of patients for whom direct eye contact is considered rude, and position yourself at or below the patient's eye level. Your posture sends a message of its own: an open stance conveys warmth, and a closed stance conveys authority.

Use plain language, and explain each procedure before you perform it. Be honest, even about pain. Address the patient by their proper name and title until they tell you otherwise. Above all, listen. Do not re-ask questions the patient has already answered, and write the answers down.

Some patients need an adjusted approach. For a patient who is hard of hearing, speak slowly and make sure they can see your mouth. For a patient who is blind or visually impaired, speak at a normal volume and describe what you are doing as you do it. When there is a language barrier, use an interpreter or a translation service. With children, come down to their level, be truthful, and involve the parents.

topics.heading: Prehospital Care Report (PCR) — 5 functions
topics.html:
The prehospital care report (PCR) is the written record of the call, and it serves five functions:

  1. It is the patient care record, and it becomes part of the permanent hospital record.
  2. It is a legal document that may be subpoenaed.
  3. It supplies administrative data for billing and insurance.
  4. It supports education and research, including trend analysis, resource deployment and the identification of training needs.
  5. It is the basis of quality improvement (QI/QA/CQI), in which reports are reviewed for conformity with the standard of care.

Complete the PCR as soon as possible, ideally before you leave the hospital, because the report is most accurate while your memory is fresh. When the full PCR cannot be completed before you leave, an abbreviated version called a drop report or transfer report is left at the hospital.

topics.heading: Narrative writing rules
topics.html:
The narrative distinguishes objective from subjective information. Objective findings are observable and measurable, such as "BP 110/80." Subjective information is a symptom the patient reports, written in quotation marks, or your own impression. Avoid opinions that go beyond your scope. Anything you did not observe yourself goes in quotation marks with its source, as in "Bystander stated 'patient passed out before crashing.'" If the patient is conscious and oriented, record the chief complaint in the patient's own words, quoted.

Document pertinent negatives, the findings you explored and found absent, such as "denies pain in right arm." A pertinent negative shows that you checked. Do not use radio codes or nonstandard abbreviations; write legibly, spell correctly and use correct medical terminology.

The rule that governs all documentation is this: "If it's not written down, you didn't do it." The same rule applies in reverse to treatment. Treat and document on the basis of the mechanism of injury (MOI) or the patient's condition, even when the patient has no pain and no complaint.

topics.heading: Legal & special documentation issues
topics.html:
The PCR is protected under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). Keep it in locked storage and distribute it only as HIPAA and state and local rules allow.

A patient refusal is the documentation situation most likely to be examined later. Document your attempts to persuade the patient, assess the patient's capacity to refuse, and inform the patient of the consequences of refusing. If the patient allows it, perform a secondary assessment and take vital signs anyway. Have the patient sign a refusal form; if the patient will not sign, document the refusal to sign and have witnesses. Suggest alternative care, and make sure a responsible person stays with the patient.

Never document care you did not give or findings you did not observe. An error of omission is a step that was left out; document only what was actually done. An error of commission is a wrong action that was performed; document what happened, the correction you made, and your notification of medical direction and the hospital.

Correcting an error depends on where the report is. On a paper report that is still intact and has not been copied, draw a single line through the error, initial it and write the correction beside it. Never obliterate the original. On a paper report that has already been submitted, draw a single line through the error, add your initials and the date, and add the correction as a separate note.

At a multiple-casualty incident (MCI), triage tags track the chief complaint, injuries, vital signs and treatment as patients move between areas, and the tags are later used to complete a standard PCR. A PCR from an MCI will not have the normal level of detail, and that is acceptable given the circumstances.

takeaways: Base station – fixed-site two-way radio. Cell phone – wireless phone via cell tower.
Drop report (transfer report) – abbreviated PCR left at the hospital.
Mobile radio – vehicle-mounted two-way radio. Portable radio – handheld two-way radio.
Repeater – retransmits low-power signals at higher power/different frequency.
Telemetry – wireless data transmission (ECG, vitals). Watt – unit of radio output power.
"If it's not written down, you didn't do it." — the core rule of documentation.

chapters.title: General Pharmacology
chapters.intro: An EMT carries a small number of medications and helps patients take a few more, and every one of them has indications, contraindications and a way of going wrong. This chapter goes through each medication and how it works, the Five Rights that guard administration, the routes by which a drug enters the body, and the categories of medication you will find in a patient's home.

sections.title: Medications an EMT Carries or Assists With

topics.heading: The 7 medications an EMT can carry/administer
topics.html:
An EMT carries or administers seven medications. The table below lists each one with its purpose and the route by which it is given.

MedicationPurposeRoute
AspirinSuspected cardiac chest painOral (chewed)
Oral glucoseConscious diabetic with AMS, able to swallowOral/buccal
OxygenHypoxia or risk of hypoxiaInhaled
Prescribed bronchodilator inhalerDifficulty breathingInhaled
NitroglycerinSuspected cardiac chest painSublingual
Epinephrine auto-injectorAnaphylaxisIntramuscular
NaloxoneNarcotic overdose with respiratory depressionIntranasal or injected

Activated charcoal is also carried in some systems as an optional medication for certain poisonings. It is system-dependent, not universal.

topics.heading: Aspirin, oral glucose, oxygen & naloxone
topics.html:
Aspirin reduces the blood's ability to clot. During a myocardial infarction (MI) it limits the damage that the clot would otherwise cause, and it has been proven to reduce mortality significantly. It is contraindicated in a patient with an aspirin allergy or gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding.

Oral glucose treats altered mental status caused by low blood sugar in a diabetic patient who is conscious and able to swallow. It is applied as a gel between the cheek and the gum and is absorbed through the digestive tract.

Oxygen treats hypoxia or the risk of hypoxia. Treat it as you would any other medication: it is given when there is a good reason to give it and withheld when there is not.

Naloxone reverses a narcotic overdose, including the loss of consciousness and the respiratory failure or arrest that come with it, and it is one of the few true antidotes in medicine. It is given by injection or as an atomized mist into the nose. Naloxone does nothing if no narcotic was taken, and the intranasal form will not work if the nasal membranes are damaged or blocked.

topics.heading: Medications EMTs assist patients with (their own prescription)
topics.html:
Beyond the medications you carry, there are several that you may help a patient take from the patient's own prescription. In every case, confirm that the medication belongs to the patient and not to a bystander or a family member.

Bronchodilator inhalers, such as albuterol and levalbuterol, are prescribed for asthma, emphysema and bronchitis. Their side effects are an increased heart rate (HR) and jitteriness. Assisting with one requires medical direction.

Nitroglycerin (Nitrostat) is prescribed for recurrent chest pain. It comes as a pill that dissolves under the tongue or as a spray applied under the tongue, and it is never swallowed. It is contraindicated when the patient has recently taken an erectile dysfunction (ED) medication such as Viagra or Cialis, because the combination risks a dangerous drop in blood pressure (BP). Its side effect is a drop in blood pressure; if that happens, lay the patient flat.

Epinephrine auto-injectors (EpiPen, Auvi-Q) are prescribed for anaphylaxis and are injected intramuscularly (IM) into the thigh. Their side effects are an increased heart rate and an increased blood pressure.

Force protection medications, such as an atropine auto-injector for a responder's own treatment in a chemical weapons scenario, are carried in some systems and not in others.

topics.heading: How asthma and anaphylaxis medications actually work
topics.html:
Understanding what a medication does at the level of the receptor explains why it is chosen. The table below compares the pathophysiology of asthma and anaphylaxis with the action of the medication used for each.

ConditionPathophysiologyMedication action
AsthmaSmall airways constrict; exhaling harder than inhaling → air trappingAlbuterol acts on beta2 receptors → airway dilation; limited cardiac side effects
AnaphylaxisHistamine release → vasodilation + shock + bronchoconstriction + edemaEpinephrine acts on alpha receptors (vasoconstriction, reduces edema) AND beta receptors (bronchodilation) — fighting both problems at once

The comparison shows why epinephrine is the drug of choice in anaphylaxis: alone among these agents it acts on alpha and beta receptors at once, so it treats the circulatory collapse and the airway narrowing together. Albuterol, acting almost only on beta2 receptors, opens the airway with limited effect on the heart.

topics.heading: General pharmacology concepts
topics.html:
Every drug has three names. The chemical name is the technical description of the molecule. The generic name is written in lowercase, as in albuterol. The trade or brand name is capitalized, as in Ventolin HFA. All drugs are catalogued in the U.S. Pharmacopoeia (USP).

Four terms describe when and how a drug acts. An indication is a condition for which the drug is appropriate. A contraindication is a condition in which the drug is not appropriate or could be harmful. A side effect is any action of the drug other than the intended one, and an untoward effect is a side effect that is harmful.

Medications come in many forms: a compressed powder or tablet, a parenteral liquid for injection, an enteral liquid taken by mouth, a vaporized or nebulized liquid, a gel, a suspension, a fine powder for inhalation, a gas for inhalation, and a sublingual spray.

topics.heading: Medication authorization & the Five Rights
topics.html:
Authorization to give a medication comes from medical direction in one of two forms. Off-line medical direction consists of pre-written standing orders, and no live contact with a physician is needed. On-line medical direction is live verbal permission given by phone or radio. When you receive an on-line order, use the "echo technique" and repeat the order back to the physician, which reduces errors.

Before administering any medication, confirm the Five Rights:

  1. Right patient
  2. Right time
  3. Right medication
  4. Right dose
  5. Right route

Always check the expiration date first as well, and document the administration fully and promptly afterward.

topics.heading: Routes of administration
topics.html:
The route by which a drug enters the body determines how fast it acts and what can interfere with it. The table below sets out the routes and what you need to know about each.

RouteNotes
Oral (swallowed)Safe, slowest — must be digested first
SublingualFaster than swallowing; impaired by poor circulation (shock)
InhaledAerosol or gas, absorbed via alveoli
IntranasalCan rival injection speed; won't work if mucosa is damaged
Intravenous (IV)Fast and precise — beyond EMT scope, but EMTs may assist
Intramuscular (IM)Fast, affected by poor circulation; typically needle-based
SubcutaneousSlightly slower absorption than IM
Intraosseous (IO)Injected into bone marrow — reaches central circulation nearly as fast as IV
EndotrachealALS-level, last resort — unpredictable absorption

A swallowed drug is the safest and the slowest, because it must be digested before it can act. The sublingual route is faster than swallowing, but it depends on circulation and is impaired in shock. Inhaled drugs, whether aerosol or gas, are absorbed through the alveoli. The intranasal route can rival the speed of an injection, but it will not work if the nasal mucosa is damaged. The intravenous (IV) route is fast and precise; it is beyond the EMT scope, although EMTs may assist. An intramuscular (IM) injection is fast but affected by poor circulation, and it is typically given with a needle; subcutaneous absorption is slightly slower than IM. An intraosseous (IO) injection goes into the bone marrow and reaches the central circulation nearly as fast as an IV. The endotracheal route is an advanced life support (ALS) measure used as a last resort, because absorption is unpredictable.

Pharmacodynamics differ with the patient. Smaller and lighter patients, which is to say pediatric patients, need less medication for the same effect, and geriatric patients often have difficulty eliminating medications. The Broselow tape helps estimate correct pediatric dosing and equipment sizing. After any medication, reassess the patient immediately and repeatedly, and document the name, dose, exact route, time given and the effects you noted.

topics.heading: Common medication categories & herbal agents
topics.html:
Much of what you learn about a patient's history comes from the medications in the home, so you need to recognize the common categories. The table below gives each category, its purpose and examples.

CategoryPurposeExamples
AnalgesicsPain reliefacetaminophen, aspirin, ibuprofen, morphine, oxycodone
AntidysrhythmicsHeart rhythm disordersdigoxin, metoprolol, propranolol, verapamil
AnticonvulsantsSeizure prevention/controlphenytoin, gabapentin, levetiracetam
AntihypertensivesLower high BPamlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, clonidine
BronchodilatorsRelax bronchial smooth musclealbuterol, ipratropium, salmeterol
Antidiabetic agentsControl high blood sugarinsulin, metformin, glipizide
AntidepressantsRegulate emotional statefluoxetine, sertraline, amitriptyline
Blood thinnersAnticoagulants or antiplateletswarfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel, aspirin

Two points deserve emphasis. Daily maintenance respiratory medications such as beclomethasone and Advair should never be used to reverse an acute attack. And ask about herbal agents specifically, naming examples such as gingko, St. John's wort, garlic, hawthorn, kava kava and valerian root. Patients often do not think to mention them, but several have real interactions with prescribed drugs.

topics.heading: Assisting with IV therapy
topics.html:
IV therapy is an ALS-level procedure. The EMT assists with it but does not perform the insertion. There are two methods: a saline or heparin lock, which is a capped port with no fluid bag, and a traditional IV bag with an administration set. The administration set consists of a drip chamber, a flow regulator, a drug or needle port and an extension set. The drip chamber comes in two sizes: a micro drip, which delivers 60 drops/mL and is used for pediatric patients, and a macro drip, which delivers 10–15 drops/mL and is used for shock and trauma.

Several problems can arise with a running IV. If it is not flowing at all, look for a constricting band left on the arm, a closed flow regulator or kinked tubing. If it is flowing too slowly, check the patient's positioning and whether the bag is held high enough. A "runaway IV" is one flowing too fast, which is dangerous, especially in children. An infiltrated IV is one in which the needle has punctured through or out of the vein; stop the flow and report or discontinue it according to protocol.

takeaways: The Five Rights – patient, time, medication, dose, route.
Indication vs. contraindication vs. side effect vs. untoward effect.
Albuterol acts on beta2 receptors (airway); epinephrine acts on alpha AND beta receptors (vessels + airway) — why epi is the anaphylaxis drug of choice.
Off-line medical direction = standing orders; on-line = live physician order ("echo technique" to confirm).
Never use a daily maintenance inhaler to treat an acute attack.
Herbal agents can interact with medications — ask about them specifically.

chapters.title: Respiratory Emergencies
chapters.intro: The first question with any patient who is short of breath is whether their breathing is adequate, because the answer decides whether they need oxygen or need you to breathe for them. This chapter reviews the physiology, the signs that separate adequate from inadequate breathing, assessment and lung sounds, CPAP, the specific conditions from asthma to pulmonary embolism, and the inhalers and nebulizers patients carry.

topics.heading: The physiology refresher
topics.html:
Inspiration is an active process. The diaphragm contracts and drops down while the intercostal muscles expand the chest wall, so the chest cavity gets bigger. As the cavity enlarges the pressure inside it drops, and air is pulled in. Expiration is passive: the diaphragm and intercostals relax, the chest cavity shrinks, the pressure rises, and air is pushed out.

Pediatric anatomy changes this picture in two ways. The rib cage of an infant or child flares outward at the bottom, which makes the diaphragm flatter and less able to move well, and the chest wall is more flexible and floppy. Adults compensate for respiratory trouble by using more chest muscle and taking deeper breaths; children compensate mainly by increasing their rate, which burns through their energy much faster.

topics.heading: Adequate vs. inadequate breathing
topics.html:
The first decision with any patient who is short of breath is whether their breathing is adequate. The table below compares adequate and inadequate breathing across six findings.

AdequateInadequate
RateAdult 12–20, school-age 18–30, infant 30–60/minAbove or below normal for age
RhythmRegularMay be irregular
Breath soundsPresent and equalDiminished, unequal, or absent
Chest expansionAdequate and equalInadequate or unequal
EffortUnlaboredLabored — accessory muscles, flaring, seesaw breathing, grunting, retractions
DepthAdequateToo shallow

Rate alone never tells the whole story. A fast rate from crying, exertion or anxiety can still be adequate. What matters is whether the rate is packaged with other findings such as altered mental status, cyanosis or a low SpO2.

topics.heading: Recognizing inadequate breathing
topics.html:
The brain has zero oxygen reserve, so a change in mental status is often the first sign of inadequate breathing. The patient becomes anxious and may describe a sense of "impending doom"; that gives way to confusion, combativeness or lethargy, and finally to unconsciousness. Cyanosis appears first around the eyes and in the nail beds, and it is a profound warning sign of severe hypoxia.

Other signs show that compensation is failing. Respirations that slow or become irregular mean the patient can no longer keep up. The patient may be unable to speak normally and cannot get more than 1–2 words out at a time. A silent chest is one in which air movement is so diminished that you hear nothing, even though the chest may still be moving. The SpO2 stays low despite supplemental oxygen. Agonal respirations, which are sporadic, gasping breaths at only a few per minute, come just before respiratory arrest.

In children, the specific signs of inadequate breathing are nasal flaring, grunting, seesaw breathing and retractions. Bradycardia in a pediatric respiratory patient is never normal. It warns of imminent cardiac arrest, because respiratory failure is the leading cause of cardiac arrest in children. Early hypoxia speeds a child's heart up just as it does an adult's; the slowing comes late, when compensation is failing.

topics.heading: Treating inadequate breathing
topics.html:
Treatment follows from the assessment. The table below matches each level of breathing to its signs and the intervention it calls for.

ConditionSignsIntervention
Adequate, needs O2Normal mental status, normal color, normal SpO2Supplemental O2 to maintain normal SpO2; treat underlying cause
InadequateAltered MS, abnormal rate/depth, cyanosis, low SpO2 despite O2Assisted (positive pressure) ventilation with pocket mask or BVM
No breathingNo chest rise, no air movementAssisted ventilation: adult ~10/min (1 breath every 6 sec), infant/child 20–30/min (1 breath every 2–3 sec)

A nonrebreather mask requires the patient to be breathing adequately. It provides no ventilation to an apneic patient; that patient needs a BVM. If you are uncertain whether breathing is inadequate, ventilate anyway. Err toward action.

Never hyperventilate the patient. Eliminating too much CO2 constricts the cerebral blood vessels and reduces perfusion of the brain. In an infant or child, a low or bradycardic pulse during ventilation means real trouble: recheck the airway positioning, the chest rise and the oxygen supply and tubing.

sections.title: Assessment, CPAP & Specific Conditions

topics.heading: Assessing the patient with breathing difficulty
topics.html:
Breathing difficulty is a subjective complaint, so assess the patient rather than relying on the patient's report alone. The primary assessment comes first. Then take the history, using OPQRST adapted to the complaint (onset, provocation, quality and cough, radiation, severity and time) together with SAMPLE.

In the physical exam, look for altered mental status, a barrel chest and the tripod position. Note retractions, accessory muscle use, flared nostrils and pursed lips, and count how many words the patient can say at a time, down to "one-word dyspnea." Assess skin color, look for pedal and sacral edema, listen for noisy breathing, and note an SpO2 below 95%.

If the pulse oximeter is ready, place the sensor before you apply oxygen so that you have a true room-air baseline. Never delay oxygen just to get a reading.

topics.heading: Lung sound auscultation
topics.html:
Auscultation of the lungs tells you where in the airway the problem lies. The table below gives each abnormal sound, when in the cycle it is heard, what causes it and the conditions it goes with.

SoundTimingCauseAssociated with
WheezesMainly expirationAir through narrowed passagesAsthma, sometimes COPD
Crackles (rales)InspirationFluid in alveoli, or opening of collapsed alveoliPulmonary edema
Rhonchi—Secretions in larger airwaysPneumonia, bronchitis, aspiration
StridorInspirationUpper airway — partial obstructionUsually audible without a stethoscope

A worsening patient can lose their wheezes entirely. That is not improvement. It means the patient has stopped moving enough air to generate the sound.

topics.heading: CPAP
topics.html:
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers noninvasive positive pressure together with supplemental oxygen (O2) through a sealed mask. The pressure is not enough to substitute for artificial ventilation. Its benefit comes from positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), which keeps the small airways and alveoli from collapsing at the end of each breath; the typical range is 5–15 cm H2O.

CPAP is indicated for pulmonary edema and drowning, for asthma and COPD, and as a bridge in respiratory failure. In every case the patient must still be breathing on their own.

The contraindications follow from what the device needs in order to work. It is contraindicated in a patient with a depressed mental status or no spontaneous respiratory rate, a patient who cannot sit up, a patient who is hypotensive with a systolic below 90, a patient who cannot maintain a mask seal, and a patient with nausea or vomiting. It is also contraindicated in chest trauma or suspected pneumothorax, in shock, and in an upper GI bleed or recent gastric surgery.

CPAP has side effects of its own. It reduces venous return, which can drop the blood pressure (BP); it carries a risk of pneumothorax in lungs that are already fragile; it can cause gastric distention with vomiting and the risk of aspiration; and it dries the corneas. Reassess constantly. If the patient's mental status or breathing worsens, remove the CPAP and go to BVM ventilation.

topics.heading: The specific conditions
topics.html:
The conditions that cause breathing difficulty each have a mechanism, a set of key signs and something particular you need to know. The table below sets them out.

ConditionMechanismKey signsSpecial notes
COPDInflamed/mucus-clogged bronchioles (bronchitis); alveolar walls break down (emphysema), stale CO2-laden air trappedSmoking history, acute worsening w/ URI, fever, colored sputumA small subset rely on low O2 (not high CO2) to trigger breathing — titrate oxygen toward their baseline, but never withhold it from a hypoxic patient — don't withhold needed O2 from a hypoxic COPD patient
AsthmaBronchiole muscle contraction + mucus overproduction narrows airwaysEpisodic, triggered by stings/pollutants/infection/exercise/stressNo hypoxic-drive concern; albuterol for rescue
Pulmonary edema (CHF)Left heart damage → pressure backs up into lungs → fluid crosses into alveoliAbrupt onset, recent weight gain, pink frothy sputum, JVD, pedal/sacral edemaKeep legs dependent (down), NOT elevated; high-conc O2; CPAP often effective
PneumoniaBacterial/viral/fungal infectionCough, fever, pleuritic pain, one-sided cracklesSupportive care, O2 if hypoxic
Spontaneous pneumothoraxRuptured bleb → lung collapsesSharp pleuritic pain, decreased/absent breath sounds one sideCPAP contraindicated; needs ALS/chest decompression
Pulmonary embolismClot/air/fat blocks a pulmonary arterySudden sharp pleuritic pain, SOB, tachycardia, leg pain/swellingHigh suspicion with recent immobilization/DVT history
EpiglottitisInfection inflames/swells the epiglottisTripod, muffled voice, drooling, stridorDo NOT inspect the throat; rapid transport
CroupViral inflammation of larynx/trachea/bronchiAges 6mo–4yr, barking cough, often at nightDon't put anything in the mouth — risk of vocal cord spasm
Bronchiolitis (RSV)Viral inflammation of small airwaysInfants and kids <2, cold-like symptoms, seasonalBulb-syringe nasal suction can meaningfully improve ventilation in infants
Cystic fibrosisGenetic — thick, sticky mucusHeavy mucus cough, frequent pneumoniaPatients/parents usually very knowledgeable about management

topics.heading: Medications — inhalers & nebulizers
topics.html:
Assisting with a metered-dose inhaler (MDI) requires medical direction. The patient exhales, places the mouthpiece past the teeth and above the tongue, presses the canister while inhaling slowly, and holds the breath for 5–10 seconds. A spacer makes the timing less critical. Wait 15–30 seconds between doses.

Inhalers fall into two groups. Rescue inhalers, such as albuterol, levalbuterol and Combivent, are for acute attacks. Maintenance inhalers, such as beclomethasone, Flovent and Advair, are for daily control and are never used for an acute attack.

A small-volume nebulizer (SVN) delivers medication as a continuous vapor over several minutes. The table below gives the medications used in it.

MedicationMechanismOnset
AlbuterolBronchodilator — beta-receptor stimulationFast-acting, usually first-line
Ipratropium bromideBronchodilator — blocks parasympathetic bronchoconstrictionSlower onset, longer duration
DuoNebCombination of both aboveFirst-line combo option

Albuterol is a bronchodilator that works by stimulating beta receptors; it is fast-acting and usually first-line. Ipratropium bromide is a bronchodilator that works by blocking parasympathetic bronchoconstriction; its onset is slower and its duration longer. DuoNeb combines the two and is a first-line combination option.

The side effects of nebulized medication mirror those of inhalers: an increased pulse, tremors and jitteriness. A patient with inadequate breathing will not benefit from a nebulizer, because the patient is not breathing deeply enough to pull in the medication.

takeaways: Adequate breathing: rate/rhythm/effort/depth all normal for age, breath sounds present and equal.
A nonrebreather requires adequate spontaneous breathing — an apneic patient needs a BVM instead.
Bradycardia during pediatric respiratory distress is always ominous, not reassuring.
CPAP contraindications: depressed MS, no spontaneous rate, can't sit up, hypotension, chest trauma/pneumothorax, shock.
Pulmonary edema: keep legs down, not elevated. Pneumothorax: CPAP is contraindicated.
Rescue inhalers (albuterol) treat acute attacks; maintenance inhalers (Advair, Flovent) never do.
Epiglottitis/croup: never put anything in the mouth or inspect the throat.

chapters.title: Cardiac Emergencies
chapters.intro: The heart has almost no oxygen reserve, so a blocked coronary artery starts injuring muscle within minutes. This chapter covers acute coronary syndrome, its signs and its management with aspirin, nitroglycerin and the 12-lead ECG, then the conditions behind it: coronary artery disease and angina, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure with pulmonary edema, and aneurysm.

topics.heading: The heart has no oxygen reserve
topics.html:
The coronary arteries branch off the base of the aorta, and they are the first vessels to receive oxygenated blood from the heart itself. Heart cells are constantly working, and without perfusion they become hypoxic and can die very quickly. This is why a blocked coronary artery is such an urgent problem.

Acute coronary syndrome (ACS), also called cardiac compromise, is a blanket term for any situation in which the blood supply to heart cells is blocked or disrupted, whether abruptly by a sudden clot or gradually by the narrowing of plaque. The resulting hypoxic condition is called ischemia. Most of the damage that ischemia causes, short of actual cell death, can be corrected by restoring perfusion.

topics.heading: Signs & symptoms of ACS
topics.html:
Chest discomfort is the most common finding in ACS, but patients describe it in very different ways: as pain, pressure, squeezing or aching. It may stay localized or radiate to the jaw, the neck, either arm or the epigastrium. It can also be absent entirely, and that is especially true in older adults, women and diabetic patients.

The other symptoms are less specific. The patient may have dyspnea, nausea or vomiting, syncope or near-syncope, vague fatigue, or sudden sweating, a combination often mistaken for "coming down with the flu." On examination you may find an abnormal pulse, whether bradycardic, tachycardic or irregular, an abnormal blood pressure, and anxiety or a "feeling of impending doom."

Because presentations vary so widely, treat any patient whose picture matches the pattern as cardiac rather than trying to talk yourself out of the diagnosis.

topics.heading: Managing ACS — assessment & 12-lead
topics.html:
Management begins with the primary assessment, followed by the history using OPQRST and SAMPLE, and then a set of baseline vital signs. Levine's sign, in which the patient clutches the chest, together with sweating, pale or gray skin, and anxiousness with a sense of impending doom, all suggest that the discomfort is from ACS.

Many states allow EMTs to acquire a 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Interpretation is outside the EMT scope, but acquiring the tracing and transmitting it speeds the hospital's diagnosis. Place the limb leads first, on the arms below the shoulder and on the legs below the hip, and then place V1 through V6 at the standard chest landmarks.

topics.heading: Treatment steps
topics.html:
Treatment of ACS follows a set sequence:

  1. Positioning. A patient with breathing difficulty is generally sat up; a hypotensive patient often feels better lying down.
  2. Oxygen. The target is an SpO2 of 94% or higher, and no higher than necessary. Give high-concentration oxygen for respiratory failure, a low SpO2 or a critical appearance. An alert patient who is not in distress and has a normal SpO2 receives no oxygen.
  3. Immediate transport if the patient has no cardiac history, has a cardiac history but no nitroglycerin on hand, or has a systolic blood pressure below the protocol threshold.
  4. 12-lead ECG, if you are trained, equipped and authorized.
  5. Aspirin, up to 325 mg by mouth (PO), chewed. Do not give it if there is an aspiration risk, if the patient already took aspirin earlier today, if the patient is allergic, if there is recent GI bleeding, or, depending on protocol, if the patient is already on a prescribed blood thinner.
  6. Nitroglycerin. Assist with it only when all of the conditions are met: the patient has chest discomfort and a cardiac history, the nitroglycerin is physician-prescribed and the patient has it, the systolic blood pressure is above the threshold, the patient has taken no erectile dysfunction (ED) medication within 48–72 hours, and medical direction authorizes it. The dose may be repeated in 5 minutes if the blood pressure remains adequate, to a maximum of 3 doses.

Drive smoothly. Sudden starts, stops and turns and unnecessary sirens add stress to a heart that is already under stress.

sections.title: CAD, Angina, AMI & Heart Failure

topics.heading: Coronary artery disease & angina pectoris
topics.html:
Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the narrowing or blockage of the coronary arteries by the buildup of plaque. Its non-modifiable risk factors are heredity and age; its modifiable risk factors are hypertension, obesity, inactivity, high cholesterol and smoking. CAD itself is usually not an emergency.

Angina pectoris is chest discomfort that occurs when a narrowed artery cannot meet the increased demand of exertion or stress. Its distinguishing feature is that the symptoms subside with rest, typically within about 5 minutes. In the field, however, angina and a myocardial infarction (MI) can look identical, so treat every symptomatic patient as a possible MI, using the same ACS protocol, until proven otherwise.

topics.heading: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI)
topics.html:
Plaque narrows and roughens a vessel, and the roughened surface promotes the formation of a clot, or thrombus. The clot may block the vessel completely, which is an occlusion, or a piece may break free and lodge downstream, which is an embolism. Either way the result is an acute myocardial infarction (AMI). An AMI has two dangerous consequences. Dysrhythmia is the most common cause of death from an MI. Mechanical failure is rarer, and it can progress to cardiogenic shock.

"Time is muscle." The faster the patient reaches the hospital and receives intervention, the less heart muscle is permanently lost. EMT treatment begins with confirming a pulse and breathing, because some AMI patients present in cardiac arrest. Transport is the single most important treatment. Contact ALS, keep an AED nearby, give aspirin and nitroglycerin per protocol, and keep the patient calm. Do not let an AMI patient walk.

topics.heading: Heart failure (HF/CHF) & pulmonary edema
topics.html:
In heart failure (HF/CHF) the heart continues to pump, but inefficiently, and the side that fails determines where the pressure backs up. In right-sided failure, pressure backs up into the vena cava, producing jugular venous distention (JVD), abdominal swelling and pedal edema. In left-sided failure, pressure backs up into the pulmonary vein, the alveolar capillaries leak fluid, and the result is pulmonary edema, with respiratory distress, crackles and possibly pink frothy sputum.

The primary assessment comes first, because a patient in heart failure can decompensate to inadequate breathing. It is followed by a detailed cardiovascular exam and continuous vital signs. Contact ALS immediately, apply CPAP if protocol allows, and note that some systems allow the EMT to give nitroglycerin for acute pulmonary edema.

topics.heading: Aneurysm & pediatric cardiac notes
topics.html:
An aneurysm is a weakened arterial wall, either congenital or related to plaque, that expands and dilates or tears in its middle layers. Rupture causes rapid, life-threatening internal bleeding. The most common sites are the aorta and the brain, and a ruptured artery in the brain is a hemorrhagic stroke.

Most pediatric cardiac conditions are congenital and are usually identified before the newborn leaves the nursery. When a child has a chronic cardiac condition that is unclear to you, consult the caregivers to establish the child's baseline and ask why EMS was called. Manage any problems found in the primary assessment the same as you would for any patient, and transport to a facility equipped for the child's condition.

takeaways: Heart cells have no oxygen reserve — a blocked coronary artery causes rapid damage.
Chest discomfort without pain is common in older adults, women, and diabetics — don't rule out ACS based on the classic presentation.
Target SpO2 ≥94% — high-concentration O2 is no longer given automatically to every chest pain patient.
Aspirin: 325 mg chewed, unless allergy/GI bleed/aspiration risk/already dosed.
Nitroglycerin: never if ED meds (Viagra, Cialis) taken within 48–72 hrs — risk of severe BP drop.
Angina resolves with rest (~5 min); if in doubt, always treat as a possible MI.
"Time is muscle" — transport is the single most important AMI treatment.
Left-sided heart failure → pulmonary edema; right-sided → JVD/peripheral edema.
Aneurysm rupture (aorta or brain) causes rapid, life-threatening bleeding.

chapters.title: Resuscitation
chapters.intro: Cardiac arrest is the emergency the EMT owns, because high-quality CPR and early defibrillation do more for survival than anything that happens later. This chapter presents the chain of survival, the difference between a mechanical and an electrical cause of arrest, recognition, the four steps of a coordinated resuscitation from first compressions through return of spontaneous circulation, and the special cases of hypothermia, submersion, implanted devices and infants.

sections.title: Cardiac Arrest Pathophysiology & the Chain of Survival

topics.heading: EMTs own CPR
topics.html:
Cardiac arrest has attracted more advanced medications and technology than almost any other emergency, yet research shows that only two interventions reliably alter its outcome: quality chest compressions and early defibrillation. Both sit squarely within the EMT's scope of practice, and that is why cardiac arrest is the emergency the EMT owns.

The systems that do best treat resuscitation as a discipline. High-performance CPR means systems planning, regimented training with feedback, incident command, and a laser focus on compressions and defibrillation. Systems that practice it can push survival from witnessed arrest above 50%, against a national average under 15%.

topics.heading: The chain of survival (6 links)
topics.html:
The chain of survival describes, in order, the six links a cardiac arrest patient must pass through, each of which depends on the one before it. The 2025 AHA guidelines went back to a single chain covering every cardiac arrest — adult or pediatric, in hospital or out of it — where there had previously been separate chains for each. The six links are:

  1. Recognition and emergency activation. Somebody identifies the arrest and calls for help.
  2. High-quality CPR.
  3. Defibrillation.
  4. Advanced resuscitation. Medications, advanced airways, and where available extracorporeal CPR.
  5. Post–cardiac arrest care.
  6. Recovery and survivorship. Rehabilitation, follow-up, and psychological support, which continue for months to years.

The second and third links, high-quality CPR and defibrillation, are the two interventions that research shows reliably change outcomes, and they belong to the EMT.

Two details of the 2025 revision are worth knowing. The symbol for the CPR link now shows compressions and breaths rather than compressions alone, because ventilation matters in pediatric arrest and in the substantial minority of adult arrests caused by drowning or opioid poisoning. And the single chain covers adult and pediatric arrest only — a newborn at delivery follows a separate Newborn Chain of Care.

topics.heading: Mechanical failure vs. electrical dysfunction
topics.html:
An arrest has one of two underlying causes. In mechanical failure, the heart stops pumping effectively because of a structural problem: loss of normal myocardial structure, as after a myocardial infarction (MI) or with chronic hypertension; loss of valve function; or direct trauma, including pericardial tamponade. Mechanical failure can occur even while the heart's electrical function is normal. When the monitor shows an organized rhythm but the patient has no pulse, the condition is called pulseless electrical activity (PEA).

Electrical dysfunction is the more common cause. When the supply of oxygen to the heart is interrupted, the sodium-potassium pump on which its electrical activity depends is disrupted. If that disruption is complete, the result is asystole. If it is partial or chaotic, the result is a dysrhythmia such as ventricular tachycardia (V-tach) or ventricular fibrillation (V-fib), and these can often be corrected rapidly by defibrillation.

topics.heading: Sudden vs. asphyxial cardiac arrest
topics.html:
Cardiac arrest can also be classified by how it begins. Sudden cardiac arrest is the abrupt collapse caused by a dysrhythmia, and asphyxial cardiac arrest is the end point of systemic hypoxia from a respiratory problem or from shock. The distinction matters because it changes what the patient needs most. The table below sets out the differences.

Sudden cardiac arrestAsphyxial cardiac arrest
CauseAbrupt-onset dysrhythmia (VF/V-tach)Systemic hypoxia (respiratory problems, shock)
% of all arrests>85%Remainder
WarningLittle to none — abrupt collapseMore warning — gradual decompensation
Ventilation priorityCompressions primaryQuality ventilations especially important

Pediatric cardiac arrest follows the opposite pattern from the adult one. It is overwhelmingly asphyxial; only about 20% of pediatric arrests result from a sudden dysrhythmia.

topics.heading: Agonal respirations
topics.html:
Agonal respirations occur when the heart stops suddenly while residual oxygen remains in the blood. The medulla continues to send occasional impulses, and the result is intermittent gasping. These gasps actually help circulation slightly, and can be thought of as the body's attempt to resuscitate itself, but they cannot sustain themselves and they cannot sustain the patient.

Because they indicate that residual oxygen is still present, agonal respirations are a good prognostic sign. They must not confuse you, however. Gasping is not breathing. If there is no pulse, or you are uncertain whether there is one, start compressions regardless.

topics.heading: Recognizing cardiac arrest
topics.html:
Recognizing an arrest sounds simple, but the stress of the moment triggers your own fight-or-flight response, and tunnel vision is a real hazard. Three features, assessed rapidly, confirm cardiac arrest: the patient is unresponsive; the patient is apneic, remembering that agonal breathing must not be mistaken for real breathing; and the patient has no pulse, checked at the carotid artery for no more than 10 seconds. Once arrest is confirmed, the primary assessment stops and compressions begin immediately.

In pediatric patients, check the brachial or femoral pulse instead of the carotid. The threshold for compressions also differs. An infant or child with a heart rate below 60 bpm and signs of poor perfusion, despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation, is treated as nonperfusing, and compressions begin.

topics.heading: Coordinated resuscitation team
topics.html: A resuscitation runs best when the first three providers on scene already know their jobs. This arrangement, sometimes called the "triangle of life," assigns predetermined roles: one provider performs compressions, one operates the AED, and one takes the head to manage the airway and ventilations. Additional providers who arrive later rotate in to relieve a fatiguing compressor or to carry out ALS interventions.

topics.heading: Step 1 — identify arrest & begin
topics.html:
The first step is to identify the arrest and begin compressions where the patient is found. Moving the patient before starting delays compressions, and it is a common and avoidable error. Once compressions have started, they must continue without pause for as much of the resuscitation as possible. The proportion of the resuscitation during which compressions are actually being delivered is the compression fraction, and the goal is to keep it high. Because the quality of compressions falls as the compressor tires, switch compressors at least every 2 minutes.

High-quality compressions are defined by five numbers, and they are the most examinable figures in the whole chapter:

AdultChild (1 year to puberty)Infant (under 1 year)
Rate100–120 compressions per minute, at every age
Depth2 to 2.4 inches (5–6 cm)About 2 inches — one third of the chest depthAbout 1.5 inches — one third of the chest depth
Ratio, one rescuer30:230:230:2
Ratio, two rescuers30:215:215:2
HandsTwo hands, heel on the lower half of the sternumOne or two hands, depending on the child's sizeTwo thumbs encircling the chest, or the heel of one hand

The infant row changed in 2025. The two-finger technique was eliminated: it did not reliably reach a third of the chest's depth. Two techniques replace it — two thumbs encircling the chest, and the heel of one hand — and when a rescuer's hands cannot physically reach around the infant's chest, the heel of one hand is the one to use.

Full recoil is the fifth, and it is the one most often lost. Let the chest come all the way back up between compressions and keep your weight off it at the top: the heart refills during the recoil, so leaning on the chest quietly reduces the blood flow from every compression that follows. Depth has an upper limit for the same reason it has a lower one — deeper than about 2.4 inches in an adult causes injury without improving flow.

Once an advanced airway is in place the ratio stops applying: compressions run continuously at 100–120 while ventilations are given about once every 6 seconds, roughly 10 per minute, in an adult (every 2–3 seconds, 20–30 per minute, in an infant or child).

topics.heading: Step 2 — integrate the AED
topics.html:
The second step is to integrate the AED. There is no benefit to delaying its application, but the order in which CPR and the AED come depends on the patient, as the table below shows.

PatientPriority sequenceWhy
Any patient, AED to handAttach and use it as soon as it arrivesDefibrillation is time-critical, and nothing is gained by holding the AED back
Lone rescuer, child or infant, arrest not witnessedAbout 2 minutes of CPR first, then fetch the AEDPediatric arrests are usually asphyxial, so oxygenation matters most — and a lone rescuer leaving to find an AED is time with no compressions at all
Lone rescuer, adult, or any witnessed sudden collapseGet the AED firstA sudden dysrhythmia is the likely cause, and a shock is the treatment

The old shorthand — “adults AED first, children CPR first” — gets this wrong. The two-minutes-of-CPR rule is about a lone rescuer having to leave an unwitnessed pediatric arrest to go and find an AED. A crew does not face that choice: one provider compresses while the other fetches and attaches the AED, at any age.

Turn the AED on first, so that it can guide you. The pads go on bare skin: remove clothing, jewelry and medication patches, shave excess hair, and offset the pads around a visible pacemaker. Do not interrupt compressions to place the pads. The analysis phase usually requires about 15 to 20 seconds during which no one touches the patient. Clear the patient before delivering a shock, and resume compressions immediately afterward without waiting for the device to prompt you. The AED reanalyzes the rhythm every 2 minutes.

topics.heading: Step 3 — continue the resuscitation
topics.html:
The third step is to continue the resuscitation through repeated cycles of compressions, analysis and shocks. In a pediatric patient, deploy the AED regardless of age; roughly 20% of pediatric arrests involve a shockable rhythm. For a child under 8 years of age, use pediatric pads if they are available, typically in an anterior-posterior placement. If no pediatric pads are available, use the adult AED anyway. It is better to over-defibrillate than not to defibrillate at all.

Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) often does not occur until the second, third or fourth shock, so stay ready for a rhythm change on any given analysis. Family presence during the resuscitation is a genuinely complicated question. The potential benefit, closure for the family, must be weighed against the risk that they interfere. Offer the option, and be ready to relocate the family if it becomes necessary.

topics.heading: Step 4 — transitioning after ROSC
topics.html:
The fourth step is the transition to postarrest care once ROSC occurs. There is no single reliable sign of it. A palpable pulse is the definition, but pulse checks are notoriously unreliable in this setting; spontaneous breathing, movement or a return of consciousness all suggest it, and where waveform capnography is in use a sudden sustained rise in end-tidal CO2 is the earliest and most objective clue. If you are in doubt, err on the side of continuing the resuscitation.

Once ROSC is confirmed, care shifts to the postarrest priorities: rapid transport, airway management that avoids hyperventilation, and oxygen titrated to a saturation of 92–98%. The target is a window, not a floor. Both ends of it matter: hypoxia after an arrest worsens the brain injury that has already happened, and so does hyperoxia, which is why the instruction is no longer to push the saturation as high as it will go. A 12-lead ECG belongs in the postarrest sequence too, if your service carries one and you are permitted to acquire it.

The resuscitated patient is at high risk of re-arrest. Recheck the pulse roughly every 30 seconds in a patient who has ROSC but remains unconscious. If the pulse is lost again, stop the vehicle if you are en route, resume CPR, analyze the rhythm, shock if indicated, and continue according to local protocol.

topics.heading: Terminating resuscitation & death notification
topics.html:
Once begun, CPR and defibrillation continue until one of four things happens:

  • Spontaneous circulation returns.
  • Care is transferred to a provider with a higher level of training.
  • You are too exhausted to continue.
  • A physician or other authority issues an order to cease resuscitation.

When resuscitation fails, the EMT is often the one who tells the family. Be straightforward and direct: "I'm very sorry, but your father has died." Allow the family privacy, be patient, and be genuine. Do not claim to know how they feel.

sections.title: Special Resuscitation Considerations

topics.heading: Hypothermia, submersion & moving ambulances
topics.html:
Several situations change the standard approach. In hypothermic cardiac arrest, defibrillate as you would for any other patient and follow the standard BLS algorithm while rewarming. The older teaching — one shock, then nothing further until the core reached 86°F (30°C) — has been dropped; withholding shocks by temperature is no longer advised. Handle the patient gently, get wet clothing off, prevent further heat loss, and transport to a facility that can rewarm actively. The window of survivability is longer in the cold patient, which is what “not dead until warm and dead” means, so do not terminate resuscitation in the field for a hypothermic patient.

Most arrests from submersion, or drowning, are asphyxial, so be aggressive with airway management and rescue breathing. Never defibrillate a soaking-wet patient. Dry the chest, or move the patient out of the wet environment, first.

Resuscitation in a moving ambulance is generally avoided. Motion reduces the quality of compressions, and some AEDs cannot analyze a rhythm while the vehicle is moving. If arrest occurs during transport, stop the vehicle to perform CPR and use the AED.

topics.heading: Implants & prior surgeries
topics.html:
Patients with implanted cardiac devices or a history of cardiac surgery are resuscitated in the same way as anyone else, with a few adjustments. The table below sets out the considerations for each.

DeviceConsiderations
Cardiac pacemakerOffset defibrillation pads several inches away, stay in the general target area
Implanted defibrillatorA firing device is a likely lifesaving sign — transport immediately; offset AED pads away from it
VAD/LVADNo palpable pulse/BP may be possible even while alive — rely on LOC/breathing; if unconscious with poor perfusion, assume malfunction and begin compressions
Cardiac bypass surgeryProvide the same standard emergency care as any other patient

topics.heading: Sudden unexpected infant death syndrome (SUIDS)
topics.html:
Sudden unexpected infant death (SUID) is the death of an infant under 1 year of age with no immediately obvious cause. It is an umbrella term covering three things: SIDS, accidental suffocation or strangulation in bed, and deaths that remain undetermined after investigation. So accidental suffocation is part of the SUID category, not something ruled out of it.

SIDS is the narrower term, and it is a diagnosis of exclusion: it is what a death is called after a full investigation, autopsy and scene review have failed to find a cause — including failing to find suffocation. None of that can be determined in the field, which is why what you are looking at on scene is a SUID until somebody else decides otherwise.

The EMT's role is to resuscitate unless rigor mortis or dependent lividity is present. As the saying goes, it is better to resuscitate when it isn't necessary than to fail to resuscitate when it is.

Support for the family is critical. Remind the parents that SUIDS happens to well-cared-for babies, and never speak to them in a suspicious tone.

takeaways: Only quality compressions and early defibrillation reliably change cardiac arrest outcomes.
Use the AED as soon as it is to hand, at any age. The “2 minutes of CPR first” rule is only for a LONE rescuer at an unwitnessed child or infant arrest who must leave to fetch one.
Compressions: 100–120/min at every age. Depth 2–2.4 in (adult), ~2 in (child), ~1.5 in (infant). 30:2, or 15:2 for two rescuers on a child or infant. Full recoil every time — do not lean.
Agonal respirations are a good sign but don't delay compressions if there's no pulse.
PEA – organized electrical rhythm without effective mechanical pumping.
After ROSC, titrate oxygen to 92–98% — a window, not a floor; hyperoxia harms the post-arrest brain too. ROSC often doesn't happen until the 2nd–4th shock — stay ready.
Never defibrillate a soaking-wet patient — dry the chest first.
Hypothermic arrest: don't terminate resuscitation in the field. Defibrillate by the standard algorithm while rewarming — the old “one shock, then wait for 86°F” rule has been dropped.
VAD/LVAD patients may have no palpable pulse even while alive.

chapters.title: Diabetic Emergencies and Altered Mental Status
chapters.intro: Altered mental status has many causes, and diabetes is one of the few an EMT can reverse on scene. This chapter covers the core approach to any patient who is not thinking clearly, the physiology of diabetes and the contrast between hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, blood glucose measurement and oral glucose, and then the other great causes of altered mentation: seizures, stroke and syncope.

topics.heading: Altered mental status — core concepts
topics.html:
Altered mental status (AMS) covers a broad spectrum of abnormal responsiveness, thought and mood, from mild anxiety to unconsciousness. Its causes fall into three groups: structural damage, such as a traumatic brain injury (TBI); chemical changes, such as toxins; and metabolic changes, such as a lack of oxygen or glucose. However subtle it may be, altered mental status is always a serious finding. Wakefulness is governed by the reticular activating system (RAS), which needs oxygen, glucose and water to function, and a deficiency of any of the three causes rapid and serious AMS.

Assessment begins with safety, because patients with altered mental status can be unpredictable. In the primary assessment, remember that hypoxia and carbon dioxide (CO2) retention are common causes of AMS, and consider shock as well. Establish the AVPU level early, and refine it later with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score. The secondary assessment includes a full history, interviews with bystanders and family, a review of the patient's medications, and a search for medical alert items.

topics.heading: Diabetes mellitus
topics.html:
Glucose is the body's basic energy source. To cross most cell membranes it needs insulin; brain cells are the exception and take up glucose without it. The pancreas secretes insulin when the blood glucose rises above roughly 90 mg/dL. Diabetes mellitus is the disease in which this system fails, and it takes two forms, compared in the table below.

Type 1Type 2
Former nameJuvenile/insulin-dependentNon-insulin-dependent
MechanismPancreas fails to produce insulinCells fail to use insulin properly
ManagementSynthetic insulin requiredDiet, oral meds, sometimes insulin

topics.heading: Hypoglycemia vs. hyperglycemia
topics.html:
The two diabetic emergencies are opposites in cause and presentation. The table below contrasts them.

HypoglycemiaHyperglycemia
OnsetRapid/suddenSlow (days–weeks)
SkinCold, pale, moist/clammyWarm, red, dry
BreathNormalAcetone/fruity (not always present)
Breathing—Deep, rapid (Kussmaul-type)

Hypoglycemia has several common causes: too much insulin or oral medication, reduced food intake, over-exercise, vomiting a meal, or an increased metabolic rate. On the other side, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and HHNS are both forms of severe hyperglycemia. You do not need to distinguish them in the field, because the treatment is the same.

Both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia can mimic intoxication. Always suspect a diabetic cause behind apparent drunkenness.

topics.heading: Blood glucose meters & treatment
topics.html:
When a diabetic patient has altered mental status, measure the blood glucose, and generally use your own device rather than the patient's own meter. A reading below 70 mg/dL is the usual threshold for hypoglycemia, and it is where treatment starts in a symptomatic patient. Protocols vary on the exact number — some services use 60 — so learn the figure your own protocol uses and treat that as authoritative on the truck. The number matters less than the pairing: a low reading in a patient who is symptomatic is what you are treating, and a patient who is clearly hypoglycemic gets treated even if the meter reads a little above the line. Below 50 mg/dL, altered mental status is often significant and the patient may be unable to take oral glucose safely. A reading above 140 mg/dL is hyperglycemia, and above 300 mg/dL the patient becomes dehydrated and the symptoms become more serious.

Low glucose is more dangerous than high glucose. Giving glucose helps a hypoglycemic patient and does no meaningful harm to a hyperglycemic one, which is why, when you are uncertain, giving it is the safer default. Oral glucose has three criteria, all of which must be met:

  • The patient has a history of diabetes.
  • The patient has an altered mental status.
  • The patient is awake enough to swallow safely.

If the patient loses consciousness at any point, stop giving oral glucose and secure the airway.

sections.title: Seizures, Stroke & Syncope

topics.heading: Seizure disorders
topics.html:
A seizure is a sudden change in sensation, behavior or movement produced by irregular electrical activity in the brain, which may follow injury, infection or disease. A seizure is a sign, not a disease in itself.

The tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizure passes through three phases. In the tonic phase, which lasts up to 30 seconds, the body becomes rigid and breathing may stop. In the clonic phase, which lasts 1 to 2 minutes, the patient jerks violently, may foam at the mouth, and the face becomes cyanotic. In the postictal phase the patient is drowsy and confused and gradually clears; a transient one-sided weakness is possible.

The most common cause of seizures in adults is a missed dose of antiseizure medication. Febrile seizures are most common between 6 months and 3 years of age. The other causes include hypoxia, stroke, TBI, toxins, hypoglycemia, brain tumor and infection.

topics.heading: Seizure management
topics.html:
While the patient is convulsing, your job is to prevent injury, not to stop the seizure. Position the patient on the floor or ground, side-lying if there is no suspicion of spine injury. Loosen restrictive clothing, clear away nearby objects that could cause harm, and protect the patient from injury. Do not hold the patient still, and never place anything in the mouth.
