After the convulsions end, protect the airway, suctioning if the patient is drooling, and place the patient in the recovery position if there is no spine injury. Give oxygen guided by pulse oximetry, and assess and treat any injuries the seizure itself caused.

Status epilepticus is either 2 or more seizures in a row without a full recovery of consciousness between them, or a single seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes. It is a high-priority, life-threatening condition that calls for immediate transport and possibly an ALS intercept.

topics.heading: Stroke
topics.html:
An ischemic stroke, the most common type, occurs when a clot or embolism blocks an artery in the brain. A hemorrhagic stroke occurs when a vessel ruptures, often as a result of chronic hypertension or an aneurysm. Because motor control is crossed, damage on one side of the brain produces hemiparesis, weakness on one side of the body.

The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale consists of three tests, set out in the table below.

TestNormalAbnormal
Facial smile/grimaceEqual movement both sidesUnequal or no movement
Arm drift (eyes closed, arms out, 10 sec)Both arms move togetherOne drifts down/doesn't move
SpeechClearSlurred, wrong words, no speech

An abnormal result on any one of the three tests indicates roughly a 70% chance of acute stroke. A transient ischemic attack (TIA) produces the same symptoms, but they fully resolve within 24 hours. You cannot distinguish a TIA from a stroke in the field, so always treat the patient as a stroke. Several conditions mimic stroke: hypoglycemia, which is why you should check the glucose if you are allowed to, postictal weakness after a seizure, and infection or sepsis in the elderly.

Management consists of calm reassurance, oxygen if the SpO2 is below 94% or the patient is in distress, and transport to a stroke-capable facility. Determining and documenting the exact time of symptom onset, or the time the patient was last known well, is one of the most valuable things an EMT can do, because thrombolytic therapy typically requires an onset within 3 to 4.5 hours.

topics.heading: Dizziness & syncope
topics.html:
Syncope is a brief loss of consciousness (LOC) with spontaneous, rapid recovery once the patient is supine. Its causes fall into 4 categories: cardiovascular, such as a dysrhythmia or a vasovagal episode; hypovolemic, such as dehydration or internal bleeding, including ectopic pregnancy, abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding; structural or metabolic, such as stroke, seizure, hypoglycemia and inner-ear problems; and environmental or toxicologic, such as alcohol, carbon monoxide (CO) and panic attacks.

Management is straightforward: lay the patient flat, loosen tight clothing, give oxygen according to saturation and distress, call for ALS if there are signs of instability, and treat any injuries from the fall. Most patients with syncope should be evaluated by ALS, because a cardiac cause always warrants consideration.

takeaways: The brain needs water, glucose, and oxygen — deficiency in any causes rapid AMS.
Oral glucose requires: diabetes history + AMS + awake enough to swallow safely.
Low glucose is more dangerous than high glucose — when uncertain, giving glucose is the safer default.
Never put anything in the mouth of a seizing patient.
Status epilepticus: 2+ seizures without recovery, or a single seizure >5 minutes.
Cincinnati Stroke Scale: face, arm drift, speech — any one abnormal = high stroke probability.
You cannot distinguish TIA from stroke in the field — always treat as stroke.
Syncope recovers rapidly once supine; anything longer is 'unresponsiveness,' not syncope.

chapters.title: Allergic Reactions
chapters.intro: An allergic reaction becomes anaphylaxis when it involves the airway or the circulation, and at that point epinephrine is the treatment and time is the enemy. This chapter explains how the reaction happens, how to tell a mild reaction from a life-threatening one, the treatment sequence and the auto-injector, and the special considerations for children and for a second dose.

sections.title: Anaphylaxis & Epinephrine

topics.heading: How an allergic reaction happens
topics.html:
An allergic reaction takes more than one encounter with the allergen. The first exposure produces no reaction at all; what it does is prompt the immune system to build antibodies specific to that allergen. On the second exposure and on every one after it, those waiting antibodies bind the allergen, and that binding releases histamine and other chemicals into the body.

Those chemicals set off the allergic response as a cascade that strikes several systems at once. The blood vessels dilate, which lowers cardiac output and puts the patient at risk of shock. The capillaries leak, producing angioedema, the swelling of the face, lips, tongue and airway. The bronchioles constrict and fill with mucus, narrowing the airways and producing wheezing. The skin breaks out in hives and itching.

The allergens responsible fall into a few familiar groups. Insects, particularly bees and wasps, cause reactions that are rapid and severe. Foods are the next group, and peanuts are especially severe and especially rapid. Then come plants such as poison ivy, medications such as penicillin, and latex. A severe reaction usually begins immediately, but it can be delayed by 30 minutes or more, and a reaction that begins mild can escalate into anaphylaxis within minutes.

topics.heading: Distinguishing anaphylaxis from a mild reaction
topics.html:
What separates a life-threatening reaction from an uncomfortable one is not how distressed the patient looks but which systems the reaction has reached. A reaction is anaphylaxis when it produces either respiratory distress or signs and symptoms of shock. Either finding alone is enough; you do not wait for both before you treat. The table below compares the two across the systems you assess.

SystemAllergic (non-life-threatening)Anaphylactic (life-threatening)
RespiratorySneezing, coughDyspnea, chest tightness, wheezing, stridor
SkinLocal hives/rednessWidespread hives, pallor, diffuse redness
SwellingLocalFace, lips, eyes, tongue, mouth
VitalsNormal/near-normalTachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, ↓SpO2
Mental statusNormal, may be anxiousSyncope, AMS, impending doom

topics.heading: Treatment & epinephrine
topics.html:
Any patient in respiratory distress, and every patient who is anaphylactic, receives high-concentration oxygen (O2) by nonrebreather mask (NRB). For anaphylaxis, though, oxygen is not the intervention that decides the outcome. Prompt epinephrine is the single most important lifesaving measure available to you.

The decision to give it rests on two things: signs of anaphylaxis — respiratory distress, swelling of the face or airway, or signs of shock — and access to the drug, either because the patient has a prescribed auto-injector of their own or because your protocol allows the EMT to carry epinephrine. A history of earlier reactions supports the picture, but a first-ever reaction is treated the same way. When both are present, administer the epinephrine in accordance with medical direction. When no auto-injector is available and your protocol does not allow EMT-carried epinephrine, treat the patient for shock, transport immediately, and request an advanced life support (ALS) intercept.

Self-administered epinephrine works on two fronts at once: it constricts the blood vessels, which raises blood pressure (BP), and it dilates the bronchioles, which improves breathing. To give it, check the expiration date, remove the cap, and press the injector firmly against the outer thigh, midway between the waist and the knee, holding it there until the dose is fully injected. Reassess the patient 2 minutes later.

topics.heading: Pediatric note & additional doses
topics.html:
The auto-injector comes in two sizes. The adult injector delivers 0.3 mg of epinephrine, and the pediatric injector, used for a child weighing less than 66 lbs (30 kg), delivers 0.15 mg. Anaphylaxis does occur in infants, and it is missed more often than it is absent. The signs are harder to read at that age — hives, swelling, persistent vomiting, coughing or wheezing, mottling and inconsolable crying — so the reaction goes unrecognized and epinephrine is under-used. Age is never a reason to withhold it.

A second dose is sometimes needed, and giving one depends on two things: having additional auto-injectors on hand, and obtaining authorization from medical direction for the repeat dose.

takeaways: Anaphylaxis criterion: respiratory distress OR shock signs — not both required.
Epinephrine is the single most important treatment for anaphylaxis — more critical than routine ABC management alone here.
Epi mechanism: alpha receptors (vasoconstriction, less edema) + beta receptors (bronchodilation).
Auto-injector dose: adult 0.3 mg, child (<66 lbs) 0.15 mg.
Confirm any assisted medication is the patient's own prescription.
Reassess 2 minutes after epi — some symptom relief and an increased pulse are expected, normal effects.

chapters.title: Infectious Diseases and Sepsis
chapters.intro: Infectious disease is both a hazard to the EMT and a category of patient. This chapter covers how diseases spread and a reference to the communicable diseases of concern, with detail on hepatitis, HIV, influenza, tuberculosis and meningitis, and then sepsis: what it is, how the SIRS and qSOFA criteria help recognize it, and how it is managed.

topics.heading: How diseases spread
topics.html:
Two kinds of microorganism account for most of the infections an EMT meets. Bacteria are living, single-celled organisms that are able to reproduce independently. Viruses are not cells at all: each one is a protein coat enclosing genetic material (DNA/RNA), and a virus can only reproduce by using a host.

Two words that sound interchangeable are not. A disease is infectious when it is caused by a microbe, and communicable when it can spread from person to person. Lyme disease shows the difference. It is infectious, because bacteria delivered by a tick bite cause it, but it is not communicable, because a patient who has it cannot pass it to you.

topics.heading: Communicable disease quick reference
topics.html:
The table below sets out the communicable diseases an EMT is most likely to encounter, how each one is transmitted and the signs that should raise suspicion.

DiseaseTransmissionKey signs
ChickenpoxAirborne, contact with soresFever, itchy rash (chest/abdomen/back)
MeaslesAirborne dropletsFever, cough, eye irritation, rash
MumpsSaliva droplets/contactPainful parotid swelling
Hepatitis AFecal-oralNausea, jaundice
Hepatitis B/CBlood, semen, other body fluidsNausea, jaundice (often asymptomatic in Hep C)
HIV/AIDSBlood, semen, breast milkFever/fatigue early; opportunistic infections later
InfluenzaAirborne droplets, contactFever, nonproductive cough, muscle aches
CroupAirborne droplets, fomitesBarking cough (kids)
PertussisAirborne dropletsSevere coughing fits, whoop on inspiration
Pneumococcal pneumoniaDropletsFever, chills, SOB, productive cough
TuberculosisAirborne dropletsCough, fever, night sweats, weight loss
Meningococcal meningitisDirect contactAbrupt fever, severe headache, nuchal rigidity, petechiae

topics.heading: Hepatitis, HIV & influenza detail
topics.html:
The hepatitis viruses share a name and a target organ but differ in how they spread and how they end. Hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route; patients usually recover fully, and a vaccine is available. Hepatitis B spreads through blood and other body fluids and can become chronic, carrying a risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer; a vaccine is available for it as well. Hepatitis C also spreads through blood and body fluids, mainly through shared needles. It is often asymptomatic for years, and there is no vaccine against it, although effective curative regimens now exist.

HIV/AIDS is transmitted by needle-sharing, by unprotected sex and from mother to newborn. How communicable it is tracks the viral load: treatment can drive the viral load to undetectable levels, which virtually eliminates the risk of transmission. If you are exposed, wash the site first, then begin postexposure prophylaxis (PEP), a course of antiviral medication taken for 28 days. Timing is what makes PEP work: start it as soon as possible, ideally within hours of the exposure, and never later than 72 hours, after which it is no longer expected to help.

Influenza spreads both by airborne droplets and by contact. Antiviral medication helps only if it is started within 48 hours of the onset of symptoms, which is why recognizing the illness early matters, and the annual vaccine is built around the strains predicted for the coming season.

topics.heading: Tuberculosis & meningitis
topics.html:
A patient with latent tuberculosis (TB) is infected but has no symptoms and is not contagious, and roughly 90 percent of these patients never go on to develop active disease. When TB is suspected, an N-95 respirator is required rather than a surgical mask, because a surgical mask does not filter the small particles that carry the organism. After an exposure, report it to the receiving hospital and have a baseline skin test done, followed by a repeat test later.

Meningococcal meningitis announces itself abruptly. The patient develops fever, a severe headache, nuchal rigidity (a neck so stiff that the chin cannot be brought to the chest), photophobia, and petechiae, small spots in the skin that do not blanch when they are pressed. The complications are severe: shock, brain damage and deafness. Standard Precautions generally protect you; only very close contact, such as mouth-to-mouth ventilation, may warrant prophylactic antibiotics.

topics.heading: STIs, Lyme disease & emerging/resistant disease
topics.html:
Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) divide by the organism responsible. The viral STIs include HIV, hepatitis A/B/C, herpes and human papillomavirus (HPV). The bacterial STIs are chlamydia, gonorrhea and syphilis, all of which can be treated with antibiotics.

Lyme disease is carried by ticks, and in most patients it announces itself with the classic bull's-eye rash within a week of the bite. It responds to antibiotics, most effectively when treatment starts early. A tick generally has to feed for at least 36 hours before it transmits the organism, so a tick found and removed promptly is much less likely to have caused infection.

Antibiotic resistance is a different kind of problem. Organisms such as MRSA, VRE and C. diff spread in patients you will often not know are carrying them, which is precisely why Standard Precautions are applied to every patient rather than to selected ones.

The recently emerged diseases (HIV/AIDS, SARS, Ebola, MERS and Zika) have all followed the same pattern: initial panic, then investigation, then protocols, and finally mitigation. When a new disease is in the news, verify what you hear against guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) or your local health department rather than relying on news reports.

sections.title: Sepsis

topics.heading: What sepsis actually is
topics.html:
Sepsis is a life-threatening condition that arises from the body's own abnormal and counterproductive response to an infection. The distinction matters: the damage to tissues and organs is done by that response, not by the infection alone. When sepsis progresses to shock, with hypotension that does not respond to intravenous (IV) fluids, it is called septic shock.

Two mechanisms drive the fall in perfusion, in varying combination. The capillaries become leaky, so fluid is lost out of the vascular space, and the vessels dilate, which prevents adequate venous return to the heart.

Infection anywhere in the body can lead to sepsis, but a few sources are common. The lungs, in the form of pneumonia, are one; the gastrointestinal tract, often after surgery, is another; the genitourinary tract, frequently in patients with urinary catheters, is a third; the skin and soft tissue, around IV catheters or pressure sores, is a fourth; and the central nervous system (CNS), as in meningitis, is a fifth. In many cases no source is ever clearly identified.

topics.heading: Assessment — SIRS & qSOFA
topics.html:
Two field tools help you think about sepsis, and they answer different questions. The first is the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria. In a patient with a documented or suspected infection, meeting two or more of the following raises the likelihood of sepsis:

  • A temperature below 96.8°F (36°C) or above 100.4°F (38°C)
  • A heart rate (HR) above 90 beats per minute
  • A respiratory rate (RR) above 20 breaths per minute
  • A white blood cell (WBC) count above 12,000 or below 4,000, a lab value the hospital obtains, not the EMT

In the field you are working with the three vital-sign criteria. Many EMS sepsis screens add a systolic blood pressure (BP) below 90 mmHg or altered mental status that is new or has worsened. Those are not SIRS criteria; they are signs that sepsis is already affecting perfusion or the brain, and your protocol may count them.

SIRS is an imperfect screen, and you should treat it as a prompt rather than a verdict: trauma patients, for example, frequently meet 2 of the criteria without being septic.

Some septic patients are hypothermic rather than febrile, so do not rule sepsis out on the basis of temperature alone.

The second tool, qSOFA, asks a different question. Its three findings are altered mental status, a respiratory rate of 22 or more and a systolic blood pressure of 100 mmHg or less, and together they do not predict who has sepsis; they predict which septic patients face a worse prognosis. No field tool is 100 percent accurate, so follow your local protocol.

topics.heading: Management
topics.html:
The EMT's care of the septic patient is supportive. Give oxygen as needed to maintain a saturation of at least 94 percent, take steps to keep the patient's body temperature normal, and call for advanced life support (ALS) as appropriate.

The most valuable thing you do may be a radio call. If the patient meets the SIRS criteria, or similar criteria used by your system, notify the emergency department (ED) of a sepsis alert. Earlier diagnosis leads to earlier treatment and to higher survival, and for a stable septic patient that notification is probably the single most valuable action an EMT can take.

takeaways: Infectious = caused by a microbe; communicable = can spread person-to-person — not the same thing.
N-95 (not a surgical mask) is required for suspected TB.
Nuchal rigidity + petechiae + abrupt fever/headache = suspect meningococcal meningitis.
Sepsis = the body's own harmful overreaction to infection, not just the infection itself.
SIRS: ≥2 of temp >100.4°F or <96.8°F, HR>90, RR>20, abnormal WBC — raises sepsis suspicion; many EMS screens add SBP<90 or new AMS.
Some septic patients are hypothermic, not febrile.
A sepsis alert to the receiving ED may be the single most valuable action for a stable septic patient.

chapters.title: Poisoning and Overdose Emergencies
chapters.intro: A poison is any substance that harms the body, and the route it takes in decides much of the care. This chapter covers the core concepts and activated charcoal, the antidotes an EMT may use, inhaled poisons such as carbon monoxide, absorbed and injected poisons, and then alcohol and the five categories of abused substances, with the signs and care for each.

topics.heading: Poisoning — core concepts
topics.html:
A poison is any substance that can harm the body, and a toxin is a poison produced by a living organism. Poisoning is most serious in three groups of patients: those who are already ill, the very young, and older adults. A poison reaches the body by one of four routes of entry. It can be ingested, inhaled, absorbed through unbroken skin, or injected through the skin by something that penetrates it.

Medical direction and poison control will want a particular set of facts, so gather them while you work. Find out exactly what the substance was, since the spelling matters and the container itself is worth bringing along when it is safe to do so; when the exposure happened; how much was taken; what has already been done for the patient; the patient's estimated weight, which is critical for pediatric dosing; and the effects the patient is showing now.

topics.heading: Activated charcoal
topics.html:
Activated charcoal works by adsorption: the poison binds to the surface of the charcoal rather than being taken up by the body. That makes it a way of preventing or reducing absorption, not an antidote, and it does nothing about poison that has already reached the bloodstream. It is used only rarely today, for specific overdoses, and always under medical direction, usually in consultation with poison control.

Several contraindications rule it out. Do not give activated charcoal to a patient who cannot swallow, who has an altered mental status, or who has ingested an acid or an alkali, and do not give it to a patient who is coughing violently, because of the risk of aspiration. Never force it on a patient who is refusing it.

topics.heading: Antidotes
topics.html:
Genuine antidotes are rare. Most of the treatment of poisoning consists of preventing further absorption and supporting the patient, not of giving a drug that undoes the poison. Naloxone is one of the exceptions: it reverses the central nervous system (CNS) and respiratory depression caused by opioids, and it has no effect at all in a patient who has taken no narcotic.

Acetaminophen poisoning deserves separate attention because its timing is deceptive. The toxic effects are delayed as the liver is progressively overwhelmed over a period of hours, and the antidote, N-acetylcysteine, works best when it is started within 8 to 10 hours of ingestion, becoming steadily less effective after that. The early symptoms, from about 4 to 12 hours, are deceptively mild: nausea and loss of appetite. Right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain and jaundice do not appear until 1 to 2 days later, by which point the best window for treatment has passed. For that reason, always suspect that acetaminophen may be involved in any overdose.

topics.heading: Inhaled poisons — carbon monoxide & smoke
topics.html:
Carbon monoxide (CO) is the most common inhaled poison. It is odorless, colorless and tasteless, and it prevents red blood cells from carrying oxygen normally. Its early signs are deceptively flu-like, with headache, dizziness and nausea, so the poisoning is easy to mistake for an ordinary illness. Pulse oximetry is no help and is actively misleading, because the readings it gives are falsely high; give oxygen regardless of a reassuring SpO2 whenever CO is suspected. The cherry-red skin of the older textbooks is a myth and is not typically seen.

Smoke inhalation combines thermal burns with chemical and irritant poisoning. The signs that the airway has been injured are coughing, a smoky or chemical odor to the breath, carbon residue in the mouth or nose, and singed nasal hairs. Give oxygen even when the SpO2 reads 100 percent, since carboxyhemoglobin reads the same as oxyhemoglobin on a standard pulse oximeter.

One inhalation hazard is directed at the rescuer as much as the patient. In a so-called detergent suicide, hydrogen sulfide gas is generated inside a small enclosed space, often a car, with the windows and doors taped shut and warning signs posted. Do not enter; call the appropriate hazmat team.

topics.heading: Absorbed & injected poisons
topics.html:
A poison that can be absorbed through the patient's skin can be absorbed through yours, which means decontamination may have to come before any contact, and a contaminated patient must never be brought into your ambulance untreated. Brush a dry powder off the skin. Irrigate a liquid, and anything in the eyes, with clean water for at least 20 minutes. Never attempt to neutralize an acid or an alkali with vinegar or baking soda: the reaction produces heat and damages the tissue further.

Poison control centers are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, anywhere in the country, at 1-800-222-1222.

sections.title: Alcohol & Substance Abuse

topics.heading: Alcohol abuse
topics.html:
Never let an assumption of intoxication cost a patient the medical care he or she needs. Diabetes, epilepsy, head injury, high fever and hypoxia can all mimic intoxication, and each of them must be ruled out rather than assumed away. A patient can also be both things at once: intoxicated and having a myocardial infarction (MI), or intoxicated and hypoglycemic.

Withdrawal from alcohol is itself dangerous. It can produce seizures or delirium tremens (DTs), with sweating, trembling, anxiety and hallucinations, and untreated it can be fatal, so every patient with seizures or the DTs must be transported promptly. Remember as well that a patient under the influence of alcohol cannot make an informed refusal of care.

topics.heading: Substance abuse — five categories
topics.html:
Abused substances fall into five categories. The table below gives the effect each category produces and the drugs most often seen in it.

CategoryEffectExamples
Opioids/narcoticsCNS depressant, intense relaxationCodeine, OxyContin, heroin, fentanyl
UppersStimulant, excitementCaffeine, meth, cocaine, bath salts
DownersCNS depressant, sedationBenzodiazepines, barbiturates, GHB
HallucinogensPerception distortionLSD, PCP, mushrooms, MDMA
Volatile chemicalsInitial rush → depressantCleaning fluid, glue, model cement

The opioid category produces the most recognizable overdose. The classic opioid triad is a coma or depressed level of consciousness (LOC), pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression. Fentanyl mixed into heroin causes overdoses that are far more potent and far more rapid than heroin alone.

topics.heading: Signs by category & care
topics.html:
Each category has a field picture of its own, and recognizing it tells you what to expect next:

  • Uppers: excitement, an increased pulse and rate of breathing, dilated pupils and sweating.
  • Downers: a sluggish patient with poor coordination and a low pulse and rate of breathing.
  • Opioids: a decreased pulse, a decreased rate and depth of breathing, pinpoint pupils, and a patient who is very sleepy.
  • Hallucinogens: a fast pulse, dilated pupils, and a patient who sees or hears things that are not there.
  • Volatile chemicals: a dazed patient, possibly in a coma, with swollen membranes in the nose and mouth.

The care is much the same whatever the substance. Begin with scene safety, watching for needles and weapons, and take Standard Precautions. Carry out the primary assessment and provide basic life support (BLS), supporting oxygenation and ventilation as the patient needs. If the patient is in respiratory failure and your protocol allows it, give naloxone intranasally. Perform a full physical exam and look for track marks, bearing in mind that their absence does not rule out injection drug use. Then transport, contact medical direction, and watch for seizures and vomiting on the way.

Many patients who have taken drugs seem calm at first and then turn violent, so stay alert throughout the call. Protect yourself from the substance as well as from the patient: many hallucinogens are absorbed through skin and mucous membranes, and you should never touch or taste any suspected illicit substance.

takeaways: Four routes of poison entry: ingested, inhaled, absorbed, injected.
Activated charcoal is an absorption-preventer, not an antidote — contraindicated with AMS or caustic ingestion.
Naloxone reverses opioid overdose only — no effect if no narcotic is present.
CO poisoning causes falsely HIGH pulse ox readings — give O2 regardless of the reading if suspected.
Never neutralize acid/alkali burns with vinegar/baking soda — the reaction generates heat.
An alcohol- or drug-intoxicated patient cannot give a valid informed refusal.
Opioid triad: coma, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression.

chapters.title: Abdominal Emergencies
chapters.intro: Abdominal pain is common, often vague, and occasionally the first sign of a condition that will kill within hours. This chapter distinguishes the types of abdominal pain and what each suggests, surveys the key conditions from appendicitis to a leaking aortic aneurysm, and sets out the assessment sequence, the physical exam and the care, with attention to the older patient whose signs are muted.

topics.heading: Types of abdominal pain — the key differentiator
topics.html:
The character of a patient's abdominal pain is the single most useful clue to where it is coming from, because the different structures of the abdomen are supplied by different kinds of nerves. The organs themselves have few nerve endings, so pain that arises in an organ is poorly defined. The parietal peritoneum that lines the abdominal cavity has a rich nerve supply, so pain that arises there is sharp and easy to point to. The table below sets out the four types of abdominal pain, where each originates and how each presents.

TypeOriginCharacter
Visceral painThe organs themselves (few nerve endings)Dull, achy, intermittent, hard to localize
Parietal painParietal peritoneum (rich nerve supply)Sharp, constant, well-localized; worsens with movement
Tearing painOnly the aorta and stomach can produce thisAAA (tearing back pain) or a perforating stomach ulcer
Referred painFelt away from the actual source via shared nerve pathwaysGallbladder → right shoulder; spleen injury → left shoulder

Two of these types deserve a particular note. Tearing pain can be produced by only two structures, the aorta and the stomach, so a patient who describes a tearing pain should make you think of an abdominal aortic aneurysm, which classically produces tearing back pain, or of a perforating stomach ulcer. Referred pain is felt away from its actual source because the affected organ shares a nerve pathway with a distant part of the body; the classic examples are gallbladder pain felt in the right shoulder and the pain of an injured spleen felt in the left shoulder.

topics.heading: Key abdominal conditions
topics.html:
A handful of conditions account for most of the serious abdominal pain you will see, and each has a presentation you should be able to recognize. Appendicitis classically begins with nausea, followed by pain that starts around the umbilicus and then migrates to become persistent pain in the right lower quadrant (RLQ). If the appendix ruptures, the patient experiences a sudden, severe spike in pain as the lining of the abdomen becomes inflamed. That inflammation is peritonitis, which is extremely painful and produces a rigid abdomen with involuntary guarding. Peritonitis is life-threatening and often requires surgery.

Cholecystitis, inflammation of the gallbladder that is usually caused by gallstones, produces severe pain in the right upper quadrant (RUQ) or the epigastrium that is often referred to the right shoulder. Because of where it is felt, it is frequently confused with cardiac pain. Pancreatitis is common in patients with chronic alcohol use and produces epigastric pain that radiates to the back or the shoulders.

Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding differs from the conditions above in that it often occurs without any pain at all. Its signs are dark, tarry stools or frank blood from the rectum and, when the bleeding is in the upper GI tract, vomit that looks like coffee grounds. Esophageal varices, which develop with chronic alcohol use, can bleed massively and compromise the airway.

An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) presents in one of two ways. A slow leak produces a gradual onset of sharp or tearing pain that radiates to the back. A sudden rupture produces excruciating pain together with shock, and the pulses may be unequal between the limbs.

A hernia is a hole in the abdominal wall through which tissue protrudes. It becomes life-threatening only when the protruding tissue causes an obstruction or becomes strangulated, and because you cannot tell that from the outside, every painful hernia is transported. Renal colic, the pain of a kidney stone, is severe flank pain that radiates to the groin. These patients are classically described as writhing, unable to find a comfortable position, which sets them apart from the patient with peritonitis, who lies perfectly still.

Finally, two of the most dangerous causes are the easiest to miss. A myocardial infarction (MI) can present as epigastric pain that the patient describes as indigestion, so treat all epigastric pain as possibly cardiac until proven otherwise. Ectopic pregnancy is the most serious female-specific cause of abdominal pain. Assume that any woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain has an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise; she will not look pregnant.

sections.title: Assessment & Care

topics.heading: Assessment sequence
topics.html:
Assessment of the patient with abdominal pain follows the standard sequence, beginning with the scene size-up. Because these patients frequently vomit, take steps to protect yourself before you approach. In the primary assessment, look for the early signs of shock before you take a single vital sign: altered mental status (AMS), anxiety, and skin that is pale, cool and moist, together with a rapid pulse and rapid respirations. Then obtain a history using OPQRST and SAMPLE, perform the physical exam, and take vital signs every 5 minutes.

For a female patient, the history must include questions that many patients will not volunteer, so ask them directly and in private. Find out where she is in her menstrual cycle, whether her period is late, whether she has had any bleeding outside her period, and whether there is any possibility that she is pregnant. Ask about pregnancy outright rather than leaving it to the patient to raise. A "yes" to any of these questions should make you suspect an ectopic pregnancy, but a set of "no" answers does not rule one out.

topics.heading: Physical exam & geriatric considerations
topics.html:
The physical exam of the abdomen consists of inspection followed by palpation, and the order in which you palpate matters. Palpate the painful area last, because pressing on it first can mask the patient's response when you examine the other quadrants. Once you have found pain or another abnormality, stop palpating that area. Watch for guarding, which the patient may show by drawing the arms across the abdomen or by tensing the abdominal muscles before you have even touched them.

Older patients call for particular caution. Decreased pain perception in the elderly makes the history harder to take, and mortality for the same abdominal condition can be up to 9 times higher than in a younger patient. Many older patients take beta blockers, which can mask the tachycardia that normally accompanies shock, so a pulse that appears normal might actually mean shock.

topics.heading: Care
topics.html:
Care for the patient with abdominal pain is supportive, and it begins with the airway. An altered mental status can compromise the airway, and vomiting is common, so keep suction ready. Give oxygen if the patient is hypoxic or in distress, or if the pulse oximeter reading is unreliable, with a target saturation of at least 94%. Allow the patient to assume a position of comfort unless shock or an airway problem overrides that choice, in which case place the patient in the left lateral recumbent position.

Never give an abdominal pain patient anything by mouth. Transport promptly, and do not let a lack of findings reassure you: the absence of abnormal findings does not mean the condition is not serious.

takeaways: Visceral pain = dull/diffuse (organ itself); parietal pain = sharp/localized (peritoneum).
Referred pain: gallbladder → right shoulder; spleen → left shoulder.
Renal colic patients writhe; peritonitis patients lie very still — a useful visual differentiator.
Assume any woman of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain has an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Treat all epigastric pain as possibly cardiac until proven otherwise.
Never give an abdominal-pain patient anything by mouth.
Palpate the painful quadrant last, and stop once tenderness is found.

chapters.title: Behavioral and Psychiatric Emergencies and Suicide
chapters.intro: A behavioral emergency is any situation in which a person's behavior is unacceptable or intolerable to themselves or others, and the first job is to rule out the medical conditions that mimic one. This chapter covers assessment and de-escalation, acute psychosis, suicide, and the safety, legal and procedural rules for restraining an aggressive patient, including excited delirium.

topics.heading: What is a behavioral emergency?
topics.html: A behavioral emergency is abnormal behavior, within a given situation, that is unacceptable or intolerable to the patient, the family or the community, and it is often potentially harmful to the patient or to others. The word "abnormal" has to be read in context, because what counts as normal depends on the situation. Cultural background matters as well: a behavior that seems unusual to you may be entirely normal within the patient's culture.

topics.heading: Physical causes that mimic psychiatric emergencies — always rule out first
topics.html:
Before you conclude that a patient's behavior has a psychiatric cause, you must rule out the physical conditions that can produce the same picture. The table below lists the most important physical mimics and the signs that point to each.

CauseKey signs
Low blood sugarRapid-onset erratic/hostile behavior, sweating, rapid pulse + normal BP
HypoxiaRestlessness, confusion, cyanosis
StrokeConfusion, impaired speech, one-sided weakness
Head traumaPersonality changes, AMS, amnesia
SeizuresPostictal AMS
Cold/heat extremesShivering/numbness/AMS or decreased LOC

Ruling out a medical cause does not mean choosing between two possibilities. Medical and psychiatric conditions can coexist, and a real medical problem can also worsen the symptoms of a chronic psychiatric illness.

topics.heading: Acute psychosis
topics.html: Acute psychosis is a severe break in the patient's ability to process reality. It is associated with schizophrenia and is defined by the presence of at least 1 of four features. The first is hallucinations; auditory hallucinations are typically psychiatric in origin, but visual hallucinations can also have a medical cause, such as drug intoxication or alcohol withdrawal. The second is delusions, which are false, fixed beliefs. The third is catatonia, in which the patient either barely interacts with the surroundings at all or moves in wildly inappropriate ways. The fourth is thought disorder.

topics.heading: De-escalation & assessment sequence
topics.html:
Your approach to the patient does much of the work of the assessment. Identify yourself and your role, speak slowly and calmly, maintain eye contact, and listen actively. Stay non-judgmental, keep your body language positive, and acknowledge the patient's feelings. Stay at least 3 feet away, and watch throughout for signs that the patient's aggression is escalating.

The assessment itself follows the usual order. The scene size-up comes first, and if the scene calls for it, the police go in before you do. Identify yourself, then perform the primary assessment, screening specifically for medical and traumatic causes of the behavior. Carry out as detailed an exam as the patient will allow, and take a thorough history, including any past psychiatric history, current medications and any missed doses, the possibility of diabetes, and substance use.

sections.title: Aggressive Patients, Restraint & Excited Delirium

topics.heading: Aggressive/hostile patients — safety precautions
topics.html:
An aggressive or hostile patient is a danger to you before anything else, and a few rules protect you. Never isolate yourself from your partner or from other help, always maintain an escape route, and never let the patient get between you and the door. Watch for weapons, and avoid kitchens in particular, because they are a common source of them.

A calm patient can turn aggressive without warning, so do not relax because the patient seems settled. Be especially alert to sudden silence in a patient who was agitated a moment before. It may not mean the patient is calming down; it can indicate that a serious medical emergency is developing.

topics.heading: Reasonable force & restraint — legal note
topics.html:
As a general rule, an EMT cannot legally restrain, forcibly move or force care on a behavioral-emergency patient, even when the family asks you to. That authority belongs to law enforcement, and in some systems to a physician acting through medical direction. Where force is authorized, it is limited to reasonable force, which means only the force necessary to prevent the patient from harming himself or herself or others.

The rule is different when the cause is medical or traumatic. A combative hypoglycemic patient, for example, may be restrained so that treatment can be given; that is a medical necessity, not a behavioral-emergency restraint. In any case, never attempt to restrain a patient without sufficient personnel. Avoid handcuffs and plastic restraints, which cause soft tissue damage; soft restraints are preferred where local protocol authorizes them.

topics.heading: Excited delirium — critical danger
topics.html: Excited delirium (now often called hyperactive delirium with severe agitation) is a state of extreme agitation and psychosis that most often arises from uncontrolled psychiatric illness, stimulant intoxication, or both. The patient shows bizarre and aggressive behavior, is insensitive to pain, displays unexpected strength and is hyperthermic. The critical danger comes after the struggle: these patients can suddenly stop struggling and, within minutes, develop inadequate or absent respirations and go into cardiac arrest. Constant monitoring is essential even after the patient appears to have calmed down.

topics.heading: Restraint procedure
topics.html:
When restraint is authorized and necessary, it is carried out as a planned procedure with adequate help. The steps are as follows.

  1. Assemble adequate help and plan the approach. Stay beyond the patient's reach until you are ready, and once the decision is made, act quickly.
  2. Assign one EMT to talk to and reassure the patient throughout. Use a minimum of 4 rescuers, one for each limb.
  3. Apply restraints approved by medical direction to all 4 limbs.
  4. Position the patient face-up. Never place a restrained patient prone or in any position that restricts movement of the chest wall, and never hog-tie a patient.
  5. Monitor the airway constantly, and contact ALS, because chemical sedation may be needed.
  6. Reassess distal circulation frequently.
  7. Never remove police restraints until you are certain that the soft restraints will hold.

Positional asphyxia from improper restraint has caused patient deaths. The face-up rule is the single most important safety rule in this chapter.

topics.heading: Medical/legal considerations
topics.html: A refusal of care from a behavioral-emergency patient carries significant risk, and the law treats it differently from other refusals. Most states allow you to transport such a patient against his or her will if the patient is a danger to self or others, which is an exception to the normal rules of consent. Whenever possible, have an EMT of the same sex as the patient attend the patient; this protects you against false accusations of misconduct. For an aggressive or violent patient, have law enforcement accompany the transport, which protects both you and the patient.

takeaways: Always rule out hypoglycemia, hypoxia, stroke, and head trauma before assuming a purely psychiatric cause.
A calm patient can turn aggressive without warning — never let your guard down.
EMTs generally cannot legally restrain a behavioral-emergency patient without law enforcement authority.
Restrained patients must always be face-up, never prone or hog-tied — positional asphyxia kills.
Excited delirium: sudden calm after struggling can mean imminent cardiac arrest, not resolution.
Most states allow transport against will only when the patient is a danger to self or others.

chapters.title: Hematologic and Renal Emergencies
chapters.intro: Blood that will not clot, blood that clots too readily and kidneys that no longer filter each produce emergencies of their own. This chapter covers coagulopathies and anticoagulant medications, anemia and sickle cell disease, and then the renal system: urinary tract infection and kidney stones, renal failure and dialysis, the emergencies particular to end-stage renal disease, and the transplant patient.

topics.heading: Blood clotting & coagulopathies
topics.html: The body stops bleeding with two systems working together. The first is platelet aggregation, the fastest and initial response, in which platelets gather at the site of the injury. The second is the clotting factors, proteins made in the liver that form the more stable, lasting clot. A coagulopathy is any abnormality of clotting. The form most relevant to the EMT is blood that clots too slowly, which produces uncontrolled bleeding, and its most common cause is a prescribed blood-thinning medication.

topics.heading: Blood thinner medications
topics.html:
Blood thinners fall into two groups according to which part of the clotting process they interfere with. The table below sets out the two types, their mechanisms and common examples.

TypeMechanismExamples
AnticoagulantsInhibit clotting factorsWarfarin (Coumadin), Eliquis, Xarelto, Lovenox
Antiplatelet agentsInhibit platelet aggregationAspirin, Plavix

Always ask trauma patients specifically whether they take a blood thinner. In a patient on one of these medications, even a seemingly minor injury, such as a minor bump to the head, carries a genuinely elevated risk of bleeding; significant intracranial bleeding can follow a mechanism that looks trivial. Notify the hospital early when a trauma patient takes a blood thinner.

topics.heading: Anemia & sickle cell disease
topics.html:
Anemia is a deficiency in the number of red blood cells (RBCs), and how it presents depends on how quickly it developed. Acute anemia, from trauma or a sudden GI bleed, produces the signs of shock rapidly. Chronic anemia, from heavy menstrual periods or slow GI blood loss, produces pallor, fatigue and pale conjunctiva, and the signs of shock appear only late.

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited defect of hemoglobin that gives the red blood cells an abnormal shape; it is most common in patients of African descent. The abnormally shaped cells clump together and block small vessels, a process called sludging, and sludging produces the complications of the disease. A sickle cell crisis, or pain crisis, causes severe pain in the arms, legs, chest or abdomen. Acute chest syndrome causes shortness of breath (SOB), chest pain and hypoxia. Sludging can also cause priapism, stroke and jaundice.

Sickle cell trait is not the same as sickle cell disease. Trait carriers usually have no complications and have a normal lifespan. In a patient with the disease, never assume that a presentation is "just another pain crisis," because the risk of infection, stroke and a chest crisis is high at the same time.

sections.title: The Renal System & Dialysis

topics.heading: UTIs, kidney stones & catheters
topics.html: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the most common disease of the renal and urinary system. They are bacterial and are usually limited to the bladder. Left untreated, the infection can ascend to the kidney, where it is called pyelonephritis; the patient then has unilateral flank pain and is sicker overall. Untreated pyelonephritis can become life-threatening by progressing to sepsis, especially in the elderly. Kidney stones cause severe unilateral flank pain that radiates to the groin as the stone descends the ureter.

topics.heading: Renal failure & dialysis
topics.html:
Renal failure may be acute or chronic. Acute renal failure, from causes such as shock or a toxic ingestion, is sometimes recoverable if the cause is corrected quickly. Chronic renal failure, from causes such as diabetes and hypertension, is progressive and often irreversible. End-stage renal disease (ESRD) requires dialysis, which takes one of the two forms set out in the table below.

TypeMechanism
Hemodialysis (HD)Blood pumped through a machine's filters via a catheter or A-V fistula, ~3x/week, 3–4 hrs each
Peritoneal dialysis (PD)Abdominal catheter, dialysis fluid dwells in the peritoneal cavity, drained ("exchange"); done more frequently at home

Never take a blood pressure on the arm with a fistula. A properly functioning A-V fistula has a palpable vibration, called a thrill.

topics.heading: ESRD emergencies
topics.html:
The patient with ESRD who misses dialysis presents much like a patient in congestive heart failure (CHF), because fluid the kidneys cannot remove overloads the circulation; the signs are shortness of breath and peripheral edema. The more dangerous consequence is elevated potassium, which can cause fatal dysrhythmias. Cardiac arrest in an ESRD patient may not respond to standard defibrillation.

Dialysis itself produces complications. A fistula may bleed or clot; for bleeding, use direct pressure, and avoid a tourniquet unless the bleeding is life-threatening — the fistula is the patient's lifeline for dialysis and is worth preserving where it safely can be. Peritoneal dialysis can lead to peritonitis, which presents with abdominal pain, fever and cloudy dialysis fluid that resembles chicken broth. Transport the drained bag with the patient so that the fluid can be tested.

topics.heading: Kidney transplant patients
topics.html: The kidney is the most commonly transplanted organ. A transplant patient must take immunosuppressant medications for life to prevent rejection of the new kidney, and those same drugs make the patient more susceptible to serious infections, including sepsis.

takeaways: Always ask trauma patients about blood thinner use — even minor injuries carry elevated bleeding risk.
Sickle cell trait is not the same as sickle cell disease — trait carriers usually have no complications.
Never take a BP on an arm with a dialysis fistula.
Missed dialysis can cause dangerous hyperkalemia and CHF-like fluid overload symptoms.
Cloudy peritoneal dialysis fluid (like chicken broth) suggests peritonitis — bring the bag to the hospital.
Kidney transplant patients on immunosuppressants are at higher risk for serious infection/sepsis.

chapters.title: Bleeding Control
chapters.intro: Uncontrolled external bleeding is one of the most preventable causes of death from trauma, and direct pressure stops most of it. This chapter presents the escalating framework from direct pressure to tourniquet and hemostatic dressing, explains why pressure works, walks through the procedure step by step — including the case that does not escalate at all, because life-threatening extremity bleeding gets a tourniquet immediately — and then covers the two things pressure cannot help with: the bleeding you cannot see, and the shock it produces.

sections.title: External Bleeding Control — Direct Pressure

topics.heading: The escalating framework
topics.html:
Bleeding control is not a single technique. It is a sequence of escalating steps, and which of them you use depends on how severe the bleeding is and on how it responds to what you have already done. Direct pressure is almost always step one, and for most wounds it is also the last step, because the bleeding stops there.

The table below pairs the situation you find with the intervention it calls for.

SituationIntervention
Wound already clotted/stoppedGauze + bandage (protect from contamination), monitor for bleed-through
Active bleedingDirect pressure → wound packing/hemostatics → tourniquet (extremity) or junctional device

topics.heading: Three kinds of bleeding, and the one that kills quickly
topics.html:
The appearance of the blood tells you which vessel is open, and that predicts how fast the patient is losing volume and how hard it will be to stop.

Arterial bleeding is bright red — it is fully oxygenated — and it spurts in time with the pulse, because it is under the pressure the heart generates. It is the hardest to control and the fastest to kill. Venous bleeding is darker red and flows steadily rather than spurting, because venous pressure is low and constant; it can still be heavy from a large vein. Capillary bleeding oozes from the surface, is dark red, and usually stops on its own.

Volume gives the urgency its scale. An adult holds roughly 5 liters of blood. Sudden loss of about 1 liter in an adult is serious; in a child the figure is around 500 mL, and in an infant as little as 100–200 mL. The same puddle on the floor means something very different depending on who is lying next to it, and a volume that an adult tolerates can be most of a small child's circulating blood.

topics.heading: Why direct pressure works
topics.html:
Pressure applied over a wound compresses the tissue around it, which diverts blood flow away from the damaged vessels and slows what still passes through them. Pressure from the outside also reduces the force of the bleeding from inside the vessel, and that gives the body's own clotting mechanism the time it needs to plug the holes in the vessel wall. In most cases this alone controls the bleeding.

Three methods deliver that pressure, and they differ mainly in how much of it you have to supply with your own hands: a gloved hand alone, a dressing held in place with a gloved hand, or a pressure dressing secured with a bandage.

topics.heading: Step-by-step procedure
topics.html:
The procedure runs in five steps, from the moment your hand reaches the wound to the point at which you decide that pressure is not working.

  1. Apply firm pressure. Use the palm of your hand for larger wounds and your fingers for smaller ones, and direct the pressure toward an underlying bone wherever one is available. If the bleeding is severe or spurting, place a gloved hand directly on the wound immediately rather than spending time hunting for a dressing.
  2. Hold the pressure firmly. For massive bleeding, maintain that pressure all the way to the hospital. For bleeding that is not massive, it is reasonable to check the wound after 5 to 10 minutes to see whether it has stopped.
  3. Do not over-layer the wound with absorbent dressings. Piling on gauze soaks up blood without stopping the bleeding, and the extra layers cushion your hand away from the wound, which weakens the pressure you are trying to apply.
  4. Convert to a pressure dressing once the bleeding is controlled. Bandage the dressing firmly in place so that the pressure is maintained without your hands.
  5. Never remove a dressing once it has been placed. Taking it off can disrupt the clots that are forming under it. If blood soaks through, treat that as your signal to escalate, either to wound packing with a hemostatic agent or, for a wound on an extremity, to a tourniquet.

Taken as a whole, direct pressure is four ideas in order: compress the wound, hold the compression, leave what you have applied undisturbed, and escalate if it fails.

topics.heading: Nosebleeds are the common exception where position does most of the work
topics.html: Epistaxis is managed by sitting the patient upright and leaning forward, then pinching the soft fleshy part of the nostrils together. Leaning the patient back, which is the instinct and the folk remedy, sends blood down the throat, where it is swallowed, irritates the stomach, and produces vomiting in a patient who is already bleeding. Forward and pinched is the whole technique.

takeaways: Direct pressure is almost always the first step in bleeding control.
For severe/spurting bleeding, put a gloved hand directly on the wound immediately — don't hunt for a dressing first.
Piling on absorbent gauze soaks up blood but doesn't stop bleeding, and can weaken your hand pressure.
Never remove a placed dressing — blood soaking through means escalate, not swap the dressing.

Escalation order for bleeding that is NOT immediately life-threatening: direct pressure → wound packing/hemostatics → tourniquet (extremity) or junctional device. Life-threatening extremity bleeding skips the ladder: tourniquet first, straight away.
Arterial: bright red, spurting with the pulse, hardest to control. Venous: dark red, steady flow. Capillary: dark red ooze, usually self-limiting.
An adult holds about 5 liters of blood. Sudden loss of about 1 L (adult), 500 mL (child), or 100–200 mL (infant) is serious.
Nosebleed: sit the patient upright, lean them FORWARD, pinch the soft part of the nostrils. Leaning back sends blood into the stomach and causes vomiting.

sections.title: Tourniquets & Wound Packing

topics.heading: The tourniquet stopped being a last resort, and the change is the point of this section
topics.html:
For decades a tourniquet was taught as the thing you tried when everything else had failed, on the belief that it cost the patient the limb. Military experience over the last two decades changed that. A correctly applied tourniquet left in place for the duration of a prehospital transport rarely costs a limb, and hesitation costs lives. Current civilian practice, reflected in the American College of Surgeons' Stop the Bleed program, is that life-threatening bleeding from an extremity gets a tourniquet immediately — not after the ladder of lesser measures has been climbed and failed.

A commercial windlass tourniquet is the device to use. Improvised tourniquets — a belt, a cravat and a stick — are a fallback when nothing else exists, and they fail more often, usually because they are too narrow to occlude the artery and merely occlude the veins, which makes the bleeding worse rather than better.

topics.heading: Applying it: where, how tight, and the two things you write down
topics.html:
Placement: about 2 to 3 inches proximal to the wound — between the wound and the heart — and never over a joint, because there is no single bone there to compress the artery against. If the wound is an amputation, if there are multiple wounds, or if you cannot see where the bleeding is coming from in a mangled limb, place it high and tight on the limb instead.

Tightness: tighten the windlass until the bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone. Both endpoints matter. A tourniquet tight enough to occlude the veins but not tight enough to occlude the artery is the failure mode that makes bleeding worse: arterial blood still enters the limb while venous return out of it is blocked.

It will hurt, often badly, and the pain is not a reason to loosen it. Tell the patient that in advance.

Write down the time of application, on the tourniquet itself and in your report, and hand it off verbally. Leave it visible — never cover a tourniquet with a blanket or a dressing, because the next person needs to see it without hunting for it. And do not loosen or remove it in the field once bleeding is controlled.

If one tourniquet does not control the bleeding, apply a second one just proximal to the first rather than tightening the first past its limit.

topics.heading: Wound packing, and the places you must not pack
topics.html:
Some wounds cannot take a tourniquet because there is no limb to put it around. The junctional areas — the groin, the armpit, the base of the neck — are where a limb meets the trunk, and bleeding there is controlled by packing the wound and holding pressure, or with a purpose-built junctional device.

To pack: push gauze, plain or hemostatic, directly into the wound, down to the source of the bleeding, filling the cavity tightly, and then hold firm direct pressure over the packed wound for at least 3 minutes. Packing that is laid on top of a wound is a dressing, not packing, and it will not work. The pressure held afterward is not optional; hemostatic gauze works by accelerating clotting at the point of contact, and it needs the contact and the time.

Do not pack the chest or the abdomen. There is no cavity floor to pack against, the gauze goes somewhere you cannot control, and neither site can be compressed. Neck wounds are also not packed in the usual sense, because the packing can compress the airway; an occlusive dressing and direct pressure that does not obstruct breathing is the approach there.

takeaways: Life-threatening extremity bleeding gets a tourniquet immediately — it is not a last resort.
Use a commercial windlass tourniquet. Improvised ones fail more often, usually by being too narrow to occlude the artery.
Place it 2–3 inches proximal to the wound and never over a joint. Amputation, multiple wounds, or an unclear source: go high and tight.
Tighten until the bleeding stops AND the distal pulse is gone. Occluding veins without occluding the artery makes bleeding worse.
It will hurt. Pain is not a reason to loosen it.
Write the time of application on the tourniquet and in the report, and say it at handoff.
Leave a tourniquet visible — never cover it. Do not loosen or remove it in the field.
If one tourniquet does not control the bleeding, add a second just proximal to the first.
Junctional bleeding (groin, axilla, base of neck) takes wound packing or a junctional device, not a tourniquet.
Pack gauze INTO the wound down to the bleeding source, fill the cavity tightly, then hold firm pressure for at least 3 minutes.
Never pack the chest or abdomen. Neck wounds get an occlusive dressing and pressure that does not obstruct the airway.

sections.title: Internal Bleeding & Hemorrhagic Shock

topics.heading: The bleeding you cannot see is the bleeding you cannot compress
topics.html:
Internal bleeding has no puddle to point at, and the patient can lose a large fraction of their blood volume into the abdomen, the chest, the pelvis, or the tissue around a femur without a drop reaching the outside. You recognize it from mechanism and from signs rather than from blood.

Look for bruising and discoloration over the trunk, an abdomen that is distended, rigid, or tender, hematemesis (vomited blood, which may look like coffee grounds), melena (black tarry stool), hemoptysis (coughed blood), pain, swelling or deformity over a long bone, and — the finding that ties them together — signs of shock with no external bleeding to explain them. A femur fracture alone can hold well over a liter; a pelvic fracture can hold far more.

There is no field intervention that stops internal bleeding. The treatment is oxygen if indicated, keeping the patient warm, handling them gently, and rapid transport to a facility that can operate. Recognizing it early and shortening the time to that facility is the whole of the EMT's contribution, and it is a large contribution.

topics.heading: Shock is recognized before the blood pressure falls, because by then it is late
topics.html:
Hemorrhagic shock progresses in a way that is worth knowing as a sequence rather than a list, because the sequence is what lets you catch it early.

In compensated shock, the body is successfully defending its blood pressure. The heart rate rises, the vessels in the skin and gut constrict to shunt blood to the brain and heart, and the patient looks pale, cool and clammy, feels anxious or restless, and is thirsty. Respirations rise. The pulse pressure — the gap between systolic and diastolic — narrows, because the diastolic rises with vasoconstriction while the systolic does not. And the blood pressure is still normal. This is the stage at which recognition changes the outcome.

In decompensated shock, the compensation has run out. The blood pressure falls, mental status deteriorates, peripheral pulses become weak or absent, and the skin may become mottled or cyanotic. Hypotension is a late sign of shock, not an early one, and waiting for it in a patient who is pale, tachycardic and anxious means waiting for the patient to get worse before acting.

Two populations distort the picture. Children compensate extremely well and then crash abruptly, so a normal blood pressure in an injured child is not reassurance. And a patient on a beta blocker may not be able to mount the tachycardia that is the earliest sign, so their heart rate stays deceptively normal while they bleed.

takeaways: Internal bleeding is recognized from mechanism and signs, not from visible blood.
Signs: bruising over the trunk; distended, rigid or tender abdomen; hematemesis (may look like coffee grounds); melena (black tarry stool); hemoptysis; pain or deformity over a long bone.
Shock with no external bleeding to explain it IS the finding.
A femur fracture can hold over a liter of blood; a pelvic fracture far more.
There is no field fix for internal bleeding: oxygen if indicated, keep the patient warm, handle gently, transport rapidly to surgical care.
Compensated shock: rising heart rate, pale/cool/clammy skin, anxiety and restlessness, thirst, rising respirations, NARROWING pulse pressure — with a still-normal blood pressure.
Decompensated shock: falling blood pressure, deteriorating mental status, weak or absent peripheral pulses, mottled skin.
Hypotension is a LATE sign of shock. Recognize it at the compensated stage.
Children compensate well and then crash suddenly — a normal BP in an injured child is not reassurance.
A patient on a beta blocker may not be able to become tachycardic, hiding the earliest sign.

chapters.title: Soft-Tissue Trauma
chapters.intro: The skin is the body's largest organ and its first line of defense, and soft-tissue injuries range from a bruise to a burn that threatens life. This chapter covers closed and open wounds and their care, including impaled objects and amputations, then burns: classification by depth and extent, burn center criteria, thermal, chemical, electrical and radiation burns, and the principles of dressing and bandaging.

topics.heading: Skin & soft-tissue basics
topics.html:
The soft tissues of the body are the skin, the fat, the muscle, the blood vessels, the connective tissue, the membranes, the glands and the nerves. The skin is the largest of them, and it does more than cover what lies beneath. It protects the deeper tissues, it maintains the body's water balance, it regulates temperature, it excretes waste, and it absorbs shock.

Skin is built in 3 layers, and how deep a wound reaches is much of what determines how serious it is. The outermost layer is the epidermis, which contains no blood vessels and no nerves. Beneath it lies the dermis, the layer that holds the vessels, the nerves and the glands; once the dermis has been opened, the wound carries a major risk of infection and of bleeding. Deepest is the subcutaneous layer, which is largely fat and which insulates the body and absorbs shock.

topics.heading: Closed wounds
topics.html:
In a closed wound the skin is not broken and the damage is entirely beneath the surface. The table below sets out the three kinds of closed wound and what distinguishes each one.

TypeDetail
ContusionBruise — epidermis intact; swelling/discoloration may be delayed up to 48 hrs
HematomaLarger vessel damage — up to 1 liter can collect
Crush injuryForce transmitted internally despite intact skin — solid organs bleed severely, hollow organ contents can leak

Care follows one pattern whatever the type. Begin with the ABCs and oxygen (O2). If the mechanism suggests bleeding inside the body, treat the patient for internal bleeding and shock. Splint painful or deformed extremities, monitor for shock to develop, and transport promptly.

topics.heading: Open wounds
topics.html:
An open wound is one in which the surface of the skin is broken, so that blood can leave the body and contamination can enter it. The table below describes the open wounds you will meet and the point that matters most about each.

TypeKey points
AbrasionOuter layer only; high infection risk from ground-in debris
LacerationSmooth or jagged cut; can't judge depth from outside
PunctureSmall entry ≠ minor — depth determines severity; check for exit wound
AvulsionFlap torn/pulled loose; avulsed tissue loses O2 supply, will die
AmputationComplete severing; bleeding may be severe OR limited
Bite woundsHigher infection rates; human bites can indicate abuse/assault

Explosions produce a pattern of injury of their own, and blast injuries are described by 4 mechanisms. The primary mechanism is the pressure wave itself, which damages organs. The secondary mechanism is shrapnel driven into the patient. The tertiary mechanism is the patient being thrown by the force of the blast. The quaternary mechanism covers the rest of what an explosion does, such as chemical exposure and burns.

High-pressure injection injuries deserve particular suspicion, because they look minor on the surface and are devastating internally. Elevate and splint the limb, never apply cold, and persuade the patient to accept transport even if there is no pain at all.

topics.heading: General open wound care & special situations
topics.html:
Care of an open wound runs in a set order. Expose the wound, then clean the surface only; controlling the bleeding takes priority over cleaning. Use direct pressure; if the bleeding from an extremity is life-threatening — spurting, pulsing with the heartbeat, or pooling fast — apply a tourniquet straight away rather than working up to it. Elevation is no longer part of bleeding control: it delays the pressure that actually works and has never been shown to stop bleeding on its own. Treat for shock and give O2, cover the wound with a sterile dressing, and hold the dressing in place with a bandage, checking the distal pulse once the bandage is on.

Three situations call for something beyond that sequence. An impaled object is never removed in the field; stabilize it where it lies with bulky dressings packed against both sides of it. With an avulsion or an amputation, save the separated part: wrap it in a sterile dressing moistened with saline and keep it cool, never placing it directly on ice and never immersing it in water, since the avulsed tissue has lost its oxygen supply and will die.

Genital injuries bleed heavily, because the tissue is highly vascular. Control the bleeding, keep the patient's dignity and privacy in mind throughout, and consider the possibility of sexual abuse or assault, particularly in a child.

sections.title: Burns

topics.heading: Classifying burns by depth
topics.html:
Burns are classified first by depth, which is to say by how far through the skin the heat has destroyed tissue. The table below gives the three depths, the layers each one involves and what each looks like on the patient.

DepthLayersSigns
Superficial (1st degree)Epidermis onlyRed, mild swelling, painful
Partial thickness (2nd degree)Epidermis + dermisDeep pain, blisters, mottled
Full thickness (3rd degree)All skin layers ± deeper structuresCharred black/white/dry; may be painless at center, painful at edges

Depth alone does not describe a burn; you also need its extent, expressed as a percentage of the body surface area. The Rule of Nines divides the adult body into regions of 9%: the head and neck, each arm, the chest, the abdomen, the upper back, and the lower back with the buttocks are 9% each, and so are the front and the back of each leg. The genitals account for the remaining 1%. A child's proportions are different, and only two regions change: the head and neck take 18% rather than 9%, and each leg takes 13.5% rather than 18%. Everything else is counted as it is in an adult, so each arm is still 9%, the chest and abdomen together and the entire back are 18% each, and the genitals are 1%. A child's head takes a larger share of the body surface and the legs a smaller one, which is why a burn of the same size is a bigger burn in a child.

topics.heading: Burn center criteria & thermal burn care
topics.html:
Some burned patients need a burn center rather than the nearest emergency department. Transport to a burn center is indicated for:

  • Partial-thickness (2nd-degree) burns covering more than 10% of the body surface area (BSA).
  • Burns of the face, the genitalia, the hands, the feet or a major joint.
  • Any full-thickness (3rd-degree) burn.
  • Electrical burns.
  • Inhalation burns.
  • Burns accompanied by other trauma.
  • Patients with special needs.

Care of a thermal burn begins by stopping the burning process. Turn next to the airway and breathing, looking for a hoarse voice, stridor, soot and singed nasal hair, any of which points toward an inhalation injury, and then complete the primary assessment. Treat for shock and give O2, classify the burn by depth and extent, and cover it with a dry sterile dressing.

Never put ointments, sprays or butter on a burn, never break blisters, and never apply ice. A cool wet dressing is appropriate only for a small isolated burn; used over more than 10% of the body surface area it risks hypothermia. Immersion and scald burns raise the possibility of abuse, especially in children.

topics.heading: Chemical, electrical & radiation burns
topics.html:
A chemical burn goes on burning as long as the chemical remains on the patient. Brush a dry chemical off first, then flush with copious flowing water for at least 20 minutes and keep flushing en route. The two families of chemicals behave differently. Acids coagulate the tissue they touch, which tends to limit their own penetration; the exception is hydrofluoric acid, which penetrates deeply while showing minimal signs on the surface. Alkalis liquefy tissue, so they reach deeper and need longer irrigation.

At an electrical injury, assume the source is still live unless it has been confirmed off. The signs to look for are entry and exit burns, paralysis, dysrhythmia or cardiac arrest, and seizures. Manage the airway and breathing with the risk of swelling in mind, have basic life support (BLS) and the automated external defibrillator (AED) ready, take spine precautions, and search for at least 2 burn sites rather than stopping at the first one you find. Cover the burns with dry sterile dressings and transport promptly, since cardiac problems can appear after a delay.

Radiation produces both an immediate and a delayed injury: burns at the time of exposure, and radiation sickness later. Do not approach a radiation incident without the proper protection and training.

topics.heading: Dressing & bandaging principles
topics.html: A dressing is the sterile material placed over the wound itself; a bandage is what holds the dressing in place, and it does not need to be sterile. A bandage is applied neither too tightly nor too loosely, and no loose ends are left hanging. Leave the fingers and toes exposed so that you can keep watching circulation, the one exception being digits that are themselves burned. Wrap from the distal end of the limb toward the proximal end.

takeaways: Never remove an impaled object — stabilize it in place with bulky dressings.

Keep an amputated or avulsed part cool in a saline-moistened sterile dressing — never directly on ice and never immersed in water. Cooling is for the separated tissue, not a treatment for the wound itself.
Rule of Nines: 9% per body region (adult) — used to estimate burn extent.
Never apply ointment, ice, or break blisters on a burn.
Chemical burns: flush with water ≥20 minutes; never neutralize with vinegar/baking soda.
Electrical burns: assume the source is still live; find both entry and exit points.

chapters.title: Chest and Abdominal Trauma
chapters.intro: The chest and abdomen hold the organs that keep a patient alive, and injuries to them can be deceptively quiet. This chapter distinguishes blunt from penetrating chest trauma, covers the care of open chest wounds and the injuries within the chest cavity such as pneumothorax, flail chest and cardiac tamponade, and then turns to open and closed abdominal trauma, including evisceration.

topics.heading: Blunt vs. penetrating chest trauma
topics.html:
Chest trauma is classified as blunt or penetrating, and the less dramatic of the two is not the safer one. Blunt chest trauma can carry a higher mortality than penetrating trauma, because minimal external evidence can mask massive internal damage. Rib fractures are the most common serious blunt injury. When 2 or more consecutive ribs are fractured in 2 or more places, the result is a flail chest: the fractured section becomes an unstable segment that moves paradoxically, in the direction opposite to the rest of the chest wall, as the patient breathes.

Penetrating trauma raises a different concern. Assume that all open chest wounds penetrate the chest cavity, and never probe a wound to check its depth. A sucking chest wound is a hole large enough that the negative pressure of normal breathing draws air directly through it into the chest.

topics.heading: Care for chest wounds
topics.html:
An open chest wound is sealed immediately. If no dressing is at hand, cover the wound with a gloved hand, then replace it with an occlusive dressing that extends at least 2 in beyond the wound on all sides. Give high-flow oxygen (O2), aiming for a saturation of 94–95%. Because of the risk of tension pneumothorax, request advanced life support (ALS) early, but do not delay transport waiting for them to arrive.

Transport the patient in a position of comfort. A patient with penetrating trauma to the chest or neck does not automatically need spinal immobilization; restrict spinal motion only if blunt trauma also occurred. In a flail chest, never restrict movement of the chest wall, even when paradoxical motion is plainly visible.

topics.heading: Injuries within the chest cavity
topics.html:
Several distinct injuries can develop inside the chest cavity, and each announces itself with a characteristic set of findings. The table below sets out the conditions you must recognize and the key signs of each.

ConditionKey signs
PneumothoraxDiminished/absent breath sounds one side, uneven chest movement
Tension pneumothoraxAbove + worsening hypoxia, shock, JVD, tracheal deviation (late sign)
HemothoraxPneumo signs + possible frothy blood cough, shock
Traumatic asphyxiaDark red/purple face-neck, bulging eyes, swollen blue tongue/lips
Cardiac tamponadeBeck's triad: JVD + muffled heart sounds + narrowing pulse pressure
Aortic injury/dissectionTearing chest/back pain, pulse/BP differences between limbs
Commotio cordisSudden collapse/arrest after chest impact — treat as VF arrest, defibrillate without delay

Bear in mind that the chest cavity can hold more than 3 quarts (3 L) of blood with zero external sign of it, so a chest that looks unremarkable can be the site of a life-threatening hemorrhage.

sections.title: Abdominal Trauma

topics.heading: Abdominal injuries
topics.html:
Evisceration is the protrusion of abdominal organs through an open wound. Among the solid organs, the liver, in the right upper quadrant (RUQ), and the spleen, in the left upper quadrant (LUQ), are the most commonly injured. Both are highly vascular, and injury to either can cause life-threatening bleeding. Hollow organs fail differently: when one ruptures, its contents spill into the abdominal cavity, the spilled contents cause peritonitis, and the abdomen becomes rigid.

Gunshot wounds to the abdomen are unpredictable because bullets deflect, fragment and tumble as they travel. Do not assume that only the structures directly beneath the entry wound are injured.
