A gunshot wound at the level of the lower ribs requires you to assume both a chest injury and an abdominal injury.

topics.heading: Care — open & closed abdominal trauma
topics.html:
Whether the abdominal injury is open or closed, the basic care is the same. Watch for vomiting and protect the airway. Position the patient supine with the knees flexed, which relaxes the abdominal muscles. Give O2 for hypoxia, treat for shock, and give nothing by mouth.

Open wounds call for additional steps. Control bleeding and dress the wounds. Never touch or attempt to replace eviscerated organs; cover them with a sterile dressing moistened with saline and re-moisten it as needed. Never use aluminum foil as an occlusive dressing, because it can cut the eviscerated organs. If an object is impaled, never remove it; stabilize it in place with bulky dressings and leave the patient's legs in the position in which they were found.

takeaways: Never probe an open chest wound to check depth — assume all open chest wounds penetrate.
Flail chest: never restrict chest wall movement, even with paradoxical motion visible.
Beck's triad (JVD + muffled heart sounds + narrowing pulse pressure) = cardiac tamponade.
Commotio cordis = sudden VF arrest after a chest impact — defibrillate immediately.
Liver and spleen are the most commonly injured solid organs — both highly vascular.
Never touch or replace eviscerated organs; never use aluminum foil as a dressing over them.

chapters.title: Musculoskeletal Trauma
chapters.intro: Fractures are rarely fatal on their own, but the blood they bleed, the damage they do to nerves and vessels, and the pain of moving them all matter. This chapter covers the four types of musculoskeletal injury, compartment syndrome and the six Ps, the principles of splinting, traction splints and pelvic injuries, and the injuries of the knee, lower leg, ankle and foot.

sections.title: Fractures, Splinting & Traction

topics.heading: Bone basics & blood loss
topics.html:
Bone is living, vascular tissue. It stores minerals, produces red blood cells (RBCs), and bleeds when it is broken, even when the fracture is closed. The periosteum, the membrane that covers the bone, contains its own vessels and nerves; if bone fragments are visible on exposed periosteum, never remove them.

The blood loss from a "simple" closed fracture is easy to underestimate. A tibia-fibula fracture bleeds about 1 pint (500 cc), a femur fracture about 2 pints (1,000 cc), and a pelvic fracture about 3–4 pints (1,500–2,000 cc) or more. The traction splint was invented specifically to reduce the blood loss from a fractured femur.

topics.heading: The four types of musculoskeletal injury
topics.html:
Musculoskeletal injuries fall into four types, distinguished by which structure is damaged. The table below defines each of them.

InjuryDefinition
FractureAny bone break — open/closed; comminuted, greenstick, angulated
DislocationBone ends displaced out of the joint; capsule/ligaments torn
SprainLigament stretch/tear (joint injury)
StrainMuscle overstretch/overexertion

You do not need to diagnose which of the four you are looking at in the field. Any extremity with pain, swelling or deformity is treated as a fracture and splinted.

topics.heading: Compartment syndrome & the six Ps
topics.html:
Compartment syndrome begins with a fracture or crush injury that causes bleeding and swelling within a muscle compartment. As the compartment fills, the pressure inside it rises until it exceeds the perfusion pressure of the tissue, and cellular damage follows. If the pressure is not relieved, the limb may be lost. The signs are pain, swelling, a sensation of pressure, and an extremity that feels hard compared with the uninjured side.

The six Ps summarize the findings of a compromised extremity: Pain or tenderness, Pallor, Paresthesia, Pulses that are diminished or absent, Paralysis, and Pressure.

topics.heading: Splinting — core principles
topics.html:
A splint immobilizes the bone ends and the joints adjacent to the injury. Doing so reduces pain, prevents further damage to soft tissue, nerves and vessels, prevents a closed fracture from becoming an open one, and minimizes blood loss.

Realignment is generally reserved for angulated long-bone shafts. Joints are splinted in the position in which they are found, with one exception: if the extremity distal to the joint is cyanotic or pulseless, attempt gentle traction to bring it to a neutral position. The order of care is fixed. Life threats come first. Then expose the injury site, assess circulation, sensation and motor function (CSM) before and after splinting, and immobilize the injury site and the adjacent joints, letting the speed of the work match the patient's priority.

The single most serious splinting hazard is "splinting someone to death": delaying the transport of an unstable patient in order to perfect a splint.

topics.heading: Traction splints & pelvic injuries
topics.html:
Traction splints are femur-specific devices. Every field traction splint uses "counter-traction" anchored against the pelvis rather than true independent traction. The indication is a painful, swollen or deformed mid-thigh with no injury to a joint or to the lower leg. The splint is contraindicated when there is an injury to the pelvis, hip or knee, an avulsion or partial amputation, or an injury to the lower third of the leg.

A pelvic injury is handled with minimal movement: move the patient as a unit, and never lift with the pelvis unsupported. A pelvic wrap is made from a sheet about 10 in wide, placed at the level of the greater trochanters and tied firmly without overcompression. Apply it for pelvic deformity or instability, and also for a high-risk mechanism of injury (MOI) even when no deformity is obvious.

topics.heading: Knee, tibia/fibula & ankle/foot injuries
topics.html:
A true knee dislocation, in which the tibia is displaced relative to the femur, can compress the popliteal artery and cut off the blood supply to the lower leg. An absent distal pulse in this setting is a true emergency, and gentle repositioning may be needed to restore the pulse. A patellar dislocation, in which the kneecap is displaced laterally, is a different injury and is less urgent.

A tibia or fibula fracture is splinted with a vacuum or air-inflated splint, and manual traction is maintained while the splint is applied. Sprains and fractures of the ankle and foot are both common and hard to tell apart, so either is treated as a fracture. Use a soft or pillow splint, or a commercial splint that extends above the knee.

takeaways: Even closed fractures can cause significant blood loss — femur ~2 pints, pelvis ~3–4 pints.
The Six Ps: Pain, Pallor, Paresthesia, Pulses, Paralysis, Pressure.
"Splinting someone to death" — never delay transport of an unstable patient to perfect a splint.
Traction splints are for isolated femur fractures only — never with hip/knee/pelvis injury.
An absent distal pulse after a true knee dislocation is a true emergency (popliteal artery compression).
Treat any suspected ankle/foot injury as a fracture — sprains and fractures are hard to distinguish in the field.

chapters.title: Trauma to the Head, Neck, and Spine
chapters.intro: Injuries to the head, neck and spine carry the greatest risk of permanent disability, and the care given in the first minutes can prevent or cause it. This chapter covers neck wounds, spinal assessment using NEXUS-based criteria to decide when motion restriction is needed, practical tips for the long backboard, when and how to remove a helmet, the traumatic brain injury whose outcome depends almost entirely on whether you keep the brain oxygenated and perfused, and the spinal cord injury whose shock looks nothing like the shock of blood loss.

sections.title: Neck Wounds & Spinal Assessment

topics.heading: Neck wounds
topics.html:
The major vessels of the neck run close to the surface, and a wound there carries two risks at once. The first is massive hemorrhage. The second is air embolism: the veins of the neck run at a pressure lower than atmospheric, so air can be sucked into an open vein, travel to the lungs, and cause cardiac arrest. Direct pressure remains a lifesaving step; the only caution is not to interfere with breathing.

Care proceeds in order. Open the airway, then place a gloved hand over the wound immediately. Replace the hand with an occlusive dressing of thick material that extends 2 in past the edges of the wound and is sealed on all 4 sides, and apply pressure to stop the bleeding. Never compress both carotid arteries at the same time. Once the bleeding has stopped, bandage the dressing in place without restricting the airway or the vessels of the neck.

topics.heading: Spinal assessment — NEXUS-based criteria
topics.html:
The NEXUS study validated a tool for judging the risk of spinal injury. It rests on five criteria, and they are written as things that must all be absent before the cervical spine can be considered low risk:

  1. No posterior midline cervical tenderness: palpate down the midline of the neck, and the rest of the spine while you are there.
  2. No evidence of intoxication: alcohol or drugs blunt the pain that the other criteria depend on the patient reporting.
  3. A normal level of alertness: the patient is fully awake and oriented, not confused, drowsy or post-ictal.
  4. No focal neurologic deficit: compare grip strength for equality, and check for paralysis, weakness, numbness or tingling.
  5. No painful distracting injury: a femur fracture or a large burn can occupy a patient's attention so completely that a broken neck does not hurt yet.

Intoxication and alertness are two separate criteria, not one. They are often taught merged into a single question about whether the patient is "reliable", which is how the list gets miscounted as four — and a patient can be fully sober and still too drowsy to assess, or wide awake and drunk.

In pediatric patients, weight the mechanism of injury (MOI) more heavily. Young children cannot reliably report pain, and because their vertebrae are more cartilaginous, a significant spinal cord injury can occur without external tenderness or deformity.

topics.heading: Long backboard application — practical tips
topics.html:
The patient is log-rolled onto the long backboard, and the EMT holding the head calls the move. Once the patient is on the board, pad the voids between the head or torso and the board. Straps are placed at the upper chest, the pelvis and the thighs, and the head is secured last, after the body has been strapped down.

A full-term pregnant patient is immobilized on the board, and the board is then tilted to the left to reduce compression of the vena cava.

For children 6 years of age or younger, pad beneath the shoulder blades to compensate for a proportionally larger head.

topics.heading: Helmet management
topics.html:
A helmet is left on when it fits snugly, there is no impending airway or breathing problem, removal would cause further injury, and proper spinal immobilization can be achieved with it in place. It is removed when it interferes with assessment or management of the airway or breathing, when it fits poorly and allows excessive movement inside, when it interferes with immobilization, or when the patient is in cardiac arrest.

With a football-, hockey- or lacrosse-style helmet worn with shoulder pads, remove both together or leave both in place. Removing only one forces the neck into hyperflexion or hyperextension.

takeaways: Never compress both carotid arteries simultaneously.
Neck wound: occlusive dressing sealed on all four sides, extending 2 in past the wound edges — the veins can entrain air.

NEXUS has FIVE criteria, all of which must be absent for a low-risk cervical spine: no midline cervical tenderness, no intoxication, normal alertness, no focal neurologic deficit, no painful distracting injury.
Intoxication and alertness are separate criteria. Merging them into one question about 'reliability' is how the list gets miscounted as four.
In young children, weight the mechanism of injury more heavily — cartilaginous vertebrae allow cord injury without tenderness or deformity.
Backboard: strap the body first (upper chest, pelvis, thighs), secure the head LAST.
Full-term pregnant patients on a backboard should be tilted left to relieve vena cava compression.
Children 6 and under: pad beneath the shoulder blades to offset the proportionally larger head.
Remove a helmet only if it interferes with airway management, fits poorly, interferes with immobilization, or the patient is in cardiac arrest.
Football-style helmet + shoulder pads: remove both together or neither — never just one.

sections.title: Traumatic Brain Injury

topics.heading: Primary injury is already done; secondary injury is the one you can prevent
topics.html:
A traumatic brain injury has two halves. The primary injury is the damage done at the instant of impact — torn tissue, bruised brain, sheared axons. Nothing an EMT does changes it; it happened before the call came in.

The secondary injury is everything that damages the brain afterward: swelling, rising pressure inside a rigid skull, and above all hypoxia and hypotension. These two are the reason head-injury care looks so much like ordinary good care. Keeping the airway open, keeping the saturation up, and keeping the blood pressure from dropping is the treatment for a brain injury, because the brain is exquisitely intolerant of low oxygen and low perfusion pressure. Adding hypoglycemia to a head-injured patient does the same thing, which is another reason the glucose gets checked.

Put plainly: the EMT cannot repair the brain, and the EMT can substantially change whether that brain is further injured in the next twenty minutes.

topics.heading: Rising intracranial pressure announces itself in a pattern that is the opposite of shock
topics.html:
The skull is a closed box. Blood or swelling inside it has nowhere to expand, so the pressure rises and squeezes the brain. Late in that process the body mounts a characteristic response, Cushing's triad, and it is worth memorizing precisely because it inverts the pattern you have been taught to look for.

Hemorrhagic shockRising ICP (Cushing's triad)
Blood pressureFallingRising, with a widening pulse pressure
Heart rateRising (tachycardia)Falling (bradycardia)
RespirationsRapidIrregular in rate and depth

A head-injured patient whose pressure is climbing while their pulse slows is not stabilizing. Other signs of rising pressure and impending herniation include a deteriorating level of consciousness — the single most sensitive indicator — vomiting, often without nausea, and a pupil that becomes dilated and unreactive on one side.

One thing not to do reflexively: do not routinely hyperventilate a head-injured patient. Driving down carbon dioxide constricts cerebral vessels and reduces blood flow to a brain that needs more of it, not less. Ventilate at the normal rate, and hyperventilate only if your protocol directs it for specific signs of herniation.

topics.heading: Skull fractures, concussion, and the drainage you leave alone
topics.html:
A basilar skull fracture, at the base of the skull, produces signs that are distinctive and, importantly, late — they can take hours to appear, so their absence early means nothing. Raccoon eyes are bruising around both eyes; Battle's sign is bruising behind the ear over the mastoid; and clear or blood-tinged fluid draining from the nose or the ear is cerebrospinal fluid escaping through the fracture.

Do not pack the nose or the ears to stop that drainage. The fluid is coming from around the brain, and blocking its exit raises the pressure inside the skull. Cover loosely with a sterile dressing and let it drain. This is also the reason an NPA is avoided in a patient with these signs.

A concussion is a transient disturbance of brain function without a structural injury that imaging will show. Expect headache, confusion, dizziness, and amnesia — either for events before the injury or for events after it — and the repetitive questioning ("What happened? Where am I?" asked over and over) that is characteristic. Most resolve. All of them are evaluated, because a concussion and a slowly expanding bleed can look identical in the first hour.

Finally, a point about where to look for shock: in an adult, a head injury alone rarely causes hypotension. An adult head-injury patient who is in shock is almost certainly bleeding somewhere else, and looking for it is the priority. Infants are the exception — their blood volume is small enough relative to their head that intracranial bleeding genuinely can cause shock.

takeaways: Primary injury happens at impact and cannot be changed. Secondary injury — hypoxia, hypotension, swelling, hypoglycemia — is what EMT care prevents.
Hypoxia and hypotension are the two biggest worsening factors in TBI. Protecting airway, oxygenation and blood pressure IS head-injury treatment.
Cushing's triad (LATE sign of rising ICP): rising blood pressure with widening pulse pressure, FALLING heart rate, irregular respirations. It is the mirror image of shock.
A deteriorating level of consciousness is the most sensitive sign of rising intracranial pressure.
A unilaterally dilated, unreactive pupil suggests herniation. Vomiting without nausea is another sign of rising pressure.
Do NOT routinely hyperventilate a head-injured patient — it constricts cerebral vessels and reduces blood flow. Only per protocol for signs of herniation.
Basilar skull fracture signs — raccoon eyes, Battle's sign, CSF from nose or ears — are LATE. Their absence early means nothing.
Never pack the nose or ears to stop CSF drainage; cover loosely and let it drain. This is also why an NPA is avoided here.
Concussion: transient dysfunction without structural injury — headache, confusion, amnesia, repetitive questioning. Evaluate every one; an expanding bleed looks the same early.
In an adult, a head injury alone rarely causes hypotension — look elsewhere for the bleeding. In infants it can, because of their small blood volume.

sections.title: Spinal Cord Injury & Neurogenic Shock

topics.heading: What the cord controls depends on how high the injury is, and breathing is the level that matters most
topics.html:
An injury to the spinal cord removes function below the level of the injury, which means the height of the injury predicts what the patient has lost. The level worth knowing by heart is the diaphragm: the nerves that drive it leave the cord at roughly C3 through C5 — remembered as "C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive." An injury above that level takes the diaphragm with it and the patient stops breathing. An injury just below it spares the diaphragm but paralyzes the muscles between the ribs, producing diaphragmatic breathing: the belly rises and falls while the chest barely moves. That pattern in a trauma patient is a cord injury until proven otherwise.

Other findings: loss of sensation or movement below a level, numbness or tingling in the extremities, loss of bowel or bladder control, and — in a male patient — priapism, a persistent erection caused by the loss of sympathetic tone, which is a specific and often-tested sign.

topics.heading: Neurogenic shock is hypotension without the tachycardia, and confusing it with blood loss is the trap
topics.html:
A high cord injury cuts the sympathetic nervous system's signal to the blood vessels. The vessels below the injury dilate, the effective size of the container becomes larger than the volume of blood in it, and the pressure falls. That is neurogenic shock, and it looks unlike any other shock on the exam.

Hemorrhagic shockNeurogenic shock
Blood pressureLowLow
Heart rateFastNormal or slow
SkinPale, cool, clammyWarm, dry, flushed below the injury

The heart rate is the giveaway. The same sympathetic signal that would normally speed the heart in response to falling pressure is the signal that has been cut, so the patient cannot mount the tachycardia. A hypotensive trauma patient with a normal or slow pulse and warm dry skin has a cord injury; a hypotensive trauma patient with a fast pulse and cool clammy skin is bleeding.

Two practical consequences. Because the patient cannot constrict their peripheral vessels, they lose heat continuously and become hypothermic quickly even in a mild environment — cover them. And because a trauma patient can have both problems at once, neurogenic shock is never a reason to stop looking for hemorrhage.

One term to keep separate: spinal shock is the temporary loss of cord function — flaccid paralysis and lost reflexes — immediately after an injury, and it may partly resolve over hours to weeks. It describes neurological function. Neurogenic shock describes the circulation. They often occur together and they are not the same thing.

takeaways: C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive. An injury above that level stops breathing.
Diaphragmatic breathing — belly moving, chest still — in a trauma patient means a cord injury until proven otherwise.
Cord injury signs: loss of sensation or movement below a level, numbness or tingling, loss of bowel or bladder control, and priapism in a male patient.
Neurogenic shock: LOW blood pressure with a NORMAL or SLOW heart rate and warm, dry, flushed skin below the injury.
Hemorrhagic shock: low blood pressure with a FAST heart rate and pale, cool, clammy skin. The heart rate is the distinguishing finding.
The patient cannot mount a tachycardia because the sympathetic signal that would produce it is the one that was cut.
Neurogenic shock patients lose heat continuously and become hypothermic quickly — cover them.
A trauma patient can have both — neurogenic shock is never a reason to stop looking for hemorrhage.
Spinal shock = temporary loss of neurological function, may resolve. Neurogenic shock = the circulatory problem. Not the same thing.

chapters.title: Multisystem Trauma
chapters.intro: A patient with injuries to more than one body system is the trauma patient most likely to die, and the decisions are about time. This chapter separates multiple trauma from multisystem trauma, explains the tension between treating on scene and transporting, presents the field triage criteria used to judge severity and choose a destination, and considers special populations and the pathophysiology of internal injury.

sections.title: Treat vs. Transport & Field Triage

topics.heading: Multiple trauma vs. multisystem trauma
topics.html: Multiple trauma means more than one serious injury, regardless of body system; a fractured arm and a fractured leg together are multiple trauma within a single system. Multisystem trauma means injury that affects more than one body system, and it is more dangerous because the physiologic reserve of several organ systems is compromised at the same time. The more systems involved, the less reserve the patient has to compensate for shock, and the more likely it becomes that field stabilization is impossible. For these patients, definitive care in the form of surgery is the actual treatment.

topics.heading: The core tension: treat vs. transport
topics.html:
Every decision in multisystem trauma balances the time spent treating against the time lost by delaying transport. An isolated musculoskeletal injury that cannot kill the patient in the next 10 minutes never takes precedence over a threat to the airway or breathing. When time is limited, interventions that address immediate life threats always come before interventions that only improve comfort.

The phrase "the well-packaged corpse" captures the failure to avoid. The goal is never to arrive at the hospital with a perfectly splinted, perfectly immobilized patient who died en route because too much scene time was spent achieving that perfection. For the truly critical patient, definitive care beats field perfection.

topics.heading: Determining severity — sequential criteria
topics.html:
Severity is judged against three sets of criteria in a fixed order: physiologic first, then anatomic, then mechanism of injury (MOI). The first "yes" determines the decision. The physiologic criteria are thresholds of the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS), systolic blood pressure (SBP) and respiratory rate (RR), set out in the table below.

FindingThresholdWhat it indicates
GCS<14Head injury or hypoxia
SBP<90Definitive sign of shock
RR<10 or >29 (infant <1yr: <20)High = compensatory shock; low = late-stage shock or head injury

The anatomic criteria predict a need for surgery regardless of the current vital signs. They are a penetrating injury to the head, neck, torso, or an extremity proximal to the elbow or knee; flail chest; 2 or more proximal long-bone fractures; a crushed, mangled or pulseless extremity; an amputation proximal to the wrist or ankle; a pelvic fracture; an open or depressed skull fracture; and paralysis.

The MOI criteria describe the forces involved: a fall of more than 20 ft in an adult, or more than 10 ft (or 2–3 times the child's height) in a child; a high-risk crash, meaning intrusion of more than 12–18 in, ejection, or a death in the same passenger compartment; a vehicle striking a pedestrian at more than 20 mph; and a motorcycle crash at more than 20 mph. A significant MOI alone does not guarantee injury. It only justifies a more cautious posture in the absence of harder evidence.

topics.heading: Special populations & pathophysiology of internal injuries
topics.html:
Age changes the thresholds. In older adults, risk increases after age 55, and after age 65 a systolic blood pressure (BP) below 110, rather than below 90, may represent shock; a "normal-looking" reading of 100 mmHg may be significant relative hypotension. Children present the opposite problem. Their bodies compensate more effectively and for longer, then decompensate suddenly and severely, so a "stable-looking" pediatric trauma patient can crash with little warning.

The internal injuries of multisystem trauma share a common physiology. In a tension pneumothorax, the compressed vena cava reduces venous return, which in turn reduces cardiac output, and shock follows. Cardiac tamponade produces similar findings, namely jugular venous distention (JVD), low BP and a narrowing pulse pressure, but it does so by external compression of the heart rather than collapse of a lung; breath sounds therefore remain bilateral, unlike the one-sided absence of a tension pneumothorax. A solid organ injury can be masked by the organ's capsule, which delays diagnosis, while a hollow organ injury causes diffuse pain as the spilled contents irritate the peritoneum.

takeaways: Multisystem trauma (injury spanning multiple body systems) is more dangerous than multiple trauma to one system.
Physiologic → anatomic → MOI criteria are checked in that order — the first "yes" decides the transport destination.
GCS<14, SBP<90, or RR<10/>29 are the three physiologic red flags for trauma center transport.
In patients over 65, systolic BP <110 (not the usual <90) may already represent shock.
Children compensate well then crash suddenly — a stable-looking pediatric trauma patient can deteriorate with little warning.
"The well-packaged corpse" — don't perfect a splint at the cost of transport time for a critical patient.

chapters.title: Environmental Emergencies
chapters.intro: The environment injures through heat, cold, water, altitude and the animals that live in it. This chapter covers how the body loses heat and the decision points in hypothermia and local cold injury, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, drowning, scuba accidents, water rescue and altitude illness, and the bites and stings of insects, spiders, snakes and marine life.

topics.heading: How the body loses heat
topics.html:
The body loses heat by five mechanisms, and each one is a route you can close off when you care for a cold patient. The table below describes them.

MechanismDescription
ConductionDirect contact heat transfer — water conducts heat away 25x faster than air
ConvectionMoving air/water strips heat (wind chill)
RadiationHeat radiates off the body — most loss from the uncovered head/neck
EvaporationLiquid→gas cooling (sweat or wet skin/clothing)
RespirationWarm air exhaled

topics.heading: Generalized hypothermia — the key decision point
topics.html:
The single question that guides the care of generalized hypothermia is whether the patient has an altered mental status. A patient who is alert and responding appropriately has mild hypothermia, and active rewarming is acceptable. A patient who is unresponsive or not responding appropriately has severe hypothermia, and only passive rewarming is used.

Shivering is present at temperatures above about 90°F. If shivering is absent, assume severe hypothermia. Factors that predispose a patient to hypothermia include shock, burns, alcohol or drugs, lying on cold ground, and being very old or very young.

topics.heading: Care — mild vs. severe
topics.html:
For the alert patient who is responding appropriately, active rewarming is allowed. Remove wet clothing, handle the patient gently, and do not let the patient walk or massage the extremities. Rewarm actively during transport with heat packs or warm air, but rewarm slowly. Central rewarming means applying heat to the lateral chest, neck, armpits and groin first, never to the limbs first, because warming the limbs first can send cold blood recirculating to the core and trigger shock.

For the unresponsive patient with severe hypothermia, rewarming is passive only. Open the airway, give high-concentration O2, warmed and humidified if available, and wrap the patient in blankets. Handle the patient gently, because rough handling can trigger V-fib. Give no food or drink, do not massage the limbs, and transport immediately.

In extreme hypothermia, check the carotid pulse for at least 60 seconds before declaring that there is no pulse. "You're not dead until you're warm and dead": the hospital will not pronounce death until the patient has been rewarmed and resuscitated.

topics.heading: Local cold injuries — frostnip vs. frostbite
topics.html:
Local cold injury ranges from frostnip, a minor injury, to frostbite, which reaches deeper tissue. The table below contrasts the two in the tissue involved, the appearance of the skin, and the care given.

FrostnipFrostbite
TissueMinor damage, good responseSkin + subcutaneous, can reach muscle/bone
Skin signsRed → blanched/whiteWhite/waxy → mottled → grayish blue; swelling/blistering
CareWarm the area (cup hands, armpits, warm breath)Cover & protect, transport ASAP; do not thaw if refreeze risk

Whatever the depth of the injury, never rub the area, rub snow on it, break blisters, massage it, or let the patient walk on it.

topics.heading: Heat exhaustion vs. heat stroke — skin is the key distinguisher
topics.html:
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are distinguished above all by the skin. The table below compares the two conditions in skin findings, mechanism, signs and care.

Heat exhaustionHeat stroke
SkinMoist, pale, normal/coolHot — dry OR moist
MechanismHeavy sweating → fluid/salt lossThermoregulation fails, sweating may stop
SignsMuscle cramps, weakness, dizziness, weak pulseAltered mental status/LOC (required for diagnosis), little/no perspiration
CareCool environment, O2 if needed, loosen clothing, small sips of water if alertCool environment, cool packs to neck/groin/armpits, high-conc O2, immediate transport

Hot skin that is moist rather than dry does not rule out heat stroke. Once altered mental status and hot skin are both present, the diagnosis is heat stroke, not heat exhaustion.

topics.heading: Drowning
topics.html:
Drowning is respiratory impairment from submersion or immersion. About 10% of victims die purely from spasm of the airway, with no water aspirated. Cold water, below 70°F, can delay biological death, so resuscitation is attempted even after an arrest of 30 minutes or more.

Rescue breathing should begin in the water if the patient can be reached there, and rescue breathing or CPR begins on land as soon as the patient is out. Suspect a C-spine injury only in water accidents with a trauma mechanism, such as diving or a strike by a boat or water ski. Simple immersion drowning without trauma rarely causes spinal injury, and in that case ventilation must not be delayed for immobilization.

topics.heading: Scuba accidents
topics.html:
Two distinct emergencies follow a scuba dive, and they differ in cause, timing and presentation even though the field care is the same. The table below compares air embolism (AGE) with decompression sickness, "the bends."

Air Embolism (AGE)Decompression Sickness ("the bends")
CauseBreath-holding on ascent → lung over-expansionToo-fast ascent → nitrogen bubbles form in blood/tissue
OnsetRapid, <15 min1–12 hr (up to 48h)
SignsAltered MS, rapid LOC, seizures, stroke-like signsConfusion, headache, joint/muscle pain, numbness/paralysis
CareOpen airway, highest-conc O2 via nonrebreather, keep warm, consider hyperbaric facility transport

topics.heading: Water rescue order & high-altitude illness
topics.html:
Water rescue follows a fixed order: Reach, Throw/Tow, Row, Go. Entering the water is the last resort, reserved for a rescuer who is trained and a strong swimmer, because untrained rescuers become patients.

Three illnesses occur at altitude: acute mountain sickness (AMS), high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). The table below sets out the key signs and the care of each.

ConditionKey signsCare
Acute Mountain Sickness (AMS)Headache + N/V, insomnia, peripheral edemaMild: rest + rehydrate. Severe: O2 + descend
HACEWorsening headache, loss of coordination, altered MSImmediate descent (priority #1), high-conc O2
HAPESOB at rest, dry cough→hemoptysis, low O2 satImmediate descent, high-conc O2, minimize exertion

sections.title: Bites & Stings

topics.heading: Insects, spiders & scorpions
topics.html: About 5% of the population has an allergic reaction to stings, and the risk of anaphylaxis is the main concern for the EMT. Treat the patient for shock even in the absence of signs. Remove the stinger and venom sac quickly; the method matters less than the speed. Remove jewelry from the affected limb, and immobilize the limb.

topics.heading: Snakebites
topics.html: Roughly 50,000 snakebites occur in the US each year. About 8,000 or more of them are from venomous species, yet fewer than 10 people die each year; more US deaths come from bee and wasp stings than from snakebites. Even so, treat all bites from unidentified or venomous species as serious. Locate the fang marks, remove constricting items, and immobilize the bitten extremity, but do not elevate it above the level of the heart. Never apply ice or a cold pack, cut and suction the wound, squeeze the site, or attempt to suck the venom out by mouth.

topics.heading: Marine life
topics.html: The sting of a jellyfish or Portuguese man-of-war is rinsed with vinegar, kept out of the mouth and eyes, and then treated with nonscalding hot water to reduce the pain. A puncture from a stingray or sea urchin is soaked in nonscalding hot water for 30–90 min, but the soak must not delay transport.

takeaways: Shivering absent = assume SEVERE hypothermia, not "not hypothermic."
Altered mental status is THE decision point for hypothermia rewarming (active vs. passive) and defines heat stroke.
Heat stroke skin = hot, dry OR moist — moist hot skin still counts once altered MS is present.
Central rewarming order: chest/neck/armpits/groin BEFORE limbs — limb-first rewarming risks shock.
60-second pulse checks in hypothermia & cold-water drowning before calling arrest.
AGE onset is <15 min; decompression sickness onset is 1–12 hrs (up to 48h).
Water rescue order is fixed: Reach, Throw/Tow, Row, Go.
Snakebite: do not elevate the limb above the heart.
"You're not dead until you're warm and dead" — don't withhold resuscitation based on cold body temp alone.

chapters.title: Obstetric and Gynecologic Emergencies
chapters.intro: Most births need no help at all, and the EMT's job is to recognize the ones that do. This chapter covers the physiologic changes of pregnancy, the three stages of labor and the transport decision, assisting a normal delivery, care and APGAR scoring of the newborn and neonatal resuscitation, and then the complications: abnormal presentations, bleeding, ectopic pregnancy, seizures, trauma and cardiac arrest in pregnancy, and gynecologic emergencies.

topics.heading: Physiologic changes in pregnancy
topics.html:
Pregnancy changes the mother's body in ways that matter to the EMT. As the uterus grows it becomes thinner-walled and less protected, and so more vulnerable to injury. The cardiovascular system adapts as well: blood volume, cardiac output and heart rate all increase, but the red blood cell (RBC) count rises less than the plasma volume does, so the added volume dilutes the cells that are present and produces a dilutional anemia.

The respiratory system is affected too. The mother's demand for oxygen (O2) rises, and in late pregnancy the fetus presses upward on the diaphragm and reduces lung volume. A pregnant patient therefore has less reserve at the very time she needs more oxygen.

topics.heading: Supine hypotensive syndrome
topics.html:
In the third trimester, the weight of the uterus and fetus can compress the inferior vena cava when the mother lies on her back. Compression of the vena cava reduces venous return to the heart, which in turn reduces cardiac output, and the mother becomes dizzy and her blood pressure (BP) drops. This is supine hypotensive syndrome.

Standard treatment for shock does not work here, because the problem is the position of the patient rather than a loss of volume. The fix is positional: transport all third-trimester patients on their left side, which takes the weight of the uterus off the vena cava.

topics.heading: Labor & delivery — 3 stages
topics.html:
Labor is divided into three stages, and the table below sets out where each begins and ends.

StageStartsEnds
1st (dilation)Regular contractions + cervical thinning beginCervix fully dilated
2ndBaby enters birth canalBaby is born
3rdAfter baby is bornAfterbirth delivered

Contractions progress from roughly 30 minutes apart to 3 minutes apart or less as delivery nears. Bloody show, the watery, blood-tinged mucus that passes from the vagina, is a normal sign that labor has begun.

topics.heading: Assessing the woman in labor — transport decision
topics.html:
When you are called to a woman in labor, the first question is whether there is time to transport. Begin with the history: ask for her due date, whether this is her first pregnancy, and whether she has had prenatal care. Then look for crowning, a visual check for a bulging or presenting part at the vaginal opening, which is best seen during a contraction. A cephalic presentation, head first, is normal. A breech presentation means the buttocks or feet present first.

The general rule is to transport unless delivery is expected within a few minutes. If crowning or other signs of imminent delivery are present, consult medical direction, and if delivery has not occurred within 10 minutes, contact medical direction again to request transport. If crowning occurs during transport, stop the ambulance and prepare for delivery.

topics.heading: Assisting the delivery
topics.html:
If the baby is coming on scene, your job is to assist a process that will happen on its own. The steps are as follows:

  1. Keep a constant view of the vaginal opening and be ready at any moment.
  2. Place one hand with slight pressure on the baby's head as it emerges. Never squeeze the head, and never pull on the baby.
  3. If the amniotic sac has not broken, puncture it with your finger and clear the membrane from the baby's mouth and nose. Check the fluid for meconium staining.
  4. Check for a nuchal cord, a cord wrapped around the baby's neck. Gently loosen it; if it cannot be loosened, clamp the cord in two places and cut between the clamps.
  5. Deliver the shoulders. Guide the head downward to deliver the upper shoulder, then upward to deliver the lower shoulder.
  6. Support the baby, who will be very slippery. Dry the baby, wrap it in a warm blanket, and suction only if needed, the mouth first and then the nose.
  7. Note the exact time of birth.

topics.heading: The neonate & the APGAR score
topics.html:
A normal newborn has a pulse above 100 beats per minute, breathes easily, cries vigorously, and shows blue coloration, if any, only at the hands and feet. The APGAR score records the newborn's condition in five categories, each scored from 0 to 2, and the table below gives the criteria for each score.

Category012
AppearanceBlue/pale all overExtremities blue, trunk pinkPink all over
Pulse0<100>100
GrimaceNo reactionFacial grimaceSneeze/cough/cry
ActivityNo movementSlight flexionMoving normally
Respiratory effortNoneSlow/irregular, weak cryGood breathing, strong cry

APGAR does not guide resuscitation and must never delay it. It is a documentation and scoring tool, not a decision-making tool in the moment. Warmth is the number one priority for the newborn.

topics.heading: Neonatal resuscitation — the inverted pyramid
topics.html:
Most neonates need only simple maneuvers, and the sequence of care is drawn as an inverted pyramid: the simple steps at the wide top are needed by almost every baby, and each step below is needed by fewer. Each step is performed for 30 seconds, and the baby is then reassessed before you move to the next. The steps are:

  1. Dry, warm and stimulate the baby.
  2. If the baby is apneic or gasping, or the heart rate (HR) is below 100, begin positive pressure ventilation at 40 to 60 breaths per minute.
  3. If the HR is below 60, begin chest compressions using the two-thumbs-encircling technique, at a compression-to-ventilation ratio of 3:1.

sections.title: Complications & Gynecologic Emergencies

topics.heading: Childbirth complications
topics.html:
Three abnormal presentations can be recognized at the scene, and in each the most important decision is what not to do. The table below sets out the findings and the critical actions for each.

ComplicationKey findingsCritical actions
Breech presentationButtocks/legs firstRapid transport; never pull on the legs
Limb presentationArm/leg/shoulder presentingCannot be delivered prehospital — immediate transport, don't pull the limb or push it back in
Prolapsed umbilical cordCord presents before the babyHead-down/pelvis-raised; push the baby's head/buttocks off the cord and maintain until relieved at the hospital

In breech and limb presentations the harm comes from pulling; in a prolapsed cord it comes from compression of the cord. Never pull on a presenting limb or on the legs of a breech, and never push a presenting limb back in.

topics.heading: Excessive prebirth bleeding & ectopic pregnancy
topics.html:
Heavy bleeding before birth usually comes from one of two problems with the placenta, and the table below contrasts them.

ConditionPresentation
Placenta previa3rd trimester, heavy bleeding often WITHOUT abdominal pain
Abruptio placentae3rd trimester, abdominal/back pain + heavy bleeding; often trauma-related

In placenta previa, the bleeding comes in the third trimester and is heavy, and it often occurs without abdominal pain. In abruptio placentae, the third-trimester bleeding is accompanied by abdominal or back pain, and the condition is often related to trauma.

Ectopic pregnancy is the other bleeding emergency you must keep in mind. Assume that any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, and especially abdominal pain with vaginal bleeding, has an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. The signs are one-sided acute abdominal pain, a rapid and weak pulse, which is a later sign, and a low BP, which is a very late sign.

topics.heading: Seizures in pregnancy & trauma
topics.html:
Preeclampsia presents with altered mental status (AMS), swelling and hypertension. When it progresses to seizures, the condition is eclampsia. Care for the seizing pregnant patient is to open the airway, give O2, transport her on the left side, keep her warm, and call for ALS.

Trauma in pregnancy raises particular concerns. The uterus acts as a natural shock absorber for minor abdominal trauma, but major forces can cause uterine rupture, abruptio placentae or organ injury. The pregnant patient's baseline pulse is 10 to 15 beats per minute faster than a nonpregnant woman's, and she can lose 30 to 35 percent of her blood volume before obvious signs of shock appear. Shock is therefore genuinely harder to detect in pregnancy, and it remains the most likely cause of prehospital fetal death.

topics.heading: Cardiac arrest in the pregnant patient
topics.html: When a pregnant patient goes into cardiac arrest, resuscitation stays focused on the mother, because a resuscitated mother is the best hope for the baby as well. If the patient is more than 20 weeks pregnant, manually displace the uterus to the left during CPR, or tilt her 27 to 30 degrees to the left lateral position on a backboard, to take the uterus off the vena cava. Place your hands in the usual position on the lower half of the sternum; current AHA guidance does not recommend moving them higher. An AED and defibrillation are appropriate in pregnancy and should be used as needed.

topics.heading: Gynecologic emergencies (non-pregnancy)
topics.html:
Vaginal bleeding in a woman who is not known to be pregnant still calls for the same thinking as before: consider pregnancy-related causes, especially ectopic pregnancy, first in any woman of childbearing age.

A call for sexual assault demands care for both the patient and the evidence. Ensure scene safety first. Be nonjudgmental, and treat life threats before anything else. Avoid disturbing evidence unless doing so is necessary for care, and examine the genitals only if severe bleeding is present. Discourage the patient from bathing or voiding, because both destroy evidence.

takeaways: Third-trimester patients are transported on their left side to relieve vena cava compression.
General rule: transport unless delivery is expected within a few minutes; crowning during transport means stop and deliver.
APGAR is a documentation tool only — never let scoring delay resuscitation.
Never pull on a baby during delivery, and never pull a limb during a limb presentation.
Assume any woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain and bleeding has an ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Pregnant patients can lose 30–35% of blood volume before showing obvious shock signs.
In cardiac arrest >20 weeks pregnant: manually displace the uterus left; use the standard hand position on the lower half of the sternum.

chapters.title: Emergencies for Patients with Special Challenges
chapters.intro: Some patients arrive with a disability, a chronic condition or a piece of medical technology that changes how they must be assessed and moved. This chapter covers the general approach to patients with special challenges, including autism, the advanced medical devices you will meet in the home from ventilators to central lines, and the recognition and reporting of abuse, neglect and human trafficking.

topics.heading: Foundational concepts
topics.html:
A disability is a condition — physical, emotional, behavioral or cognitive — that interferes with a person's everyday activities. Diseases that leave a patient disabled are described by when they began. A congenital disease is present at birth, while an acquired disease develops afterward, whether from an infection, another medical condition or trauma.

A chronic disease complicates the picture in two different ways, and you should be prepared for either. The chronic condition itself can worsen acutely, or the patient can develop an entirely unrelated acute illness that hits harder than it otherwise would because of the coexisting chronic condition. The same illness is simply a larger insult to a patient who has less reserve to absorb it.

topics.heading: Common chronic conditions
topics.html:
A handful of chronic conditions turn up often enough in the field that you should know in advance what each one changes about your assessment, your equipment and the way you communicate. The table below sets out those conditions and the points that matter most.

ConditionKey points
AutismImpaired social function/communication; spectrum from normal language/intellect to language delay
Cerebral palsyPermanent motor control impairment; don't assume cognitive impairment
Hearing impairmentFace the patient directly (lip-reading); some use hearing aids/sign language
Kidney failureNever take BP on the dialysis access arm; access devices can bleed
Neuromuscular disorders (MD, MS, ALS)Risk: pain, communication difficulty, UTI, respiratory paralysis
Spinal cord injuryNo sensation/function below the injury level; high injuries → ventilator-dependent, pneumonia risk
Vision impairmentAsk how to help; explain actions before doing them; bring cane/service animal

topics.heading: Autism — the ABCS approach
topics.html:
Patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are encountered often enough that a structured approach is worth committing to memory. The ABCS approach gives you four things to attend to on every such call:

  • Awareness. Patients with ASD react differently from what you may expect, and stress narrows their range further. Even a patient who normally speaks may go silent when frightened or in pain, so consider picture cards when speech fails.
  • Basic. Keep everything simple. Give direct instructions, ask closed-ended questions, and minimize sensory stimulation by turning down radios, reducing lights and shutting off sirens wherever you can.
  • Calm. Calm creates calm. Avoid anything that looks like a show of force, designate one primary contact person to speak with the patient, keep a familiar caregiver alongside you, and allow extra time.
  • Safety. A familiar environment is a source of security, so preserve as much of it as the situation allows. Narrate each step before you carry it out. Restraint is a last resort, used only when there is imminent danger.

Overstimulation can produce an escalation, or meltdown: involuntary, tantrum-like behavior that is not defiance and must not be treated as misbehavior. Assessment calls for the same patience, because patients with ASD may voice atypical complaints and may have a high tolerance for pain. A careful, unhurried examination is what keeps a serious condition from being missed in a patient who is not able to report it in the usual way.

topics.heading: General approach principles
topics.html:
Establishing a baseline comes first. What counts as normal is specific to the patient, so the most useful question is the one put directly to the patient or the family: what is different today. The answer is often the most efficient path to the real problem, and it keeps you from mistaking a long-standing deficit for an acute change.

Routine care still applies. Patients with special challenges get the same everyday illnesses as everyone else, and the priorities of the primary assessment are universal, whatever diagnosis or device you find in front of you.

Finally, follow your protocols. If the care a patient needs falls outside your training or your scope of practice, confer with medical direction rather than improvising.

topics.heading: Respiratory devices
topics.html:
Respiratory technology in the home ranges from a mask the patient wears at night to a machine that breathes for the patient entirely. The table below lists the devices you are most likely to meet and what each one means for your care.

DevicePurposeNotes
CPAP/BiPAP (NIPPV)Keeps airway openUnlikely device-related emergency; bring the device even if not used during transport
Tracheostomy tubeSurgical airway via stomaDisplacement (rare) vs. obstruction (mucus — most common)
Home ventilatorBreathes for the patientDOPE mnemonic for problems (see below); battery backup ~1hr+

When a ventilated patient deteriorates, the causes to work through are recalled with the mnemonic DOPE: displacement of the tube, obstruction of the tube, pneumothorax or pneumonia, and equipment failure. Your first action tests several of them at once. Remove the ventilator circuit and ventilate the patient with a bag-valve mask (BVM), which rules out equipment failure while checking for displacement and obstruction at the same time.

topics.heading: Cardiac devices
topics.html:
Implanted and wearable cardiac devices are common in the community, and each one changes something about your assessment or your resuscitation. The table below summarizes the four you are most likely to encounter.

DeviceFunctionKey points
PacemakerPrevents HR from going too slowFelt as a lump under the skin, usually below the left collarbone; the pulse should still be palpable. Place AED pads about an inch away from it, not over it
AICDDetects V-fib/V-tach, delivers a shockEnergy far less than an AED — safe to touch the patient during discharge
WCD (LifeVest)External vest version of an AICDAlerts before shocking; CPR OK unless a voice command says otherwise
VADImplanted pump for a failing ventriclePulse may be absent/unusual even with the device working — assess via pump sound, mental status, skin color

When you apply AED pads to a patient with an implanted pacemaker or AICD, or with a central line, offset the pads away from the device rather than placing them directly over it.

topics.heading: Gastrointestinal & urinary devices & dialysis
topics.html:
A patient who cannot take food by mouth may be fed through a nasogastric, gastrostomy or jejunostomy tube (NG/G/J-tube). Dislodgement of the tube, infection at the site and clogging of the tube all warrant evaluation at the hospital. Do not attempt to replace a tube that has come out; cover the opening with an occlusive dressing and transport the patient.

An indwelling urinary catheter, or Foley, asks only one thing of you: keep the drainage bag below the level of the patient at all times, including while you move the patient to the stretcher.

Patients in kidney failure are maintained on one of two forms of dialysis, and each brings its own concern. In hemodialysis, the blood is filtered through a surgically created fistula, most often in an arm. Never take a blood pressure (BP) on the fistula arm. A fistula that bleeds can bleed massively, so apply direct pressure and do not release it until a physician advises you to.

In peritoneal dialysis, fluid is exchanged through a catheter in the abdomen, and the two problems to watch for are dislodgement of the catheter and peritonitis. Fluid that drains cloudy suggests infection, so bring the bag with you to the hospital for testing.

topics.heading: Central IV catheters & VP shunts
topics.html:
A central intravenous catheter — a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC), a Groshong catheter or an implanted port — delivers medication into a large vein. EMTs generally do not access these lines. Handle them gently, avoid tugging on the catheter or contaminating the site, and hold a high suspicion for sepsis in any patient who has one, since a central line is a direct route for infection into the bloodstream.

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt drains excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the brain to the abdomen. When the shunt malfunctions, the fluid accumulates, intracranial pressure (ICP) rises, and the patient presents with altered mental status, seizures or respiratory compromise. Management is supportive: standard airway care and prevention of hypoxia, transport, and consultation with medical control.

sections.title: Abuse, Neglect & Trafficking

topics.heading: General principle & child abuse
topics.html:
Patients with special needs, at any age, are more vulnerable to abuse than the population at large, for the plain reason that they depend on other people for their daily care. Certain findings raise suspicion whatever the patient's age: a story that is inconsistent with the injury you are looking at, multiple injuries at different stages of healing, a pattern of repeated injury, and a caregiver who is indifferent to what has happened. Suspicion is not accusation. You never accuse anyone at the scene; you report according to the rules of your jurisdiction.

In children, the physical findings have a characteristic look. Patterned marks may match the shape of the weapon that made them, and fractures may be found at various stages of healing. Head injury is among the most lethal of abuse injuries, and in shaken baby syndrome it shows itself as a bulging fontanelle and unconsciousness. Burns with a specific line of demarcation, such as a cigarette burn or a glove or stocking pattern, point the same way.

Behavior tells you as much as the injuries. Be alert to a caregiver who will not leave you alone with the child, to a story that conflicts between tellers or changes in the retelling, to a child who is afraid to explain what happened, and to injuries found both front and back or on both sides of the body.

topics.heading: Elder & dependent adult abuse
topics.html:
Elder abuse is conventionally divided into 3 types — physical, psychological and financial — with physical neglect standing alongside them as a further form of harm. Falls are genuinely common in the frail elderly, which is exactly what makes them convenient cover, so do not assume that an injury is a simple fall merely because a fall would explain it.

Dependent adults face the same risks. These are adults whose developmental or physical disability leaves them reliant on a caregiver, and the red flags cluster around that caregiver: an unexplained absence, a patient who is malnourished, and interference with the care you are trying to provide.

topics.heading: The EMT's role in suspected abuse
topics.html:
Your role is a bounded one. The EMT is not the police, not an investigator, not a social worker and not a judge. Where the scene allows it, interview the caregiver and the patient separately, and conduct both interviews without judgment. Control your own emotions while you do it: make no accusations, and let nothing in your face or your voice show suspicion.

In many states the EMT is a mandated reporter, and you should know whether yours is one of them. Report and document in the language of possibility, describing the abuse as suspected or possible. Record the facts you observed and the statements you heard, and leave the conclusions to the agencies whose job it is to draw them.

topics.heading: Intimate partner violence & human trafficking
topics.html:
Intimate partner violence (IPV) follows a pattern the EMT needs to understand rather than judge. The moment of greatest risk to a victim is the moment of leaving, which is much of the reason a patient may stay in the relationship or refuse your help even when the injuries are plain. Assess the patient away from the partner, and away from the children, whenever the scene allows it. Offer advocacy and hotline information every time, including on repeat calls to the same address.

Human trafficking is exploitation through force, fraud or coercion, and it is present in every U.S. state. The warning signs are found in the scene as much as in the patient: a companion who controls the encounter, a companion who insists on speaking for the patient, ID documents held by someone other than the patient, and a submissive or fearful affect.

Treat the medical problem first. Never disclose your suspicion to the victim or to anyone else on the scene, and report immediately to law enforcement instead. The National Human Trafficking Hotline is 1 (888) 373-7888.

takeaways: Never take a BP on the dialysis access (fistula) arm.
DOPE mnemonic for a home ventilator emergency: Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax/Pneumonia, Equipment.
AICD/pacemaker shocks are safe to touch — energy is far less than an AED's.
AED pads should be offset away from any implanted device or central line.
Bulging fontanelle + unconsciousness in an infant strongly suggests shaken baby syndrome.
Never disclose suspicion of trafficking to the victim or anyone on scene — it escalates danger.
The highest-risk moment for an intimate partner violence victim is when they try to leave.

chapters.title: EMS Operations
chapters.intro: An ambulance call has five phases, and the work of being ready begins long before the tones drop. This chapter covers ambulance readiness and inspection, receiving and responding to a call, the law and the limits of warning lights and sirens, safety at highway incidents, transferring and transporting the patient, and when and how to use air medical resources.

topics.heading: 5 phases of an ambulance call
topics.html:
Every ambulance call passes through the same five phases, and each has work of its own:

  1. Preparation for the call.
  2. Receiving and responding to a call.
  3. Transferring the patient to the ambulance.
  4. Transporting the patient to the hospital.
  5. Terminating the call.

The first of them takes place before any call comes in; the other four follow in order once it does.

topics.heading: Ensuring ambulance readiness
topics.html:
The ambulance is inspected every shift, and the inspection is tracked on a checklist rather than left to memory. Begin by taking a shift report from the crew going off duty.

The inspection itself runs in a sequence. With the engine off, check the body of the vehicle, the tires, the fluid levels and the battery, and look over the cleanliness of the interior. With the engine running, check the dash indicators, the brakes, the lights and the communications equipment. Finish in the patient compartment with an item-by-item inventory, checking the oxygen (O2) pressure and testing the automated external defibrillator (AED).

If a call comes in while the check is half done, respond to the call and finish the check afterward. The exception is essential equipment that is missing, in which case the unit is declared out of service until the equipment is replaced.

topics.heading: Receiving & responding to a call — the EMD
topics.html:
A call reaches the crew through an emergency medical dispatcher (EMD), who is certified through a medical priority dispatch system. The EMD questions the caller and assigns the call a priority from the answers, gives the caller prearrival instructions, and dispatches and coordinates the resources that respond.

The questioning follows a set pattern. The EMD establishes the exact location, a callback number, the chief complaint, and the patient's age and sex, and then asks whether the patient is conscious and whether the patient is breathing. If the patient is not breathing, the EMD sends the maximum response the system can give and talks the caller through CPR over the telephone.

sections.title: Operating the Ambulance & Air Rescue

topics.heading: The law & warning devices
topics.html:
The exemptions from traffic law that an emergency vehicle enjoys apply only while you are responding to an emergency or transporting a sick or injured patient; they do not apply during nonemergency operations. They also depend on the proper use of the warning devices, and they never grant immunity from reckless driving. After a collision the law asks two questions: whether you used due regard for the safety of others, and whether this was, to the best of your knowledge, a true emergency.

The siren is the most misused device on the ambulance. Drivers often neither see nor hear an ambulance until it is within 100 feet of them, so never assume that a motorist has heard the siren or will yield to it. The visual devices are used continuously: headlights on by day and by night, and the full emergency lighting package whenever the vehicle is in emergency mode.

topics.heading: Safety at highway incidents
topics.html:
If you are not the first-arriving unit at a highway incident, stay off the highway and stage near an on-ramp until you are called in. The first unit blocks the incident. Whichever unit you are, keep the ambulance on the same side of the road as the incident, and avoid driving over debris and skid marks.

The personal protective equipment (PPE) you wear depends on the work going on around you. Where there is no extrication, wear an American National Standards Institute (ANSI) safety vest and a helmet; where extrication is in progress, wear full turnout gear.

topics.heading: Transferring & transporting the patient
topics.html:
Packaging a patient takes a minimum of 3 straps: one across the chest, one across the hip or waist, and one across the lower extremities. Every patient is secured before being transferred to the ambulance, including a patient receiving CPR.

En route, a minimum of 1 EMT rides in the patient compartment, and 2 is preferable. Notify the hospital by radio, and reassess vital signs every 5 minutes if the patient is unstable and every 15 minutes if the patient is stable. Lights and siren are used far more often than they are needed: less than 5% of transports genuinely require them, so ask on each call whether this one does.

The call ends with a formal transfer of responsibility. Wheeling a nonemergency patient in, placing them in a bed and leaving without handing over care to hospital staff is abandonment.

topics.heading: Air rescue
topics.html:
Air rescue is reserved for high-priority patients, and the clinical criteria for requesting it are:

  • Shock.
  • A Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of less than 10.
  • Head injury with altered mental status.
  • Chest trauma with respiratory distress.
  • Penetrating injury to a body cavity.
  • Amputation proximal to the hand or foot.
  • Extensive burns.
  • Return of a pulse after cardiac arrest.

The landing zone (LZ) measures roughly 100 feet by 100 feet, sits on a slope of less than 8 degrees, and is clear of wires, towers, vehicles and loose objects. Mark it with one flare placed upwind.

Approach the helicopter only when a member of the flight crew escorts you, and stay clear of the tail rotor at all times. Keep traffic at least 100 feet away from the aircraft, and allow no smoking within 200 feet of it.

takeaways: Emergency vehicle exemptions apply only during an actual emergency response/transport, with due regard for others' safety.
Never assume other drivers hear your siren or will yield.
Less than 5% of ambulance transports genuinely require lights and siren.
Leaving a nonemergency patient at the hospital without a formal transfer of care is abandonment.
Air rescue: never approach a helicopter unescorted; always stay clear of the tail rotor.

chapters.title: Hazardous Materials, MCIs, and Incident Management
chapters.intro: Some incidents are too large or too dangerous for a single crew, and they demand a system. This chapter covers hazardous materials: the zones, the EMT's role and identifying the substance; then multiple-casualty incidents: disaster plans, the Incident Command System, triage priorities and the START method, and the logistics of staging and transport.

topics.heading: Zones & EMT responsibilities
topics.html:
A hazardous materials scene is divided into three zones, and which one you may stand in depends on your level of training. The table below describes them.

ZoneDescription
Hot zoneImmediately surrounding the incident — contamination/danger area; only Technician-level+ personnel with PPE enter
Warm zoneAdjacent to the hot zone — decon corridor located here
Cold zoneSafe area — command post, staging, EMS treatment area

EMTs are typically trained to the Awareness level and sometimes to the Operations level, but not to the Technician level; it is the Technician-level responders who actually plug and patch a release. Your responsibilities are to recognize that an incident involves hazardous materials, to call for the resources it will take, to control the scene, and to identify the substance safely from a distance. Treat every patient who leaves the site as contaminated until it is proven otherwise.

topics.heading: Identifying the substance
topics.html:
Identify the substance only by methods that keep you away from it. Read placards through binoculars rather than approaching them, and use the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 704 numeric and color coding, the Department of Transportation (DOT) placards, the shipping papers and the Safety Data Sheets (SDS). No one source can be trusted on its own: studies show that 25 to 50% of placards can be incorrect, so always cross-confirm the substance against several sources.

Several references are available to you. The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is the first of them, CHEMTREC can be reached at 800-424-9300, and poison control centers, which are often overlooked at these incidents, can give useful guidance on decontamination and treatment.

topics.heading: Decontamination
topics.html:
Patients at a hazardous materials incident sort into 4 types: those who are uninjured and not contaminated, those who are injured and not contaminated, those who are uninjured and contaminated, and those who are both injured and contaminated.

Decontamination itself happens in phases. Gross decontamination removes the majority of the material, secondary decontamination removes most of what remains, and tertiary decontamination is carried out at the hospital. Throughout, keep hold of one principle: water dilutes, it does not neutralize most substances.

Some parts of the body hold residual contamination and are easily missed. Pay particular attention to the scalp and hair, the groin, the buttocks, the armpits, the spaces between the fingers and toes, the ear canals and the navel.

sections.title: Multiple-Casualty Incidents & ICS

topics.heading: MCI definition & disaster plans
topics.html:
A multiple-casualty incident (MCI) is not defined by any fixed number of patients. What defines it is that the patients challenge or hamper the ability of the EMS system to respond to them, so the same number of casualties may be an MCI in one system and routine in another.

The response to such an incident rests on a disaster plan, and a plan is worth having only if it meets four conditions. It must be written for the events that are conceivable locally, it must be well publicized, it must be realistic, and it must be rehearsed.

topics.heading: Incident Command System (ICS)
topics.html:
The Incident Command System (ICS) is a subset of the National Incident Management System (NIMS). It divides an incident into Command, Operations, Logistics, Planning and Finance, and it keeps span of control, the number of people reporting to any one supervisor, to between 3 and 7.

Command takes one of two forms. Under single incident command, one agency controls everything. Under unified command, several agencies cooperate while each keeps control of its own resources, and that arrangement works best at a large or complex incident.

Communication follows the same discipline. Only Command speaks to dispatch and only Command requests resources; everyone else speaks to their own direct supervisor. The alternative is freelancing, meaning uncoordinated activity by people acting on their own, and freelancing is a leading cause of injury and death on scene. Organizing early and aggressively is what prevents it.

topics.heading: Triage — priority categories
topics.html:
Triage sorts patients by how urgently they need care, and each patient is tagged with a color that tells everyone who reaches them where they stand. The table below gives the priorities and what puts a patient in each.

PriorityTag colorCriteria
1RedLife-threatening but treatable — airway/breathing issues, severe bleeding, shock
2YellowSerious, not life-threatening
3Green"Walking wounded" — minor injury
4/0BlackDead/fatal

The priorities depend on the resources available. A patient in cardiac arrest is tagged Priority 4, black, while resources are limited, and can become Priority 1 if resources later become available.

topics.heading: START triage — RPM
topics.html:
START triage is meant to be fast: about 30 seconds with each patient. What you assess is captured by the mnemonic RPM, for Respiration, Pulse and Mental status. Only 3 treatments are permitted while triaging: opening the airway and inserting an oropharyngeal airway (OPA), controlling bleeding, and elevating an extremity.

The table below gives the criteria that place a patient in each category.

PriorityCriteria
Red (1)Altered mental status OR absent radial pulse OR RR >30
Yellow (2)Alert AND radial pulse present AND RR 30 or less
Black (4)Not breathing after airway opened, or no pulse + not breathing

Patients who can walk are assigned Priority 3, green, at the outset, but they must be triaged again, since they can deteriorate.

topics.heading: Transportation & staging logistics
topics.html: No ambulance transports a patient until the transportation supervisor approves the move. It is the transportation officer, and not the individual EMTs, who communicates with the hospitals. Routing it all through one person keeps radio traffic to a minimum and stops any single hospital from being sent more patients than its surge capacity can absorb.

takeaways: EMTs are usually trained to Awareness/Operations HazMat level, not Technician.
Water dilutes contamination, it does not neutralize it — decontamination is never truly complete.
Freelancing (uncoordinated activity) is a leading cause of on-scene injury/death — early organization prevents it.
Cardiac arrest patients become Priority 4 (black) in an MCI when resources are limited.
START triage: RPM (Respiration, Pulse, Mental status), only 3 allowed interventions.
The transportation supervisor — not individual EMTs — decides which hospital receives each patient.

chapters.title: Highway Safety and Vehicle Extrication
chapters.intro: A highway is one of the most dangerous places an EMT works, and the vehicle itself stays hazardous long after the crash. This chapter covers highway operations and scene positioning, protective equipment and scene hazards including downed electrical wires, vehicle fires and alternative-fuel vehicles, the ten phases of extrication, stabilizing a vehicle, gaining access and disentangling the patient.

topics.heading: Highway emergency operations
topics.html:
The greatest hazard at a highway crash is the traffic still moving past it, and highway operations are organized around that fact. Only the first-arriving unit goes directly to the scene. Every other unit stages off the highway and waits there until it is requested, so that the roadway does not fill with apparatus that nobody is using.

The first unit parks to protect the people who will be working. The technique is called upstream blocking: the apparatus is positioned between oncoming traffic and the work zone, so that a vehicle which fails to stop strikes the apparatus rather than the crew. Crew members then step out only into the safe zone, and only after the whole crew has confirmed that traffic has in fact stopped.

Night operations add a hazard you can create for yourself. Your own headlights shine into the eyes of oncoming drivers, and a driver who is blinded cannot see your reflective vest either, so the vest stops protecting you. The correct setup after dark is red and amber warning lights on, headlights off, and directional boards operating.

topics.heading: PPE & managing hazards
topics.html:
Personal protective equipment (PPE) is selected according to the zone you are working in. Working in traffic calls for a reflective vest meeting the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standard and a helmet; the high-visibility vest is federally mandated. Active extrication calls for full turnout gear, a helmet and eye protection. As a rule of thumb, match the level of protection worn by the workers around you.

The vehicle holds two hazards that catch rescuers out. An airbag that did not deploy in the collision remains a real danger during extrication, and turning off the ignition does not disable it; the battery must be disconnected. Energy-absorbing bumpers are the second. After an impact a bumper can be left loaded, holding the energy of the collision in its compressed state, so never stand directly in front of one.

topics.heading: Electrical hazards — the most dangerous invisible threat
topics.html:
Electricity is the most dangerous hazard on a crash scene precisely because there is nothing to see. Wood utility poles can carry up to 500,000 volts, and once a pole or its wires are involved you should assume that the entire area, including the ground you are standing on, could be energized. Treat every downed wire as live until a utility professional confirms otherwise, and never move a wire yourself.

Current spreading outward through the earth produces a ground gradient, a difference in voltage from one footstep to the next. The warning sign is a tingling in your legs, and it means you are already standing on energized ground. If you feel it, turn 180 degrees and shuffle away, keeping both feet in constant contact with the ground. Never hop, and never let your feet come together.

topics.heading: Vehicle fires & alternative-fuel vehicles
topics.html:
Call the fire department yourself for any vehicle fire, and never assume that someone else has already done it. An A:B:C dry chemical extinguisher will handle most vehicle fires. Where you stand matters as much as what you are holding: never stand in front of a truck wheel, because the tires can blow apart.

Alternative-fuel vehicles — hybrid, electric, natural gas and propane — carry hazards that a conventional gasoline vehicle does not, and when you are in doubt about one, do not intervene if intervening puts your own safety at risk. Confirm that the vehicle is truly off rather than merely silent. With a keyless ignition that means locating the fob and moving it well away from the vehicle.

sections.title: Stabilization, Access & Disentanglement

topics.heading: 10 phases of extrication
topics.html:
Extrication is taught as a sequence of ten phases, worked in this order:

  1. Prepare.
  2. Size up the scene.
  3. Recognize and manage hazards.
  4. Stabilize the vehicle.
  5. Gain access to the patient.
  6. Assess the patient.
  7. Disentangle the patient.
  8. Immobilize and extricate.
  9. Transport.
  10. Terminate the incident.

The phases do not change with the patient's condition, but the pace does. A stable patient can tolerate the slower techniques, while an unstable patient needs rapid extrication straight to a long board. The spinal principles are the same either way; only the speed is different.

topics.heading: Stabilizing a vehicle
topics.html:
The core rule is that every vehicle involved in a collision is unstable, regardless of how settled it appears. A car sitting squarely on its wheels can still roll or shift once rescuers begin working in and around it.

For a vehicle on its wheels, confirm that the engine is off, that the transmission is in park and that the parking brake is set, then take out the remaining movement with step chocks. A vehicle on its side or its roof demands more. Never let bystanders try to push it upright, and stabilize it with cribbing or struts before anyone attempts access.

topics.heading: Gaining access
topics.html:
Once the vehicle is stable, the guiding phrase is "try before you pry." Always try the door in the ordinary way first, because a door that simply opens costs nothing and saves the time that mechanical tools would take.

When the doors will not open, a window is the next choice. Most side and rear windows are tempered glass, which breaks into small rounded pieces, and that makes them the preferred access point over the laminated glass of the windshield. Cover the occupants with an aluminized blanket before you break a window near them.

topics.heading: Disentanglement — three-part plan
topics.html:
Disentanglement follows a plan in 3 parts, taken in order. Part 1 is the doors, part 2 is the roof, and part 3 is displacing the entire front end of the vehicle as one unit.

Taking the doors and then the roof buys you several things at once. It gives full access to the interior so that care can continue while the work goes on, it opens a large exit should a new hazard appear, it brings fresh air to the patient and the crew, and the faster access it provides improves the patient's chance of survival.

Displacing the front end brings the work close to the airbag system, so the sequence there is fixed. Disconnect the negative battery cable first. Stay clear of the airbag module and out of its deployment path, since a residual charge can remain even after the battery has been disconnected. Never cut or drill into the module itself.

topics.heading: The Nader pin
topics.html: Every car sold in the United States since 1966 has a Nader pin, a case-hardened pin in the door latch that keeps the door from flying open in a crash and so prevents occupants from being ejected. It does that job well, and in doing it, it locks rescuers out as effectively as it holds occupants in. The crowbar method that once opened a door will not defeat it, and hydraulic spreaders are required instead. That trade is the recurring lesson of extrication: every improvement in occupant safety creates a new challenge for the rescuer.

takeaways: Only the first-arriving unit goes directly to a highway scene — others stage off-highway until requested.
Night operations: headlights OFF, red/amber warning lights ON — headlights blind drivers and defeat your reflective vest.
Always call the fire department yourself for a vehicle fire — never assume someone else has.
Downed wires and ground gradients: treat all wires as live; shuffle away with both feet on the ground if you feel tingling.
"Try before you pry" — always attempt the door normally before mechanical extrication.
Assume every collision vehicle is unstable, in any position, until it's actually stabilized.
Disconnect the negative battery cable before any airbag-related extrication work.
